Go-kit (Oregon OEM checklist) Medications and medical devices · glasses · food and plenty of water · important documents · phone chargers · battery AM/FM radio · first-aid kit · flashlight · N95 masks · long sleeves, long pants, sturdy shoes, hat. Plan two routes out. Move livestock early.

Around the house (defensible space) - First 5 ft around the house: nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away (OSFM, p. 13; the ODF Josephine County handout says at least 20 ft). - Within 100 ft: grass mowed to 4 in or less, 10 ft between tree crowns, limbs 10 ft from the chimney, no "ladder fuels" (brush under trees). - Clean roofs and gutters; cover vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh; clear around propane tanks; keep the driveway clear enough for a fire engine.

Smoke Make one cleaner-air room (windows shut, AC on recirculate). A DIY air cleaner = a box fan (made 2012 or later, UL/ETL label) + a MERV-13 furnace filter. Unplug it when you leave the house. Use N95 masks outdoors. Details: the Wildfire\ folder (Ready-Set-Go guide, OSFM defensible-space guide, OSU fire-resistant plants, EPA/OHA smoke sheets). Fire news: swofire.com (ODF Southwest Oregon). 📚 Go deeper: Evacuation levels flyer and checklist — print for the fridge; ODF Josephine County handout — defensible space on one page; EPA Wildfire Smoke Guide, p. 61 — setting up a cleaner-air room; Wildfire prep for pets and livestock.

🌎 Earthquake (Cascadia) and tsunami - A Cascadia magnitude-9 quake would shake for 4–6 minutes, with aftershocks for months (CREW scenario, p. 10). Drop, Cover, Hold On. - Expect landslides on mountain roads and damage to bridges. Coast-to-inland routes like US-199 are exactly the kind expected to be cut, so the valley may be isolated for a long time. - State estimates for inland western Oregon: power out 1–3 months, water/sewer 1 month to 1 year, main highways 6–12 months to partly reopen, fuel shortages (Oregon's fuel hub is near Portland) (Oregon Resilience Plan, p. 6). - Plan to be on your own for at least 2 weeks — longer in rural areas. - At the coast (Brookings, Gold Beach, Crescent City): if you feel a long quake, walk to high ground immediately. The first waves can arrive in 15–30 minutes; surges continue 12+ hours and the first is not the largest. Details: Earthquake-Tsunami\ (Living on Shaky Ground, 2 Weeks Ready toolkit, Cascadia scenario, tsunami evacuation maps for Brookings-Harbor, Gold Beach, Crescent City, Smith River). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA P-530 Earthquake Safety at Home — strapping the water heater, bolting the house; Living on Shaky Ground — Oregon's quake and tsunami guide.

☢️ Nuclear fallout - Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Fallout is dust; put mass between you and the roof and outside walls. It loses 90% of its strength in 7 hours and 99% in 2 days (FEMA H-20, p. 8). - A one-story wood house with no basement is poor shelter. Know now where you'd go: a basement or masonry building nearby, a shielded crawl space, or a trench shelter. - Potassium iodide (KI) protects only the thyroid, from radioactive iodine — adults 130 mg, children less (FDA, p. 9). - Everything else — shielding, how long to stay in, decontamination, food, water, livestock, homemade fallout meter: Nuclear Fallout Guide and Nuclear-Radiation\. 📚 Go deeper: CDC: Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned — where to shelter, on one page; Nuclear War Survival Skills — expedient shelters and fallout meters.

🦌 Hunting and 🎣 Fishing While seasons and tags are still enforced, the 2026 rule booklets are in Hunting\ and Fishing\ (big game, fishing) (the 2027 big game and fishing booklets come out around December 2026 — see Keeping this current). With or without rules, the units, waters and seasons below tell you where game and fish are, and when — and leaving breeding animals and spawning runs alone is what keeps them there next year. Hunting units: US-199 is the line. West of the highway (Illinois River canyon, Kalmiopsis) is Chetco Unit 27 (82% public land). East of it (Lake Selmac, Takilma, Oregon Caves, Williams) is Applegate Unit 28 (57% public land). In Cave Junction, Kerby, Selma and O'Brien, which side of the highway you're on decides the unit. North of the Rogue at Grants Pass is Evans Creek Unit 29. 2026 general seasons, for orientation (check the current booklet): western Oregon buck rifle Oct 3–Nov 6 · archery deer & elk Aug 29–Sep 27 · Unit 28 coast elk rifle Nov 14–17 and Nov 21–27 (Unit 27 is controlled hunts only) · black bear Aug 1–Dec 31 · cougar all year (quotas) — bear and cougar must be checked in at ODFW within 10 days · grouse and quail Sep 1–Jan 31 · fall turkey Sep 1–Jan 31 · spring turkey Apr 15–May 31. 🪤 Trapping How-to: start with the national Trapper Education Manual and the NY trapper manual (trap types, baits, water and land sets, snares, running a trapline, fur handling), then the species guides (beaver, coyote, raccoon, bobcat, gray fox). For improvised traps with no store-bought gear, see the 1907 Deadfalls and Snares (illustrated) and the snare and deadfall chapters of the Army survival manuals (Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals; FM 21-76, p. 95). Hides and furs: USDA Home Tanning of Leather and Small Fur Skins. - Check traps at least daily — animals spoil, suffer, or get taken by other predators. - Beaver, raccoon, muskrat and rabbits are the most dependable meat from traps here; wear gloves for rabbits and rodents (tularemia), and cook all wild meat thoroughly. - Don't catch your own dogs: the AFWA dog-friendly guides show sets that avoid pets. While Oregon's rules are still enforced (details in the 2026–2028 furbearer booklet in Trapping\): - License: trapping needs an Oregon Furtaker's License — that includes "unprotected" animals like coyote, skunk, opossum and porcupine. A landowner can get a free license for land they own and live on (register the land with ODFW first). - Trapper education (free, online at hunter-ed.com/oregon/trapper) is required if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time — except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to

if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time — except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to livestock or crops. - Every trap and snare must carry your ODFW brand number. Check traps at least every 48 hours. - Banned: toothed jaws; oversized footholds and land killing traps (size limits are in the booklet); game meat as bait; visible bait within 15 ft of a foothold set for carnivores. In the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest west of I-5 (that includes the Illinois Valley), no traps or snares hung in trees. On public land, stay 50 ft from trails and 300 ft from trailheads, campgrounds and picnic areas. - 2026–27 seasons: bobcat Dec 1–Feb 28 (needs a record card) · gray fox Oct 15–Feb 28 · raccoon, river otter and beaver Nov 15–Mar 15 · mink and muskrat Nov 15–Mar 31 · marten closed west of I-5 · fisher and ringtail closed all year. - Wolves are federally endangered here. Use coyote traps no bigger than #3 and snares with breakaways. A wolf track is about 5 in long; a coyote's is about 2.5 in (furbearer booklet, p. 16). ⚡ Off-grid power and creek hydro Start with the US Navy NEETS modules (electricity basics, AC, circuit protection, wiring, generators) in Off-Grid-Power\Electrical-Basics, then the solar guides, then the micro-hydro handbooks in Off-Grid-Power\Micro-Hydro. Generators - Never run one indoors, in a garage, crawlspace or shed, even with doors open. Carbon monoxide kills in minutes. Keep it outdoors, away from windows and vents, and use battery-powered CO alarms. - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding"). It sends power back through the lines and can kill anyone working on them. Wire into the house only through a transfer switch. - Store fuel outside living areas, in proper cans. Let the engine cool before refueling. - Engine won't start, carburetor gummed up, generator makes no power? See the Engines, Motors and Generators guide — it also covers chainsaws, rewinding motors, and turning motors and car alternators into generators. - Fuel: how long gas and diesel keep, rescuing stale or watery fuel, and getting fuel out of station tanks, drums and vehicles with no power: Fuel Guide. - EMP or solar storm: protecting solar gear, inverters and spares, and Faraday containers: EMP Guide. Sizing a solar system (Sandia and IEA guides) - Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan

Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan 7–9 days of storage for a solar-only system, and vent battery rooms at the top (hydrogen rises). - System voltage: 12 V under 1 kWh/day, 24 V for 1–4 kWh/day, 48 V above that. Low voltage over long wires needs very heavy wire. Sizing creek hydro (NRCan, NCAT) - Real output (watts) ≈ flow (liters/second) × drop (meters) × 9.8 × 0.5. In US units: kW ≈ flow (cubic ft/min) × drop (ft) ÷ 709 × 0.5. Example: 50 gallons/minute falling 100 ft ≈ 470 W around the clock ≈ 11 kWh a day, more than solar gives most of the year here. - Design for late-summer low flow (the flow you have 95% of the time). Size the pipe so friction eats less than 10% of the drop. Screen the intake and leave water in the creek. - A hydraulic ram pump (Clemson plans) lifts creek water uphill with no fuel or power. While Oregon's water laws are enforced: hydropower needs a state water right, and most Illinois Valley creeks are closed to hydro by state rule, including the Illinois River and its forks, Althouse, Sucker, Deer, Josephine, Rough and Ready and many more (OAR 690-515-0050). Firewood (OSU, heat per cord when dry): Oregon white oak and madrone ≈ 30 million BTU, Douglas-fir ≈ 21, alder ≈ 18, ponderosa pine ≈ 17. Each 1% of extra moisture costs about 1% of the heat: split and stack wood through one dry summer (two is better) and keep it covered through the rains. A good stove is 60–80% efficient; an open fireplace 10–15%. Carbon monoxide kills. Never run a generator, grill, charcoal, camp stove or a wood-gas unit indoors, in a garage or near windows. CO feels like flu without a fever. A battery CO alarm near the bedrooms is cheap insurance. A wood-gas generator keeps making CO-rich gas for ~20 minutes after the engine stops. Lye (for soap and biodiesel): wear gloves and goggles, keep children away, add lye to cold water a little at a time (never water to lye), never use aluminum pots. On skin or in eyes: flush with lots of

keep children away, add lye to cold water a little at a time (never water to lye), never use aluminum pots. On skin or in eyes: flush with lots of water for a long time (not vinegar). Methanol (for biodiesel): very flammable, vapors creep along the ground to flames, absorbed through the skin, and swallowing it causes blindness. Work outdoors, away from any flame. Stored fuel: gasoline stays good about 6 months (longer with stabilizer), diesel 6–12 months. Approved cans, outside the house, in a tub to catch spills. Sanitation is what keeps disease away when water and sewer stop: the OSU twin-bucket toilet, then a proper latrine (Army FM 21-10, the WHO notes) at least 100 ft downhill from any well or creek, and handwashing with soap every time. While laws are enforced: making fuel alcohol needs a free federal TTB permit first; Oregon requires permits for graywater systems and composting toilets/privies; and burning needs a Josephine County burn permit and a burn day ((541) 476-9663). 🧰 Make-Do Household Guide How to make or replace everyday necessities when the store is gone — from basic supplies, things you can scavenge, and what grows around the Illinois Valley. Each section points to the detailed manuals in Homestead-Skills\ (especially Household-Make-Do\, Soap-Candles\ and Sanitation-Water\) and Electronics-Repair\. The links open each book on the drive at the right page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never mix cleaning chemicals. Bleach + ammonia (or urine) makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach + vinegar or any acid makes chlorine gas. Use one product, rinse, then the next. - Lye (from ashes or the store) burns skin and blinds. Gloves and eye protection; flush any splash with plenty of water for 15 minutes. Never use aluminum pots with lye. - Label every container. Never store chemicals or fuel in food or drink bottles, and never reuse a container that held chemicals or fuel for food or water. - Never put gasoline in a lamp, stove or heater, and never burn charcoal, a camp stove or a generator indoors (carbon monoxide). - Never throw water on burning wax or fat — it spreads the fire. Cut the heat and smother it with a metal lid or damp cloth.

🧽 Cleaning and disinfecting - Most cleaning is just soap, hot water and scrubbing — it removes most germs along with the dirt. Homemade lye soap works fine (see the soap section below). - Scouring powder: baking soda, fine wood ash, or fine sand on a damp rag. - Glass and hard-water film: white vinegar mixed half and half with water (not on marble or stone, and never together with bleach). - Disinfecting with bleach (for kitchen surfaces, sickrooms, after flooding): plain unscented household bleach, 5 tablespoons (⅓ cup) per gallon of water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Clean first, leave it wet for at least a minute, and mix it fresh every day — diluted bleach loses strength. Drinking water needs a much weaker dose — use the table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (p. 2). - No bleach? Boiling water, scrubbing with soap, and drying things in full sun all kill germs. - Wash hands with soap before handling food or eating, after the toilet, after cleaning up a child or caring for a sick person, and after touching animals or garbage. Hand sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol) only works on hands that aren't visibly dirty. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, p. 4) 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies — chlorine, latrines and hygiene after disasters; Army FM 21-10 Field

dirty. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, p. 4) 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies — chlorine, latrines and hygiene after disasters; Army FM 21-10 Field Hygiene and Sanitation — keeping a group healthy in the field; EPA Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, p. 2 — the bleach-drops table.

🧼 Soap from fat and ashes 1. Make lye from ashes. Use hardwood ashes (they make the best lye); ashes of paper, cloth or garbage won't work (VITA, p. 342). Fill a bucket with ashes, pour on boiling water and stir, top up with ashes and water, then let it stand 12–24 hours and carefully pour off the clear liquid (Practical Action Soapmaking, p. 2). 2. Check the strength. Lye that floats a fresh egg or a potato is right. Too weak? Run it through fresh ashes again, or boil it down. (VITA, p. 343) 3. Make soft soap. Boil ½ cup of ash lye for every cup of clean fat until it is thick, rubbery and foamy. Age the brown jelly at least a month before use. (VITA, p. 344) Ash lye is potash, which only makes soft soap; hard bars need store lye (caustic soda), or boiled soap "salted out" with salt water (USDA 1940, p. 3; Practical Action, p. 4). Hard soap with store lye (USDA): weigh 2½ lb clean fat, melt it and let it cool to lukewarm. Dissolve 5½ oz lye in 11 oz cold water (lye into water, never water onto lye), pour it into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after 24 hours; let them harden

into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after 24 hours; let them harden a week or more out of the sun. (USDA 1940, p. 3) - Clean kitchen grease first: melt it with about an equal amount of hot water, stir, let it cool, and lift the clean fat off the top (USDA 1940, p. 3). - Is it done? Cool a drop on a plate. Clear = ready. Weak and grey = needs more lye. A grey skin that slides on the plate = too much lye — add more fat (Practical Action, p. 3). - New ("green") soap is still caustic. Wear gloves to handle it and let bars cure at least 3 weeks (Practical Action, p. 4). - Keep children away and don't breathe the fumes. Splashes: water, lots of it (some old books say vinegar — use water). | Soap problem | Likely cause (Practical Action, p. 4) | | Won't thicken | Not enough lye, too much water, too cool, not stirred enough, or too much liquid oil | | Oily layer on top as it cools | Too much fat or not enough lye | | Hard and brittle | Too much lye | 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Soapmaking — lye from ashes, soft and hard

Too much fat or not enough lye | | Hard and brittle | Too much lye | 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Soapmaking — lye from ashes, soft and hard soap, recipes; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 342 — leaching lye and soft soap with drawings; CAWST Soap Making Fact Sheet — modern measured recipes; MSU Making Soap at Home — store-lye bars.

👕 Laundry - Laundry soap: grate one bar of soap and mix with 1 cup washing soda (add 1 cup borax if you have it). Use 1–2 tablespoons per load, dissolved in hot water first. - Make washing soda from baking soda: spread baking soda in a pan and bake at 400 °F (200 °C) for about an hour, stirring now and then, until it turns dull and grainy. It's stronger than baking soda — wear gloves. - Ash water (old-time "lye wash"): soak hardwood ashes in water, let it settle, and use only the clear liquid for greasy or very dirty clothes. It's caustic — gloves, and never on wool or silk. - Washing by hand: soak overnight, agitate with a clean plunger in a bucket (or a washboard), rinse twice, wring hard, and dry in the sun — sunlight helps disinfect. Stains (USDA Stain Removal from Fabrics): - Treat it while fresh, and try cold water first — hot water and soap set many stains. Test any remover on a hidden seam. (pp. 4, 6) - Blood: soak in cold water until the stain turns light brown, then wash in warm soapy water. Strong salt water (about 2 cups salt per gallon) loosens old stains. Never hot water. (p. 15) - Grease: rub in cornstarch, chalk or talc, let it soak up the grease, brush off (p. 8).

Skip the bulletin's gasoline and carbon tetrachloride — fire and poison hazards. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Stain Removal from Fabrics, p. 4 — an A-to-Z of stains; Household Discoveries (1909) — washing, soap and laundry methods.

🪥 Personal care - Teeth: how you brush matters more than the paste. Brush twice a day with water, a little baking soda, or salt (or a 50-50 mix of the two). No brush? Chew the end of a fresh green twig until it frays into bristles, or wrap rough towel around a finger. Use thread as floss. (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17, p. 2; Medical\Manuals-PDF\Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63) - Deodorant: wash daily; dust on baking soda or cornstarch (baking soda can irritate some skin). - Salve: melt 1 part beeswax with 4 parts oil or clean tallow (by weight) over low heat and pour into small tins. Lip balm is firmer: about 1 part wax to 2 parts oil. - Hair: wash with soap, then rinse with a cup of water with a spoonful of vinegar in it to remove soap film. 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63 — gum care and keeping teeth without a dentist; Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17 — teeth, gums and mouth.

🩲 Menstrual pads and diapers - Reusable pads: several layers of absorbent cotton (old flannel or towel) sewn or folded into a pad, held in underwear. Rinse in cold water first, wash with soap, and dry in the sun. See Where Women Have No Doctor (Medical\). Change pads several times a day; a homemade tampon must be changed at least 3 times a day or it can cause a serious infection (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5, p. 4). - A pad that buttons on: a sleeve of heavy cotton about 4½ × 9½ inches with two button wings, plus removable folded towel liners about 6 × 8 inches. Wash and add bleach if you have it; dry in the sun, never under the bed — damp pads mold and cause itching. (WASHplus pattern) - Cloth diapers: absorbent cotton folded in layers, with a wool or plastic cover. Rinse, soak in a lidded bucket, wash hot with soap, dry in the sun. 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus Making Reusable Menstrual Pads — sewing pattern with drawings; Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5 — periods and staying clean.

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives - Water: a squeeze bottle of water, then wash your hands with soap — the cleanest option. - "Family cloth": cotton squares, used once, kept in a lidded bucket and washed hot, separately from other laundry. - Leaves: big soft thimbleberry leaves (common along roads and forest edges here in summer) or first-year mullein leaves. - ⚠️ Learn poison oak first — it's everywhere in the Illinois Valley. Leaves in threes, lobed like small oak leaves, shiny or dull, red in fall. The bare stems in winter still cause the rash. It grows as a shrub or a climbing vine, and the roots and stems carry the oil too (OSU EM 9184, p. 24). Also avoid stinging nettle. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9184, p. 24 — poison oak photos and control; FM 3-05.70 Survival, p. 514 — poison oak and other plants to avoid.

🚽 Toilets when the water is off - Don't flush if the sewer lines might be broken, even if your pipes look fine. A septic system can keep working if nothing leaks or backs up. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, pp. 4–5) - Twin-bucket toilet: two 5-gallon buckets marked "pee" and "poo". The poo bucket is lined with a heavy (3 mil or thicker) black bag; after each use, cover it with about ½ cup of sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper or peat. Keeping urine out of the poo bucket is what stops the smell. (OSU, pp. 2–3) - Emptying: dilute urine with wash water and pour it on the ground, a different spot each time. Fill the poo bucket no more than half, then double-bag it with gloves on and store it sealed, away from food and water. In the country you can bury it — never within 100 feet of a well, spring or creek. (OSU, p. 3) - Hand-washing station: a jug of clean water with a spigot, a catch bucket, and soap in the toe of a sock tied to the jug — one by the toilet, one by the kitchen (OSU, p. 3). - Trench latrine for longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. Cover each use with soil; fill it

longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. Cover each use with soil; fill it in when the contents are 1 foot from the top (WHO/WEDC, p. 56). Hot ashes tipped into a pit cut smell and flies (Practical Action VIP Latrine, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics: Sanitation — twin-bucket setup and supply list; WHO/WEDC Technical Notes, p. 55 — trench, family and borehole latrines; Practical Action Compost Toilets — longer-term options; EPA Composting Toilets — how they work.

🔥 Fire and light without stores - Fire starters: cotton balls rubbed with petroleum jelly; fatwood (resin-soaked heartwood from old pine or fir stumps — smells like turpentine and lights even when damp); dry bark and pine pitch. - Char cloth (catches a spark): put squares of 100% cotton cloth in a metal tin with a small nail hole in the lid, set it in a fire until smoke stops coming out, then let it cool before opening. - No matches: a ferro rod or flint-and-steel onto char cloth (steel struck on flint, quartz or pyrite throws sparks); a magnifying glass in sun; touching a 9-volt battery (or two AAs) to fine steel wool; or a bow drill — drill about ⅝ in thick and a foot long, of dry cedar, fir, cottonwood or basswood, on a board of the same wood with a notch cut to the center of the pit; tinder of dry grass with shredded cedar bark (Seton's Book of Woodcraft, pp. 192–194, and the Army survival manuals — FM 21-76, ch. 7). - Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\. - Dipped candles: dip wicks in melted tallow, cool, dip

or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\. - Dipped candles: dip wicks in melted tallow, cool, dip again until thick enough (Household Discoveries, p. 98). 2 parts beeswax to 1 part tallow is firmer than plain tallow (p. 99). Melt wax in a pot set in hot water, not over the flame (Practical Action Candlemaking, p. 3). - Rushlights: peel rushes and dip the pith in tallow like a candle (Household Discoveries, p. 99). How much light you get (lumens, roughly — Practical Action Rural Lighting, p. 3): candle 1 · wick oil lamp 1–10 · hurricane lantern 10–100 · mantle lamp ~1,000 · a 1-watt white LED 25–50. 📚 Go deeper: FM 21-76 Army Survival Manual, ch. 7 — tinder, fire lays and fire without matches; Seton Book of Woodcraft, p. 192 — the classic bow-drill method; Practical Action Candlemaking — dipping, pouring and molding; Practical Action Rural Lighting — lamps, LEDs and batteries compared.

🪵 Glue, patching and waterproofing - Pine pitch glue: gently melt pine resin (it's flammable — heat beside the fire, not in it), stir in powdered charcoal (about 1 part to 3–4 parts resin) plus a pinch of fine plant fiber, and use while warm. Sets hard — for hafting tools, patching containers and seams. Plain heated resin works as glue too (FM 3-05.70, p. 455). - Flour paste: cook flour and water to a thick paste — for paper and labels. - Casein (milk) glue — skim-milk curd mixed with slaked lime and two other chemicals — makes wood joints as strong as the wood — water-resistant but not waterproof. Full recipe: VITA, p. 313. - Waterproof cloth or leather: rub in beeswax, tallow or a beeswax–oil mix, then warm it so it soaks in. - Waterproof boots (USDA): melt together 1 lb petroleum jelly + 2 oz beeswax, or 12 oz tallow + 4 oz cod oil. Apply warm (never hotter than your hand can bear), working it into the welt and sole edge, where shoes leak most. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 12–13) 📚 Go deeper: Henley's Twentieth Century Formulas (1916) — hundreds of glues, pastes and cements; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 313 — casein glue; USDA Care of Leather, p. 10 — oiling and waterproofing shoes and harness.

👟 Clothing and footwear - Mending: running stitch for seams, backstitch where it must be strong, whipstitch for edges, and darning for holes (weave thread back and forth across the hole, then across the other way). Patch from the inside for strength. Needles from stiff wire; thread from unraveled fabric, dental floss or fishing line. - Mend early — a few stitches on a weak seam or loose button save a big patch later. Shrink new patch cloth first and cut it on the straight of the weave. Darn with yarn raveled from a seam allowance, and don't pull it tight (it puckers). (USDA ABCs of Mending, pp. 4–8) - Sandals from old tires: trace your foot on tire tread, cut with a very sharp knife wetted with soapy water (steel belts make it slow — choose worn tread with no wire showing), sand the edges, and tie on with straps cut from an inner tube or with cord through slots. - Shoe care: work grease in well where the sole meets the upper, and let shoes dry somewhere warm, not hot. Re-sole before the welt and insole wear through — after that they're rarely worth fixing. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 10–11) - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it in cold rain. 📚 Go deeper: USDA ABCs of

Leather, pp. 10–11) - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it in cold rain. 📚 Go deeper: USDA ABCs of Mending — patches, darns and tears for every fabric; Bower Practical Shoe Repairing — soles, heels and stitching; Leland Manual of Mending and Repairing — fixing almost anything in the house; USDA Knitwear Make-Overs — reusing worn sweaters.

🔧 Simple plumbing - Dripping faucet: shut the water off first, then replace the washer. A temporary washer can be cut from leather (cold taps) or rubber (hot taps). If the washer screw is stuck, put on a drop of kerosene and tap it; if the head splits, deepen the slot with a hacksaw. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, pp. 4–5) - Toilet tank keeps running: usually a leaky, waterlogged float or a worn flapper/ball. A tank should empty in about 10 seconds. (pp. 9–11) - Clogged drain: put a little water in the sink and plunge hard; if that fails, open the trap under the sink and dig out the grease and hair with a bent wire (p. 12). - When you shut off the water for repairs, open the highest faucet so a vacuum can't suck dirty water back into the pipes from a tub or toilet (p. 12). - Frozen pipe: open the faucet and thaw from the faucet end back toward the supply — never from the middle, where trapped water can burst the pipe. Thaw drains from the low end upward. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, p. 14.) 📚 Go deeper: USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs in the Home — faucets, valves, tanks, clogs and thawing, with drawings; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater — using wash water on the garden.

Test a part in the circuit before you desolder it. Bulging or leaking capacitors are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. - Look before you plug in — about 2 minutes finds most visible faults: loose or corroded connections, stray solder or wire bits (shake it and listen), charred resistors, and a white crust at an electrolytic capacitor's seal. A discolored or leaking transformer means a short somewhere. If anything smokes or sizzles when powered, pull the plug at once. (NEETS 6, pp. 210–211) - The simplest explanation that fits all the symptoms is usually right (Kuphaldt, p. 37). Multimeter quick tests (touch the probes together first — the meter should read near zero ohms — Kuphaldt Multimeters, p. 30) - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires. - Diode: conducts one way only — about 0.5–0.7 V on the diode setting forward, nothing backward. Both ways = shorted; neither = open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56–57). - Transistor: test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. Avoid the lowest ohms range (R×1), which

(NEETS 7, pp. 56–57). - Transistor: test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. Avoid the lowest ohms range (R×1), which can damage small transistors. (NEETS 7, p. 111) - Capacitor (discharged first): on the ohms setting a good one shows a brief "kick" then rising resistance; no kick = open, steady low reading = shorted. (NEETS 6, p. 171) Resistor color code: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Bands 1–2 are digits, band 3 is the number of zeros, the last band is tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%). Example: yellow–violet–orange–gold = 47,000 Ω ±5%. (Kuphaldt vol. 5, pp. 26–27) Soldering: use rosin-core solder (never acid-core plumbing solder); a 25-watt iron for circuit boards. Make the wires hold mechanically first, heat the joint, not the solder, and don't move it while it cools. Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. - Put the iron's tip on the bigger piece of metal (the pad or lug), not the thin wire; a little fresh solder on the tip helps the heat flow. (Kuphaldt Soldering, pp. 24–26) - 63/37 tin-lead solder is best for electronics; zinc-chloride (acid) fluxes corrode circuit boards (NEETS 14, p. 80; Navy 2M, p. 195). What to salvage before throwing anything out: - Radios and clock radios: power transformers, cords, switches, knobs, speakers. - Computer power supplies: 12 V and 5 V power, fans, heat sinks, wire, connectors. - Printers and scanners: small motors, gears, rods, belts, switches. - Microwaves (after discharging!): fan and turntable motors, door switches, fuses, magnets. - Cars: batteries, alternators (12 V charging), lights, wire, fuses, relays — see Army TM 9-8000 in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals (charging systems, p. 304). - Also: LEDs, magnet wire from motors and transformers, fuses, batteries, cords. - Motor run capacitors can be reused; motor start capacitors can burst if used continuously. - Insulators for antennas: plastic or glass is best (spoons, buttons, bottle necks), then dry wood, then rope. 🍲 Hay-box cooking (saves fuel) Bring the pot to a full boil, then nest it tightly in hay, wool, newspaper or blankets in a box with a padded lid; it keeps cooking for hours on its own heat. Bring food back to a boil before eating if it has cooled below hot (food is safest kept above 140 °F). - Building one (Haybox): a wooden box, old trunk or bucket with at least 4 inches of packing all round the pot, below it and in a thick cushion on top. Crumpled newspaper, packed hard, is the best cheap packing. Use a pot with straight sides and a tight lid, sized to the food — a big half-empty pot cools fast. (USDA FB 771, pp. 6–9) (The 1919 bulletin suggests asbestos — never use it.) - Times: boil beans or meat 20–25 minutes first, then 2–2½ hours in the box; soft foods need only a few minutes' boil and about 25 minutes in the box. It cuts fuel use by about 40%. (Practical Action Fireless Cookers, pp. 2, 5) - Meat and beans are the riskiest — don't leave them in the box too long, and reboil before eating (p. 5). - A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p. 6). 📚 Go

- A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p. 6). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 771 Homemade Fireless Cookers — building plans and recipes; Practical Action Fireless Cookers — a basket cooker from scraps; Aprovecho Capturing Heat — haybox, rocket stove and solar cooker plans.

🫙 Containers and storage - Food-grade buckets (recycling number 1 or 2 on the bottom, from bakeries and restaurants), glass jars and metal cans with lids. Wash with soap, then rinse with the bleach solution above. Never store food in trash bags, paint cans or chemical drums. Containers of 20–30 lb are easy to lift and get used up before bugs move in. (USU Food Storage in the Home, pp. 11–12) - Keep mice out: metal cans or glass; hang sacks from wire. Set snap traps along walls. Seal cracks, keep food off the floor, and keep the store room between freezing and 70 °F — cooler keeps longer (USU, p. 9). - Clay-pot cooler (zeer): a small clay pot inside a bigger one with wet coarse sand between, and a wet cloth on top. Evaporation keeps vegetables cool — it works best in hot, dry weather, which suits our summers. Keep it in shade with a breeze and wet the sand three times a day. (Practical Action Clay Pot Cooler, pp. 1, 6) 📚 Go deeper: USU Food Storage in the Home — containers, storage rooms and shelf life; Practical Action Clay Pot Cooler — making and using a zeer pot; WSU Root Cellars — storing vegetables and fruit without power.

💧 Clean water from plastic bottles (SODIS) Fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 liters or less with clear water, lay them on a roof or shiny surface in full sun for 6 hours (two full days if it's more than half cloudy). Doesn't work with cloudy water — let it settle or filter it first. Details: Sanitation-Water\ and Water\. - Clear enough? Stand the full, open bottle on a page of large print (letters about ½ inch high) and look down through it. If you can read it, the water is clear enough. - Fill ¾, shake 20 seconds, then top up — the air helps kill germs. Lay bottles flat, on metal roofing if you have it. Drink straight from the bottle so it isn't re-contaminated. - Not green or brown bottles; replace scratched, cloudy ones (about yearly). SODIS does nothing for chemical pollution. (Eawag SODIS Manual, pp. 26, 86–87) - In long rainy spells, boil or use stored or rainwater instead (p. 27). 📚 Go deeper: Eawag SODIS Manual, p. 26 — step by step, with a question-and-answer section from p. 85; OSU Survival Basics: Water, p. 3 — boiling and bleach; CAWST Biosand Filter Manual — build a filter for cloudy water.

🐜 Pests - Roaches and ants: powdered borax mixed with sugar or flour, dusted into cracks (roaches), or a sponge soaked in borax-and-sugar syrup in their trail (ants). Keep borax away from children and pets. - Mosquitoes: screens, netting over beds, and smoke; homemade repellents are weak. Cover water barrels and screen their vents so they don't breed there (Practical Action Household Water Treatment, p. 2). - Lice: comb wet hair with a fine-tooth (nit) comb every day for two weeks; wash bedding hot. Body lice live in clothing seams — wash clothes and bedding at least weekly (FM 21-10, p. 96). - Ticks: check every evening, especially after brush; pull straight out with tweezers. Grip close to the skin and pull with gentle, steady force without crushing it, and protect your fingers with cloth or gloves (FM 21-10, p. 98). 📚 Go deeper: Army FM 21-10 Field Hygiene and Sanitation, p. 96 — lice, ticks, mites and other pests; USU Food Storage in the Home, p. 13 — pantry pests.For hundreds more recipes — cleaners, polishes, glues, inks, waterproofing, pest control and home remedies — see the classic formula books in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do\. They are old: use their methods, but follow the modern safety rules above, and skip any recipe using mercury (bichloride), arsenic, cyanide, lead, benzene, carbon tetrachloride or carbolic acid, or any "remedy" taken by mouth that contains

follow the modern safety rules above, and skip any recipe using mercury (bichloride), arsenic, cyanide, lead, benzene, carbon tetrachloride or carbolic acid, or any "remedy" taken by mouth that contains kerosene — those are poisons. 🌾 Food From Scratch How to make staple ingredients — flour, masa, leavening, salt, sweetener, fat — from what grows or can be raised around the Illinois Valley, and how to turn them into bread, tortillas, pasta, crackers and other everyday food. Details and more recipes are in Food-From-Scratch\ (grain, wild and local staples, breads and staples) and Gardening-Food\. The links open each book on the drive at the right page. ⚠️ Two foods here can kill if you get them wrong: camas has a deadly look-alike (death camas), and acorns and lye/ash-cooked corn must be processed properly. Follow the steps exactly, and never eat a wild plant you can't identify with certainty.

🌾 Flour from grain - Grow hulless varieties of oats and barley if you can — hulled types need dehulling. Wheat and corn are the easiest staples to grow and grind. Winter grains are sown in fall and cut the next summer: ¼–½ inch deep, about 1 foot apart each way (SARE, p. 2). - Harvest when the heads are fully tan and nodding and the kernels are too hard to dent with a fingernail. Cut about 10 inches below the heads. - Thresh by stomping the heads in a clean bin or on a tarp; winnow by pouring the grain slowly in front of a fan (or in a breeze) so the chaff blows away. Repeat. (SARE handout, p. 1) - Dry to 12–13% moisture before storing — wetter grain heats, molds and draws insects. Field test: a dry kernel resists your thumbnail and cracks sharply between your teeth. (Peace Corps Small Farm Grain Storage, p. 55) If you dry it with heat, keep eating grain below 140 °F and seed grain below 113 °F (p. 53). - Store whole grain, grind as needed. Whole grain keeps for years; flour goes rancid within months once milled. A hand grain mill is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones (a quern: a turning top stone on a fixed bottom one) and sift out the bran (Shifts and Expedients, p. 519).

mill is worth owning; otherwise grind between two stones (a quern: a turning top stone on a fixed bottom one) and sift out the bran (Shifts and Expedients, p. 519). - Kill pests in stored grain: freeze small bags 2–3 days, or heat a ½-inch layer at 140–150 °F for 30 minutes (may weaken bread rise). Store airtight, and only when dry. (USU Food Storage in the Home, p. 14) - A sealed, full container kills bugs on its own — they use up the oxygen. Keep the grain you dip into daily in a separate small container (Peace Corps, p. 279). 🌰 Acorn flour Our oaks — tanoak (the traditional favorite), California black oak, Oregon white oak and canyon live oak — all make good flour, but every acorn must be leached to remove bitter tannins. A tanoak can drop over 200 pounds in a good year and bears some crop every year (NRCS Tanoak, p. 1). 1. Gather the second fall (late September–October); the first acorns down are mostly wormy. Dry them 2–5 days in the sun or 20 minutes in a 175 °F oven, door ajar. Whole, dry acorns keep several years — in sacks or jars, not plastic. (UCCE, p. 2) 2. Crack and shell them, and remove any moldy or wormy ones. Grind the nutmeats to a coarse meal or flour. 3. Leach — any one of these: - Hot: soak in hot water for an hour, drain, repeat several times (fastest). - Running water: a cloth bag of meal in cold running water for several hours. - Daily change: 3 parts water to 1 part meal in jars, kept cool; pour off the dark water and refill every day for about a week. - Traditional: pour nearly scalding water over fine flour in a hollow scooped in clean sand (Hupa, p. 38). 4. It's done when it tastes sweet, not bitter or puckery. Cold leaching keeps more of the starch's binding power (better for bread); hot

in clean sand (Hupa, p. 38). 4. It's done when it tastes sweet, not bitter or puckery. Cold leaching keeps more of the starch's binding power (better for bread); hot is faster. 5. Use it wet as mush/porridge, pat it into flatbread on a hot stone or pan, or dry it and replace ¼ to ½ of the wheat flour in bread (acorn flour has no gluten on its own). 6. Ground meal goes rancid in a warm room — grind only a few weeks' worth and keep it cold (UCCE, p. 2). Other local nuts need no leaching: hazelnuts (June–July, dry and eat raw) and sugar pine nuts (October; pound the cones to free the seeds) — Hupa, pp. 39–40. Bay nuts (Oregon myrtle) must be roasted at 350 °F for 30–45 minutes until dark-chocolate brown; they taste of coffee and contain a caffeine-like stimulant (UCCE, pp. 2–3). 📚 Go deeper: UCCE Foods from the Tanoak Forest, p. 2 — modern acorn and bay-nut processing step by step; Goddard, Life and Culture of the Hupa, p. 37 — how acorns were gathered, ground, leached and cooked just south of us; NRCS Tanoak guide, p. 2 — storage, leaching and acorn bread.

🌿 Camas, cattail and other local starches - Camas bulbs (Camassia quamash — meadows, blue flowers in spring) were a major food here. They must be pit-roasted or slow-baked 24–36 hours — long cooking turns the indigestible starch sweet. Dry cooked bulbs or cakes for storage. ⚠️ Death camas grows in the same meadows and its bulbs look the same. Flower color is not a safe test. Only harvest from a bed you have watched bloom and learned plant by plant; if there's any doubt, leave it. (USDA Great Camas guide, pp. 1–2; Wild-Plants\ death camas guide) - Dig after flowering, take only the big bulbs, replant the small ones, and rest each patch a few years. Fresh bulbs don't keep; dried camas cakes are soaked overnight before eating (Camas guide, pp. 1–2). | | Camas (edible) | Death camas (deadly) | | Flowers | Blue-violet to creamy white, on a tall leafless stalk | Greenish to yellowish-white, in a pointed cluster | | Height | 24–48 inches | 6–18 inch stem | | Leaves | Long, narrow, grass-like | Grass-like, V-shaped, edged with stiff hairs | | Bulb | Edible only after long cooking | Blackish scales, no onion smell — every part poisonous | Sources: Camas guide, p. 2; PNW 104, pp. 1–2. Death camas symptoms start 1–8 hours after eating (drooling, vomiting, weakness, irregular heartbeat): get help at once. - Cattail (Typha latifolia): young shoots and stem bases (boiled or roasted), green flower spikes (boiled like corn), pollen to stretch flour, and rhizome flour (the root core is 30–46% starch — pound, soak, let the starch settle, dry it). Harvest only from clean water; cattails take up pollutants. (Cattail guide, p. 1) - ⚠️ Western waterhemlock grows in the same wet ground — the most poisonous plant in North America; a walnut-sized piece of root can kill a cow. Its stem base and roots are hollow with cross-walls and ooze yellow, oily juice. Never dig roots in wet ground unless you're sure. (PNW 109, p. 1) - More: USDA Food Plants of the North American Indians lists about 1,100 native food plants and how each was prepared (p. 6). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Great Camas guide — harvest, cooking, drying; PNW 104 Meadow Deathcamas — identification photos; PNW 109 Western Waterhemlock, p. 3 — photo comparison with look-alikes.

🌽 Corn: masa, tortillas and hominy Always cook dried corn with lime or wood ash ("nixtamal") before making it a staple — it unlocks the corn's niacin. People living mostly on untreated cornmeal get pellagra (FAO Maize, p. 13). - Masa with lime (food-grade slaked lime, cal): use lime 1% of the dry corn's weight (5 g of lime per 500 g of corn — weigh it if you can) and water 1½ times the corn's volume. Heat to just below a simmer (200–210 °F) until the skins slip off but the center is still firm (often under 30 minutes). Rest 8–12 hours in the liquid, then rub and rinse off the skins. Grind while cold (a metate or stone mill, with a little cold water); use the masa within a day. (Smithsonian method, pp. 1–3) Fresh corn needs less lime and cooking; old, hard corn more (FAO, p. 66). - With wood ash instead: boil shelled corn 15–30 minutes in weak lye water made from hardwood ashes until the hulls loosen, then rinse very thoroughly in running water until no lye remains. Lye is caustic — gloves and eye protection; never taste it. - Lye hominy with store lye (USDA): 5 oz lye in 6 quarts cold water; stir in 5 quarts whole corn and let stand 15 hours. Wash and rub the corn in a cloth bag until

(USDA): 5 oz lye in 6 quarts cold water; stir in 5 quarts whole corn and let stand 15 hours. Wash and rub the corn in a cloth bag until hulls and black tips are gone, then boil 3–4 hours in salted water, changing the water once or twice to remove the lye taste. Makes 15–20 quarts. (FB 1236, pp. 20–21) - Corn tortillas: knead masa with a little water to a soft, play-dough feel, press balls flat between plastic or cloth, and cook on a hot dry griddle about a minute a side. Keep the masa under a damp cloth — dry masa cracks (Smithsonian, p. 3). - Hominy (whole kernels) and cornbread, mush, polenta and corn pone recipes: USDA Corn and Its Uses as Food (FB 1236, p. 11). To stretch wheat, use a scant cup of cornmeal per cup of flour in quick breads and bake longer. - If the kernels go mushy all the way through, they're overcooked and won't make masa — stop sooner next time (Smithsonian, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: Smithsonian Nixtamalization — the full masa method; USDA FB 1236 Corn and Its Uses, p. 11 — mush, pone, cornbreads and hominy; FAO Maize, p. 96 — tortillas and other corn recipes; Parker, Iroquois Uses of Maize, p. 115 — hominy, samp and old corn dishes.

🍞 Leavening without store yeast or baking powder - Wild sourdough starter: mix equal weights of flour (whole-grain or rye starts fastest) and unchlorinated water in a jar. Every day, discard all but a little and feed it equal weights of flour and water (twice a day from day 4). Keep it at 70–82 °F. Usable around day 7, strong in 2–4 weeks — it's ready when it doubles within 4–6 hours of feeding and smells yeasty and pleasant. Throw it out if mold appears. (Illinois Sourdough 101, pp. 1–3) - Keep it going: save ½ cup each time you bake; the night before, feed it equal parts flour and water and leave it warm 6–8 hours. Store in glass, not metal, with the lid loose. (Alaska's guide warns against all metal; Illinois allows stainless steel but never copper, iron or galvanized.) (UAF Sourdough, p. 2) - Back-up: spread some starter thin, dry it until brittle, and store it airtight. Revive by crumbling into warm water overnight, then feeding. - Sourdough pancakes and muffins get ½ tsp baking soda dissolved in 1 Tbsp water, stirred in last. Never put soda in the starter itself — it can kill the yeast (UAF, pp. 2–3). - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807, p. 10) — liquid yeast keeps about two

(UAF, pp. 2–3). - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807, p. 10) — liquid yeast keeps about two weeks in a cool, dark place. - Quick breads: sour milk or buttermilk + ½ tsp baking soda per cup replaces sweet milk and baking powder (FB 1136, p. 22). Homemade baking powder = 1 part baking soda : 2 parts cream of tartar (Fannie Farmer, p. 92). | Starter trouble | Fix | | Not rising after a week | Somewhere warmer; switch to rye or whole-grain flour; avoid very hard or chlorinated water (Illinois, pp. 1–2) | | Dark liquid on top ("hooch") | It's hungry — pour it off or stir it in, then feed (Illinois, p. 3) | | Any mold | Throw it out; restart from your dried back-up (Illinois, p. 3) | 📚 Go deeper: Illinois Sourdough Bread 101, p. 4 — step-by-step loaf and schedules; UAF Sourdough, p. 3 — hotcakes, muffins and bread; USDA FB 807, p. 10 — potato yeast and saved dough.

🧂 Salt, 🍯 sweeteners and 🥓 fat - Salt from seawater: seawater is about 3.5% salt — roughly 4–5 gallons per pound of salt in practice. Collect it away from harbors and outfalls, filter through cloth, boil down to a slush, then finish drying slowly; pour off the last bitter liquid for better taste. - Bigleaf maple syrup (OSU 2025 guide): tap after leaf drop and a hard freeze, through winter freeze–thaw days, until buds break. 5/16-inch spile in a 2-inch hole; collect sap daily and boil it within 24 hours. Bigleaf sap is thin — about 80 gallons of sap per gallon of syrup (20 gallons ≈ 1 quart after ~8 hours of boiling). Syrup is done at 7 °F above the boiling point of water where you are — about 216 °F around Cave Junction's elevation (219 °F at sea level). (OSU EM 9163, pp. 2–8) Keep buckets lidded — "ropey" (stringy) sap is spoiled. Let syrup settle and pour it off the gritty "sugar sand"; to keep it on a shelf, bottle it at 180–190 °F into just-boiled jars (pp. 6, 8–9). - Honey: strain through progressively finer cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it — blow air over a pan instead. Solid ("granulated") honey is fine. (pp. 3–4)

wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it — blow air over a pan instead. Solid ("granulated") honey is fine. (pp. 3–4) Honey replaces sugar cup for cup in baking (FB 1136, p. 23). - Lard and tallow: chill fat and render it within about a week. Melt slowly with a little water, stirring, at 235–245 °F (no copper pots), until bubbling stops and the cracklings float and turn chestnut-brown; strain into clean jars, fill full, store cool and dark. (Minnesota, pp. 2–3) Leaf (kidney) fat makes the best lard; strong-tasting gut fat is for soap. Slightly rancid lard can be rescued by heating it with sliced potatoes until they're dark brown, then straining (pp. 2, 4). - Nut oil (hazelnuts, acorns): grind, boil with water, and skim the oil as it rises; clarify and store cool (Practical Action brief, p. 2). Discard moldy nuts first; store oil dark and airtight, never in copper (pp. 1, 6). - Butter: sour the cream mildly at 65–75 °F, churn at 52–66 °F until grains the size of wheat form, drain, wash twice in cold water, and work in ¾ oz salt per pound (USDA FB 876, pp. 23–24). - ⚠️ Homemade vinegar (FB 1424) is fine for cooking, but never for canned pickles — its acid strength is unknown, and canning recipes need tested

FB 876, pp. 23–24). - ⚠️ Homemade vinegar (FB 1424) is fine for cooking, but never for canned pickles — its acid strength is unknown, and canning recipes need tested 5% vinegar (USDA Canning Guide 1, p. 28). 📚 Go deeper: OSU Making Bigleaf Maple Syrup, p. 3 — tapping, sanitation and bottling, with photos; Minnesota Making Lard at Home — rendering and what spoils lard; Practical Action Honey Processing — straining, moisture and wax; USDA FB 876 Making Butter — cream, churning and storage.

🥩 Jerky - Heat the meat to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F) before or right after drying — drying alone doesn't kill E. coli, Salmonella or trichinosis. Ten people caught trichinosis from cougar jerky in 1995 (PNW 632, p. 8); cougar and bear are hunted in our units (ODFW, pp. 67–68). Either dip strips 1½–2 minutes in simmering brine before drying, or heat the dried strips 10 minutes in a 275 °F oven (pp. 9, 17). - Dry at 145–155 °F (check with a thermometer; an oven with the door propped open works). Sun drying isn't recommended. Done when a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (pp. 9, 18). It keeps 1–2 months. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 632 Making Jerky at Home Safely — tested methods and the hot-brine recipe; NDSU Preservation of Game Meats and Fish, p. 5 — game jerky, smoking and curing.

🥖 Staples - No oven thermometer? Put a scrap of white paper or ½ tsp flour on a tin plate in the oven; if it turns light golden brown in 5 minutes, it's right to start bread (FB 807, p. 15). Over a fire, cook on coals, not flames (OSU EM 9331, p. 4). - Danger zone: cooked food left between 40 °F and 140 °F for over 2 hours can make you sick (OSU EM 9331, p. 5). Basic yeast bread — per loaf (USDA FB 807, pp. 13–17): 1 cup lukewarm liquid, about 3 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 1 Tbsp sugar or honey, up to 1 Tbsp fat, and yeast (or ½ cup active sourdough starter in place of yeast and part of the liquid). Knead until smooth and springy, let it double, shape, let it rise again, and bake at about 400 °F for 40–50 minutes, until it sounds hollow when tapped. Stop adding flour once the dough doesn't stick to unfloured hands — too much flour makes heavy bread. Rise it covered, at about 80 °F; it's ready for the oven when a light touch leaves a slight dent. Simple sourdough loaf: 1 cup active starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about

starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about 425 °F for 35–45 minutes. Poke test: a floured finger-dent that springs back halfway means bake now; one that stays means over-risen — bake at once. A preheated Dutch oven (lid on 30 minutes, then off) gives a good crust without a real oven (Illinois, pp. 5–6). Flour tortillas / flatbread: 2 cups flour, ¼ cup lard, 1 tsp salt, about ¾ cup warm water. Knead, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cook on a hot dry pan 30–60 seconds a side. Works with part acorn or barley flour. Barley flatbread with no yeast: FAO Barley, p. 63. Biscuits (USDA FB 1136, p. 23): 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp baking powder (or the soda and sour milk swap above), 2 Tbsp fat, ⅔–¾ cup liquid. Bake hot (about 450 °F) 12–15 minutes. Keep it all cold and handle it lightly. Too much soda makes them yellow and bad-tasting (p. 22). Crackling bread: for each cup of cornmeal, ¾ tsp salt and ½ cup cracklings left from rendering lard; pour on boiling water until you can mash it by hand, shape into cakes and bake (FB 1236, p. 12). Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg +

pour on boiling water until you can mash it by hand, shape into cakes and bake (FB 1236, p. 12). Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg + 2 yolks, ½ tsp salt, about ⅓ cup water (or the old way: one egg, a pinch of salt and enough flour for a very stiff dough). Knead 8–10 minutes, rest 10–20, roll paper-thin, cut ⅛–¼ inch strips. Cook fresh 2–4 minutes, dried 10–12. To store, dry until the noodles snap; keep airtight about a month (longer frozen). (Illinois Extension, p. 2; Fannie Farmer 1896, p. 167) Because of the raw egg, Illinois says don't air-dry over 2 hours — finish them at about 135 °F. Hardtack (keeps for years): 3 parts flour to 1 part water (no salt — salt draws moisture and mold), stiff dough, ½ inch thick, prick with holes, bake 1 hour at 375 °F, then dry 3 more days. Soak or crumble into soup to eat. (City of Alexandria) Beans: soak overnight (6 cups water + 2 tsp salt per pound) or quick-soak (boil 2 minutes, stand 1 hour), then simmer 2–4 hours. Old beans take longer; lentils and split peas need no soak. Beans + corn (or wheat) together make complete protein. Add tomatoes or vinegar only after they're tender — acid stops beans softening (USU, pp. 2–4). Canning beans needs a pressure canner:

+ corn (or wheat) together make complete protein. Add tomatoes or vinegar only after they're tender — acid stops beans softening (USU, pp. 2–4). Canning beans needs a pressure canner: at Cave Junction's elevation a weighted-gauge canner runs at 15 lb (OSU EM 9435, p. 3). Porridge and mush: cracked wheat, oats, barley, cornmeal or leached acorn meal simmered in about 3–4 times their volume of water with a pinch of salt. Hominy grits can finish overnight in a hay box after a 10-minute boil; coarse hominy needs longer on the fire first (FB 1236, p. 19). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 807 Bread and Bread Making, p. 12 — kneading, rising and baking; USDA FB 1136 Quick Breads and Biscuits, p. 22 — biscuits, muffins and griddle cakes; Fannie Farmer 1896, p. 92 — hundreds of everyday recipes; Practical Action Fireless Cookers, p. 5 — hay-box cooking times.Old recipes in these books are fine for methods; for food safety (canning, curing, storing) follow the modern USDA guides in Gardening-Food\.

🪵 Firewood: Cutting, Splitting, Seasoning & Burning How to keep a household warm and cooking with wood: which local trees give the most heat, how much you'll need, felling and bucking safely, splitting, drying wood in our wet winters, burning it cleanly, keeping the chimney from catching fire, handling ashes in fire country, and growing your own firewood from oak, madrone and tanoak stumps. The manuals are in Firewood\ (Cutting-Felling, Splitting-Seasoning, Burning-Stoves-Chimneys, Woodlot); saws, axes and sharpening are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws and the Blacksmithing guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst injuries and fires - Felling kills more woodcutters than anything else. Leave snags and dead trees to someone experienced, never cut alone, and keep everyone two tree-lengths away (WorkSafeBC Part 1, p. 13). - Plan your escape before you cut, about 45° back and away from where the tree will fall. - Never use an axe as a wedge or to drive one; wear eye protection when striking steel wedges (U. of Minnesota, p. 12). - Ashes start wildfires. Lidded metal can, on bare ground, well away from the house, for days. - Carbon monoxide and chimney fires — a CO alarm near the bedrooms, and a clean chimney.

🔥 Which wood, and how much All dry wood gives about the same heat per pound (~9,000 BTU) — so heavier (denser) wood gives more heat per cord (PNW-GTR-810, p. 9). | Local tree | Heat per cord (million BTU, dry) | How it burns | | Oregon white oak | ~30 | Hard to light, long-lasting coals — best overnight wood | | Pacific madrone | ~30 | Same; dries slowly and checks | | Tanoak | ~24–27 (estimated from density) | Excellent coals | | California black oak | ~22–24 (estimated) | Good coals | | Douglas-fir | ~21–24 | Easy to light, hot, some sparks | | Bigleaf maple | ~20–24 (estimated) | Good all-round | | Red alder | ~17–18 | Fast, clean; spring and fall fires | | Ponderosa pine / sugar pine | ~15–22 | Lights easily, burns fast, poor coals | | Incense cedar | ~15–17 (estimated) | Kindling — lights instantly, sparks a lot | (Oak, madrone, fir, alder and pine from OSU EC1628, p. 4 and PNW-GTR-810; burn traits from U. of Minnesota, p. 14.) Use the right wood for the job: cedar and pine for kindling and quick spring or fall fires; oak, madrone and tanoak for cold nights and overnight burns (rule of thumb). Creosote comes mostly from wet wood and smoldering fires, not from the kind of tree

fall fires; oak, madrone and tanoak for cold nights and overnight burns (rule of thumb). Creosote comes mostly from wet wood and smoldering fires, not from the kind of tree (E-1388, p. 2). How much: - A cord is a stack 4 ft × 4 ft × 8 ft (128 cubic ft). A face cord is 4 ft high by 8 ft long with shorter pieces — three face cords of 16-inch wood make one full cord (CMHC, pp. 62, 64). A cord of green wood weighs roughly 5,000 lb (Cornell). - A whole house heated only by wood: 2–4 cords a winter; a stove that helps out: 1–2 cords (CMHC, p. 64). Add a cord or two if you also cook with wood, and keep a year ahead so next winter's wood is drying now (rule of thumb). - Trees per cord (trunk width at chest height): 10-inch ≈ 0.15 cord; 14-inch ≈ ⅓ cord; 22-inch ≈ 1 cord (Cornell, p. 1). 📚 Go deeper: PNW-GTR-810 Fuelwood Characteristics — tables for every Northwest tree; CMHC Guide to Residential Wood Heating; OSU EC1628.

🌲 Felling trees safely (OSU EC 1124 Safe and Effective Use of Chain Saws, written for Oregon woodland owners; USFS sawyer course) 1. Size it up. Don't fell in gusty wind, fog, snow or ice. Check the lean from two sides (a weight on a string works), look up for dead limbs ("widow-makers") and vines tying it to other trees, and bore in once to check for rot. Alder and maple often have rotten hearts (EC 1124, pp. 3–4). 2. Dead trees and snags are a different job. They can fail across a circle 1–1½ times their height, farther downhill (USFS FS-1273, p. 36). Tanoak killed by Sudden Oak Death rots fast and can snap before it's fully dead — treat it as very high risk, and don't move infected tanoak wood to new areas (FS-1273, p. 181). 3. Clear an escape path about 45° back and away from the fall direction, and clear brush around the trunk (EC 1124, p. 5). 4. Notch (undercut) on the side it will fall, about one-third of the way through the trunk. The two cuts must meet exactly — if they don't, the trunk can split up and kick back ("barber chair"). An open-face notch (about 90°) is the most controlled (EC 1124, pp. 6–7). 5. Back cut from the other side, level and about 1 inch higher than the floor of the

open-face notch (about 90°) is the most controlled (EC 1124, pp. 6–7). 5. Back cut from the other side, level and about 1 inch higher than the floor of the notch. Stop to leave a hinge of uncut wood 1–1½ in thick — the hinge steers the tree. Wedge the back cut early. When it goes, set the saw down and walk out your escape path (EC 1124, pp. 7–8). 6. Hung up in another tree? Don't cut the tree it's leaning on and don't work under it — see the professional fallers' methods for hang-ups and leaners (WorkSafeBC Part 2). With hand tools: a sharp crosscut saw and axe still fell and buck trees when fuel runs out — the USFS Crosscut Saw Manual, Saws That Sing and An Ax to Grind cover it, and the Engines guide covers chainsaw care. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1124 — the whole felling sequence with drawings; WorkSafeBC Faller Standard Part 1; USFS hazard-tree guide — reading snags and rot.

🪚 Bucking and limbing - Stand uphill of the log. Cut the side that's being squeezed (compression) first with a shallow cut, then finish from the side that's being stretched (tension) — this keeps the saw from pinching (EC 1124, pp. 8–9). - Log supported at both ends (it sags in the middle): cut down from the top first, then up from below. Supported at one end: cut up from below first (U. of Minnesota, p. 11). - Bent-over saplings ("springpoles") whip when cut. Stand to the side and shave the inside of the bend with shallow cuts (EC 1124, p. 10). - Cut length to fit your stove — usually 16 in, a little shorter than the firebox. - Fire season: saws start fires. Cut early in the morning, keep the spark arrester in place, carry a shovel and extinguisher, and stay a while after you stop (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: WorkSafeBC Part 2 — binds and safe bucking; U. of Minnesota — bucking without pinching, p. 11.

🪓 Splitting (UW-Extension Harvesting Firewood, pp. 15–16; U. of Minnesota, pp. 11–12) - Tools: a 6–8 lb splitting maul handles nearly everything; two steel wedges and a sledge for tough rounds. Keep wedge heads ground smooth — mushroomed steel throws chips. - Set up: a big round as a chopping block, at a height where the maul handle is level when it hits. An old tire bolted on top holds pieces upright. - Technique: swing with your legs and body, all the way through — half swings stick the maul. Aim for existing cracks, put knots at the bottom, and work slabs off the edges of big rounds before trying the middle. - Size: split everything to 6 inches or less so it dries — rounds of 6–10 in at least in half, 10–14 in at least in quarters. - Safety: goggles, boots and shin protection; bystanders 20 ft away. - Easiest when: green wood splits easier than dry for most species; frozen wood splits easier still (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: UW-Extension Harvesting Firewood from Your Woods; An Ax to Grind — axes and mauls.

☀️ Seasoning: drying wood in a wet climate Wet wood wastes heat — a ton of wood at 60% moisture gives about 5.6 million BTU; dried to 20% it gives about 10.7 million (U. of Minnesota, p. 14). It also makes creosote and smoke. - How long: softwoods about 6 months, hardwoods about 12 (EPA Wet Wood is a Waste, p. 2); big oak and madrone pieces up to 2 years (CMHC, p. 61). In western Oregon: cut and split by spring, stack through a dry summer, cover before the rains — two summers is better (OSU EC1628, p. 2). - Cut early. Wood split in August is only half dry by November, and wood that isn't dry by November won't dry outdoors over the winter — move it under cover (USFS 1943 test). - Stacking: single rows, off the ground on rails or pallets (4–6 in), bark side up, in sun and wind. Cover only the top — side tarps trap moisture. Wood dried inside a closed shed takes nearly twice as long as wood in sun and wind (UW-Extension, pp. 16–18; EPA, p. 2). - Keep the woodpile at least 30 ft from the house so it can't carry a wildfire to the walls (UW-Extension, p. 17). - Is it dry? Cracks in the ends, faded gray color, a hollow knock when two pieces are struck together, lighter

carry a wildfire to the walls (UW-Extension, p. 17). - Is it dry? Cracks in the ends, faded gray color, a hollow knock when two pieces are struck together, lighter weight, no hissing in the fire — or a moisture meter reading 20% or less on a freshly split face (CMHC, p. 61; EPA, p. 2). - Woodsheds and racks: plans for a 1-cord shed and cheap pallet or block racks (EPA shed plans; EPA 4 simple racks). 📚 Go deeper: EPA Wet Wood is a Waste; UW-Extension — stacking and drying; CMHC — drying tests, p. 61.

🏠 Burning safely: stoves, chimneys, ashes Burn hot and dry. Smoldering fires and wet wood coat the chimney with creosote, which condenses below about 250 °F and turns to sticky tar below 150 °F (E-1388, p. 2). Flaky, dry creosote means you're burning well; black, shiny tar means you're not (CMHC, p. 46). Chimney cleaning: at least once a year; some say every 3 cords. After cleaning, check after 2 weeks, 1 month and 2 months to learn how fast yours builds up, and check the stovepipe every 2–3 months (E-1388, pp. 3, 5). A stiff brush on rods or a rope, from the top down, with the stove sealed below (rule of thumb). Chimney fire — roaring sound, shaking pipes, sparks out the top (E-1388, p. 3): 1. Close every air inlet and the damper to starve it. 2. Get everyone out; have someone watch the roof for sparks and check the attic. 3. A dry-chemical (ABC) extinguisher or baking soda thrown into the firebox can knock it down. 4. Chimney fires reach 2,000–3,000 °F — inspect the chimney before using it again; metal chimneys can be ruined after 2–3 fires. Clearances: follow the stove's label. For an unlabeled stove: 36–48 in from anything that burns, 18 in for stovepipe, and a non-combustible floor pad reaching 18 in in front (CMHC, p. 31; U. of Minnesota, p. 24). Keep

stove: 36–48 in from anything that burns, 18 in for stovepipe, and a non-combustible floor pad reaching 18 in in front (CMHC, p. 31; U. of Minnesota, p. 24). Keep wood, furniture and drying clothes 3 ft away (USFA card). Ashes in fire country (Crystal Lakes fire district; USFA): - Leave ashes in the stove 4+ days if you can; then into a metal can with a tight metal lid, set on dirt or concrete at least 10 ft from anything that burns, for at least a week — or soak and stir them with water. - Never a plastic bucket, cardboard box, or the garden in fire season. Buried "dead" coals have started wildfires. - Cold, wet wood ash is useful: lye for soap, nixtamal for corn, and potash for the garden. Carbon monoxide: smoke and CO alarms near bedrooms; both wear out after about 10 years (Crystal Lakes, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: E-1388 The Creosote Problem; CMHC — stoves, chimneys and clearances; Aprovecho Capturing Heat — homemade stoves; Arkansas Basics of Heating with Firewood.

🌳 Growing your own: thinning and coppicing Our hardwoods regrow from the stump — cut once, harvest again and again ("coppicing") (USFS PSW-GTR-185): - Black oak, tanoak and madrone all resprout from the root crown, and it's almost impossible to stop them. - Cut stumps low — under 8 inches. Sprouts from tall stumps attach weakly and rot early (p. 35). - Cut in winter or spring: black oaks cut December–May sprouted 92% of the time; cut June–November, only 45% (p. 36). - In full sun, black oak and tanoak sprout clumps reached about 20 ft tall in 10 years (p. 36). Thin clumps to 3–4 of the best stems after a few years. - Bigleaf maple resprouts strongly; red alder only from young stumps (rule of thumb). Thin for firewood and fire safety at the same time: remove small, crowded trees and lower limbs ("ladder fuels") and space out the crowns — the cut becomes firewood, and the woods burn less hot in a wildfire (OSU EC 1573, p. 3; EC 1574). In oak woodland, removing the Douglas-fir crowding the oaks gives both firewood and healthier oaks (KBO/Lomakatsi oak guide). 📚 Go deeper: PSW-GTR-185 — sprouting of black oak, tanoak and madrone; OSU EC 1573 — thinning; Restoring Oak Habitats in Southern Oregon; Wikipedia: coppicing.

📆 A firewood year (rule of thumb) | When | Do this | | Jan–Mar | Fell and coppice hardwoods (best resprouting, sap down, easy to see the woods). Buck to length. | | Mar–May | Split and stack everything for next winter, in sun and wind. Clean the chimney after the heating season. | | June–Sept | Fire season: little or no saw work; let the woodpile dry. Clear brush around the house and woodpile. | | Oct | Cover the tops of the stacks before the rains; move a month's wood into the shed or porch. Check the stovepipe. | | Nov–Feb | Burn last year's wood; check the chimney after the first month. Haul ashes to the metal can.
