🚰 Water Purification — With What You Have How to make creek, spring, rain or well water safe to drink when there's no store and no power: settling and straining, homemade sand, biosand and clay-pot filters, charcoal (what it does and doesn't do), boiling, bleach and pool shock, sunlight, solar stills, simple tests, and safe storage. The manuals are in Water-Purification\ (Filters-Sand-Charcoal-Ceramic, Disinfection, Settling-Coagulation, Overviews-Testing), Water\ and Homestead-Skills\Sanitation-Water. Getting the water out of the ground is in the Wells & Pumps guide. ### The four rules of safe water 1. Clear it, then kill the germs. Settle or filter muddy water first; then boil or disinfect. 2. Charcoal and sand filters alone do NOT make water safe. They clear water and improve taste; charcoal beds even grow bacteria and shield them from chlorine. Charcoal goes last, after disinfection (WHO, pp. 51–52; Wilderness Medical Society, p. 6). 3. Boiling kills germs but removes no chemicals — not fuel, metals, salt or fire-retardant runoff. 4. Keep treated water clean: covered container with a spout, never dip a cup into it.

🧭 Which method does what From CAWST's comparison of household methods (CAWST Fact Sheets): | Method | Germs (bacteria / viruses / Giardia-Crypto) | Muddy water | Chemicals | Notes | | Settling, three-pot storage | some | very good | no | First step for muddy water | | Cloth straining | larger organisms only | some | no | Quick first step | | Alum, wood ash, Moringa seed | some (lab good, field ~50%) | very good | no | Clears water fast | | Biosand / slow sand filter | good / fair / very good | very good | no (some iron) | Needs a living top layer | | Ceramic pot filter | very good / fair / very good | very good | no | Needs silver coating for best results | | Boiling | kills all | no | no | Uses fuel | | Chlorine (bleach, pool shock) | kills bacteria & viruses; weak on Crypto | no | no | Cheap, protects stored water | | Sunlight (SODIS) | good | needs clear water | no | Free; sunny months only | | Solar still / distilling | kills all | yes | removes salts & metals | Slow, ~1 gallon/day per 12 sq ft | | Charcoal / "activated" carbon | poor — not a germ barrier | some

| yes | removes salts & metals | Slow, ~1 gallon/day per 12 sq ft | | Charcoal / "activated" carbon | poor — not a germ barrier | some | taste, odor, many organic chemicals | Use last | WHO's bar for a "protective" method is removing about 99% of bacteria and protozoa and 99.9% of viruses; most homemade methods reach that only in combination (WHO Evaluating Household Water Treatment, p. 11). Best simple combination: settle or filter → boil or chlorinate → (optional) charcoal for taste. 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Household Water Treatment Fact Sheets — every method with removal data; WHO Managing Water in the Home; Practical Action Household Water Treatment.

🫙 Step 1 — Clear the water - Let it settle. Three-pot method: fill pot 1 from the source; each day pour pot 1 gently into pot 2, and pot 2 into pot 3 (your drinking pot) — water sits at least 2 days and much of the dirt and some germs settle out. Still disinfect it (CAWST, p. 4). - Strain through cloth: old, soft cotton folded 7–8 times catches particles bigger than about 20 microns — silt, worms, the plankton cholera rides on — but not bacteria or viruses. Wash the cloth after each use (CAWST, pp. 14–15). - Make the mud drop (coagulants): - Alum (pickling alum): about ⅛ tsp per gallon; stir fast 1 minute, slowly 5 minutes, settle at least 30 minutes, pour off through cloth (WMS, p. 7). - Wood ash, lime, crushed beans also work as rough coagulants (same source). - Moringa seed: about 1 crushed kernel per liter of muddy water — shake the paste in a cup of water, strain it in, stir 1 minute fast and 5–10 minutes slow, settle 1–2 hours (ECHO note; WEDC, p. 3). Moringa won't grow here (frost) — stockpile seed if you want it. - Coagulants clear water; they don't make it safe. Always disinfect afterward. - Is it clear enough? Look down through a clear 2-liter bottle of the water at large print —

Coagulants clear water; they don't make it safe. Always disinfect afterward. - Is it clear enough? Look down through a clear 2-liter bottle of the water at large print — if you can read it, it's under about 50 NTU, clear enough for filters, SODIS and chlorine (CAWST Testing, p. 81). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST — settling, coagulants and cloth, pp. 4–15; WEDC Moringa seed coagulant.

Biosand filter (best household filter you can build) A concrete or plastic box of sand with a living layer on top (the "schmutzdecke") that eats germs (CAWST Biosand Construction Manual): - Layers, bottom to top: 2 in of drainage gravel (¼–½ in), 2 in of small gravel, then fine washed sand (0.7 mm or finer) filled with water already in the box so no air gets trapped (pp. 59, 92). - About 2 in of water must stand above the sand when it stops flowing — more starves the living layer of air; letting it dry out kills it. A diffuser plate keeps poured water from digging up the top (pp. 18–19). - Use it every day, one bucket (12–18 L) at a time, 6–12 hours apart. The living layer takes up to 30 days to grow — disinfect the output until then and always for babies and the sick. When flow gets slow, stir the top inch and scoop off the dirty water ("swirl and dump") (CAWST Fact Sheets, pp. 18–19). - Results once mature: bacteria about 88–98% removed in the field, Giardia-type parasites over 99.9%, viruses less reliable (p. 19). - Cold winter water slows the living layer — filter slower and disinfect (EPA slow sand, p. 9).

Slow sand filter (for a group or homestead) The same idea, bigger: water trickles down through about 3 ft of fine sand at 0.1–0.2 m per hour; build two beds so one can be cleaned (scrape off the top inch). A mature filter removes 95–100% of fecal bacteria and nearly all viruses and cysts. Takes about 3 weeks to "ripen" when new (IRC Slow Sand Filtration, pp. 38, 48).

The bucket "layer filter" — gravel, sand, charcoal A bucket of gravel, sand and charcoal clears and improves water but is not a germ barrier. The right way to use charcoal is the three-stage system: gravel roughing filter → slow sand biofilter (germs) → crushed charcoal (chemicals and taste) → covered storage; replace the charcoal yearly (Aqueous Solutions Biochar Water Filter, pp. 2–9).

Clay pot (ceramic) filter Clay mixed with sawdust or rice husk (about 50:50 by volume to start) is pressed into a pot and fired to about 900 °C (1,650 °F) — the sawdust burns out and leaves tiny pores (CMWG Ceramic Pot Filters, p. 62; RDIC handbook). It sits in a covered bucket with a tap and gives 1–3 liters an hour. Test local clay first (clay testing); flow-test each pot (at least 1 liter in the first hour, not too fast — too fast means cracks) (CMWG, p. 114). They work best with a colloidal silver coating, which you can't make from raw materials — without it, still disinfect. Replace every 1–2 years or when cracked. Kiln plans: Mani kiln. 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Biosand Filter Construction Manual; IRC Slow Sand Filtration; CMWG ceramic filter manual; Wikipedia: biosand filter · slow sand filter · ceramic water filter.

⚫ Charcoal: making it and using it right - What it does: soaks up taste, odor and many organic chemicals (pesticides, some fuel residues). What it doesn't: reliably remove germs — WHO doesn't recommend it for germs, and bacteria grow in the bed (WHO, pp. 51–52). - Plain vs. activated: ordinary charcoal has its pores clogged with tar, so it adsorbs poorly. Factories "activate" it by heating to about 800 °C in steam, which opens the pores (FAO Industrial Charcoal Making, p. 28). - Homemade water-treatment charcoal (Aqueous Solutions Char Drum Oven): 1. Pack dry wood pieces (1–2 in thick) tightly in a steel drum, set a chimney drum on top, and light it from the top. It burns about 2 hours down to faint blue flames. 2. Quench with plenty of water — the steam partly opens the pores (crude activation, not true activated carbon). 3. Crush and sieve to 1–5 mm pieces; wash out the dust. - Use it as the LAST step after the water is filtered and disinfected, or in a column after a sand filter; replace it yearly. Hardwood (oak, madrone) makes good charcoal. Chemical activation (acids, zinc chloride) isn't a safe home method (rule of thumb). - Charcoal-making in bulk: Practical Action brief and the Peace Corps charcoal manual. 📚 Go deeper: FAO — what activated charcoal is, p. 28; Aqueous Solutions — charcoal

of thumb). - Charcoal-making in bulk: Practical Action brief and the Peace Corps charcoal manual. 📚 Go deeper: FAO — what activated charcoal is, p. 28; Aqueous Solutions — charcoal oven; Wikipedia: activated carbon.

🔥 Step 3 — Kill the germs Boiling — the surest method. A rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft — we're far below that) kills bacteria, viruses and parasites even in cloudy water. Let it cool covered; don't add ice (WHO Boil Water, p. 1; OSU, p. 5). Fuel cost: about 0.2 kg (½ lb) of wood per liter — a family's 4 gallons a day is about 7 lb of wood a day (WHO Bulletin, p. 4) — see the Firewood guide. Bleach (plain unscented, 6–8.25% sodium hypochlorite) — EPA, p. 1: | Water | 6% bleach | 8.25% bleach | | 1 quart, clear | 2 drops | 2 drops | | 1 gallon, clear | 8 drops | 6 drops | | 1 gallon, cloudy or very cold | 16 drops | 12 drops | Stir, wait 30 minutes. It should smell faintly of chlorine; if not, dose again and wait 15 more minutes. Cold water needs longer: 1 hour at 50–65 °F, 2+ hours below 50 °F — winter creek water (CAWST, p. 59). Bleach loses strength — use it within a year. Chlorine is weak against Cryptosporidium: settle or filter first. Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) — stores for years as dry granules. Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution; then use 1 part stock

Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) — stores for years as dry granules. Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons of water to make a stock solution; then use 1 part stock to 100 parts water (1 pint per 12½ gallons), wait 30 minutes (EPA, p. 2). Use plain granules (no algaecide or stabilizer), mix outdoors with eye protection, and make stock in small batches — it lasts about a month in heat, longer cool and dark (CDC Safe Water Systems, p. 62). Iodine: 5 drops of 2% tincture per quart (10 if cloudy), wait 30 minutes — fine short-term, not for months on end or for pregnant women (EPA, p. 2). Sunlight (SODIS): clear plastic (PET) bottles of clear water, lying flat in full sun 6 hours (2 days if more than half cloudy). Works well here March–September, poorly in the winter rains (EAWAG SODIS manual, p. 23). Solar pasteurizing: water held at 65 °C (150 °F) is pasteurized — a solar box cooker can do several gallons on a summer day (Ciochetti & Metcalf). A lump of beeswax in a sealed tube melts at about 62 °C and shows when it's done (CAWST, p. 76). 📚 Go deeper: EPA Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water; CDC Safe Water Systems handbook — making and storing chlorine; Wilderness Medical Society guidelines; Wikipedia: SODIS.

☀️ Salty or chemical water: the solar still A shallow black basin under sloped glass or clear plastic: the sun evaporates the water, it condenses on the cover and runs into a gutter — leaving salt, metals and germs behind. Expect about 1 gallon a day per 10–12 sq ft of glass (CAWST, p. 71; Aprovecho, p. 43). Some fuel-type chemicals can carry over (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST — solar distillation; Wikipedia: solar still.

🔬 Simple tests - Turbidity tube: a clear tube with a black-and-white disk at the bottom — pour water in until the disk disappears; the depth tells cloudiness (disk gone at 18 cm ≈ 50 NTU; at 85 cm ≈ 5 NTU) (Myre & Shaw, pp. 11–16). - H₂S bacteria test: a paper strip with a special medium in a bottle of water turns black in 1–2 days if fecal bacteria are present — keep it warm (above 77 °F). Agreed with lab tests about 90% of the time; sulfur well water can give false alarms (WHO, pp. 16, 33). The test bottles must be bought ahead. - Chlorine check: a faint chlorine smell 30 minutes after dosing means enough was added. - Sanitary check: look at the source — animals, outhouses, runoff upstream? Fix the source first (CAWST Testing). 📚 Go deeper: CAWST Introduction to Drinking Water Quality Testing; Turbidity tube.

🪣 Storing water safely - Covered container with a tap or narrow spout, opaque, easy to clean; never put untreated water in it; clean it with soap or chlorine; keep it off the ground in shade; pour, don't dip (CAWST, pp. 83–84). - Don't reuse milk jugs — they can't be cleaned well (OSU, p. 2). - Chlorinated water keeps best; boiled water can be recontaminated — drink it within a day or two.

🔥 After a wildfire Burned slopes send ash, metals, nitrate and organic chemicals into creeks after storms — levels jumped 10 to 10,000 times after a Colorado fire (USGS, p. 1). Boiling, chlorine, sunlight and sand or clay filters do not remove these. Fire-damaged plastic pipes can leach benzene, and boiling doesn't remove it (WQA). After a fire, prefer springs or wells outside the burn, or rainwater; distilling and charcoal are the only partial chemical barriers here. 📚 Go deeper: USGS Wildfire Effects on Source-Water Quality; OWRD — your well after wildfire.

💧 Water Wells, Pumps, Springs & Cisterns How to keep water coming when the power is out for good: understanding your well, running the well pump from a generator or solar, getting water up by hand, moving creek water uphill with no fuel (ram pumps), developing a spring, catching rain in a cistern, and keeping it all clean. The manuals are in Water-Wells-Pumps\ (Wells, Pumps-No-Grid, Hand-Ram-Rope-Pumps, Springs-Cisterns, Water-Quality, Oregon) and Water\. Making water safe to drink is in the Water Purification guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst problems - Never pour outside water into a well and never leave a well open — one bucket of creek water or a drowned animal can contaminate it (OWRD Wells and Drought). - Well pumps run on 240 volts. Shut off the breaker before touching the pressure switch or wiring, and connect a generator only through a transfer switch — never backfeed. - Don't run a flooded pump until it's dry and checked (EPA). - Test the water — clear, cold water can still carry bacteria or arsenic.

🕳️ Know your well Three kinds of wells (USGS Ground Water and the Rural Homeowner, pp. 16–17): - Dug wells: wide and shallow, often lined with rock or concrete rings. Easy to contaminate and the first to go dry in drought — but you can lower a bucket into them. - Driven wells (sand points): a pipe with a screened tip driven into shallow sand or gravel. Cheap, shallow, easily contaminated. - Drilled wells: a steel or plastic casing (usually 6 in) sealed into the ground, often hundreds of feet deep, with an electric submersible pump at the bottom. Most valley homes have this kind. About 5 gallons a minute is a normal household supply. Find your well's records. Oregon has driller's reports for most wells drilled since 1955 — Josephine County well IDs start with "JOSE". The report gives the depth, where water was found, the static water level and the tested yield — all things you need to plan a hand pump or generator (OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook, pp. 27, 30). Print it and keep it with this drive. Look it up on OWRD's Well Log Query (by owner, location or well ID) while the internet works (rule of thumb). What the ground here gives (Grants Pass area, the nearest USGS study): river gravels 5–50 gpm but easily polluted when shallow; weathered granite up to 50 gpm,

(rule of thumb). What the ground here gives (Grants Pass area, the nearest USGS study): river gravels 5–50 gpm but easily polluted when shallow; weathered granite up to 50 gpm, solid granite under 5; serpentine rock — common around the Illinois Valley — gives few if any good wells, and high-magnesium water (USGS HA-480 Plate 1; Plate 2). In summer a household uses several times its winter water. Measure your water level twice a year (spring and fall), from the same point on the casing, after the pump has rested several hours, and keep a log. A ¾-in slotted PVC measuring tube taped to the pump pipe lets a tape get past the wires (OWRD Handbook, pp. 15–16). A chalked weighted tape shows the wet line (rule of thumb). Rules worth knowing: household use up to 15,000 gallons a day, livestock water and up to ½ acre of garden need no water right (OWRD Exempt Uses). Wells must be at least 50 ft from septic tanks and 100 ft from drain fields, with the top at least 12 in above ground (OWRD Handbook, pp. 23–24). 📚 Go deeper: OWRD Water Well Owner's Handbook — Oregon's complete owner guide; USGS Ground Water and the Rural Homeowner; Wikipedia: water well.

🔌 Running the well pump without the grid From a generator (Franklin Electric AIM Manual, pp. 8–9) — a well pump needs far more power to start than to run: | Pump size | Minimum generator — 2-wire pump | 3-wire pump (has a control box) | | ½ hp | 3 kW | 2 kW | | ¾ hp | 4.5 kW | 3 kW | | 1 hp | 6 kW | 4 kW | | 1½ hp | 7.5 kW | 5 kW | - Example: a ½ hp pump runs on about 670 watts but draws over 6 times that for a moment when it starts (AIM, p. 41). The pump's size is on the control box or the well report. - Start the generator first, then the pump; switch the pump off before stopping the generator. Never let the generator run out of fuel with the pump on (AIM, p. 8). - Pump into storage — run the generator an hour or two and fill tanks, instead of running it all day. From solar: a DC solar well pump with its own panels pumps whenever the sun shines. Store water, not electricity — a tank holding about 3 days' water beats batteries for cost and upkeep (NRCS Solar-Powered Water Pump Systems, pp. 27, 29). Choose a brushless pump; brushed ones need new brushes about every

holding about 3 days' water beats batteries for cost and upkeep (NRCS Solar-Powered Water Pump Systems, pp. 27, 29). Choose a brushless pump; brushed ones need new brushes about every 2 years (Practical Action, p. 4). Pressure tank and switch (UNL G2152, pp. 2–3): the switch starts the pump at a low pressure (often 30 or 40 psi) and stops it at a high one (50 or 60). A bladder tank's air charge should be 2 psi below the start pressure, checked with the tank empty and power off. | Problem | Usual cause (AIM, p. 28) | | Pump starts and stops every few seconds | Waterlogged tank (low air charge), leak, stuck check valve | | Pump runs and won't stop | Water level below the pump, worn pump, clogged screen, broken pipe | | No water, pump silent | Breaker, pressure switch contacts, control box, wiring | | Sputtering, air in the water | Water level dropping to the pump — rest the well, use less | 📚 Go deeper: Franklin Electric AIM Manual — the pump-maker's troubleshooting bible; UNL Pumps and Pressure Tanks; NRCS solar pump design; Engines guide — generators.

✋ Getting water up by hand The suction limit: a pump at the top of a well doesn't "lift" water — air pressure pushes it up. In practice a pitcher pump or any suction pump stops working at about 20–22 ft of lift, a little less at our elevation (USDA FB 1448, p. 27; Peace Corps Wells Construction, p. 262). Deeper than that, the pumping part must be down in the water — there's no limit on pushing water up from below. | Water level | Options | | Under ~20 ft | Pitcher pump; rope pump; bucket and windlass on a dug well | | 20–150 ft | Rope pump (to about 115 ft); deep-well lift handpumps (Afridev, India Mark II up to about 160 ft) | | Deeper | Generator or solar on the existing submersible; well bucket (below) | - Rope pump: an endless rope with small pistons every meter runs up a pipe over a hand wheel. About 35 liters a minute at 33 ft, 10 at 115 ft; fits a 3-in borehole; can be built from local materials (Practica Rope Pump Handbook, pp. 8–9). - Deep-well handpumps: a cylinder set below the water on rods. Set the cylinder below the lowest water level you've measured while pumping (Afridev manual, p. 26; India Mark II manual). Commercial deep-well hand pumps can be fitted beside the electric

Set the cylinder below the lowest water level you've measured while pumping (Afridev manual, p. 26; India Mark II manual). Commercial deep-well hand pumps can be fitted beside the electric pump in a 6-in casing (rule of thumb). - Well bucket (bailer): a narrow tube about 3 in wide with a flap valve in the bottom fits down a 4–6 in casing beside the pump pipe and brings up 1–2 gallons a trip on a rope and pulley. You must open the well cap and keep everything clean — sanitize the bucket and rope, and close the well between uses (rule of thumb; no manual found). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Human-Powered Handpumps, p. 5 — which pump for which depth; Practica Rope Pump Handbook — building one; Peace Corps Wells Construction — digging and lining a well by hand; Wikipedia: rope pump.

🔁 Ram pumps: creek water uphill with no fuel A hydraulic ram uses the force of falling water in a long pipe to push part of that water much higher — day and night, with no fuel (Practical Action Hydraulic Ram Pumps). - Rule of thumb: water delivered ≈ water going in × fall ÷ lift × about 0.5. Example: 10 gallons a minute falling 20 ft into the ram can push about 0.8 gpm — roughly 1,200 gallons a day — up 100 ft (Peace Corps Hydrams, p. 66). Another: 3 gpm with a 12-ft fall lifts about 780 gallons a day to 48 ft (USDA FB 1448, pp. 24–25). - The drive pipe from the source to the ram must be straight, rigid (steel is best) and long — about 3–7 times the fall, and at least 100 times its own width (Practical Action, p. 3). - You need: a reliable flow and a few feet of fall — a creek with a small dam or a spring above the ram. The water that doesn't get pumped flows back out the waste valve. - Tune the waste valve's stroke for the best output; build one from pipe fittings with the Peace Corps manual. - Oregon water law and fish screens apply to diverting creek water — see the Engines guide creek-power section. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps Hydrams

with the Peace Corps manual. - Oregon water law and fish screens apply to diverting creek water — see the Engines guide creek-power section. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps Hydrams workshop manual — build and repair one; USDA FB 1448 — rams and windmills; Wikipedia: hydraulic ram.

🌬️ Windmills Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed (twice the wind = 8 times the power); a water-pumping windmill pays off where the average wind is above about 7 mph, and needs a storage tank for calm days (Practical Action Wind Pumping, p. 2). Sheltered valley floors here may be too calm — ridges and open ground are better (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Wind Pumping; USDA FB 1448 — windmills.

⛲ Springs A spring box collects spring water before animals and surface runoff can foul it (Virginia Tech Spring Development, p. 5): - Dig back to where the water comes out of the ground and lay a gravel-packed collection pipe or trench. - A concrete box at least 4 ft deep, sticking up 1 ft above ground, with a tight overlapping lid, an outlet pipe, a screened overflow (so animals and insects can't crawl in) and a drain for cleaning. - Dig a ditch upslope to steer surface runoff away, and fence livestock out of the area above the spring; keep outhouses and corrals at least 100 ft away. - Measure flow with a bucket and a watch; test the water and shock-chlorinate a new box (Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination). - Spring water runs by gravity to the house or garden — no pump at all if the spring is uphill. 📚 Go deeper: Virginia Tech Spring Development and Protection; EPA Manual of Individual Water Supply Systems — springs, wells and cisterns.

🛢️ Cisterns and rainwater Our winters are wet: every square foot of roof catches about 0.6 gallons per inch of rain (Texas Rainwater Harvesting, p. 34). A 1,500 sq ft roof in a 10-inch rain month could fill a 9,000-gallon tank (rule of thumb arithmetic). - First-flush diverter: dump the first dirty water off the roof — about 13–49 gallons per 1,000 sq ft (Texas, p. 13). A standpipe of 4-in pipe holds about 1 gallon per 18 in. - Size the tank for summer: almost no rain falls June–September, so store enough to carry you through. - Opaque, covered, screened tanks; clean gutters; treat roof water before drinking (Water Purification guide). Oregon rules for rain tanks: OSU EM 9448. 📚 Go deeper: Texas Manual on Rainwater Harvesting; OSU Harvesting Rainwater for the Garden.

🧪 Keeping well water clean - Test yearly for coliform bacteria and nitrate, and at least once for arsenic (treat at 10 ppb or more) (OWRD Handbook, p. 34). Without a lab, a home H₂S bacteria test helps — see the Water Purification guide. - Shock chlorination after repairs, floods or a bad test: for 5.25% bleach, about 2½ quarts for a 4-in well with 100 ft of water, 4 quarts for a 6-in well with 100 ft, 1½ gallons for 6-in with 200 ft. Run every tap until you smell chlorine, leave it 12–24 hours, flush it away from the septic system, and retest in 1–2 weeks (Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination, p. 3; OHA bulletin). - After a flood: wells under 50 ft deep or over 10 years old are probably contaminated (EPA, p. 1). - After a wildfire: check the wellhead, wiring and pipes, and test before drinking (OWRD after wildfire). - "Dry" well? Often the water only dropped below the pump — lower the pump (not to the very bottom) and fit a pump-saver switch (OWRD Wells and Drought). - Protect the wellhead: tight sanitary cap, ground sloping away, no fuel, manure or chemicals nearby (OSU Twelve Simple Things). 📚 Go deeper: OWRD Handbook — testing schedule, p. 34; Virginia Tech Shock Chlorination; OSU Twelve Simple Things to Protect Your Well Water.

⚡ EMP, Solar Storms & Faraday Cages What a nuclear electromagnetic pulse (EMP) or a severe solar storm would really do, how to protect radios, solar gear and this library, how to build and test a Faraday container, what to do when a solar-storm warning comes, and how to check and repair equipment afterward. It's based on what government tests actually measured, not internet stories. The reports are in EMP-Solar-Storms\ (Effects-and-Threat, Protection-Shielding, Grounding-Surge, Recovery). ### The short version - The danger comes in through long wires — power lines, antennas, long cables. Small gear that isn't plugged into anything mostly survives. - Unplugged, switched-off cars and trucks were not affected in tests; a few running ones stalled and restarted. - A solar storm threatens the power grid, not your phone. You'd get 1–3 days' warning. - The real long-term problem is the grid going down for months. Plan for that (see the off-grid power section of the Illinois Valley guide). - Keep spares and a second copy of this library in a metal container, sealed at the seams.

⚡ Two different threats | | Nuclear EMP (a bomb exploded high above the U.S.) | Solar storm (geomagnetic storm, like 1859, 1921, 1989, May 2024) | | Warning | None | 18–72 hours after the Sun erupts; 20–45 min final warning (CISA, p. 21) | | Parts | E1: a pulse rising in billionths of a second — hits electronics through wires and antennas. E2: like lightning over a huge area. E3: slow, seconds to minutes — like a solar storm (EMP Commission 2004, p. 13) | Like a weak, hours-long E3 only — no fast pulse | | What it hits | Electronics connected to wires/antennas; computers and control systems; the power grid | Very long conductors: power lines, big transformers, pipelines, long phone cables. Also GPS and HF radio | | What it doesn't | People (a high-altitude burst puts no radiation on the ground) | Unplugged phones, laptops, radios, cars, solar panels | Why only long wires matter in a solar storm: the storm induces a few volts per kilometer — measured worst cases are about 7–20 V/km, and under 1.1 V/km in Colorado during the May 2024 storm (Meta-R-319; LANL 2024 storm study). A 6-ft cord sees hundredths of a volt; a 100-mile power line sees hundreds to thousands (rule of thumb arithmetic). In 1989 that was enough to collapse Quebec's grid in 90 seconds

cord sees hundredths of a volt; a 100-mile power line sees hundreds to thousands (rule of thumb arithmetic). In 1989 that was enough to collapse Quebec's grid in 90 seconds and destroy a large transformer in New Jersey — and big transformers take about a year to replace (Meta-R-319, p. 149). E1 isn't the same strength everywhere: it's strongest south of the point under the burst, and averages only about a tenth of the peak over the affected area (Meta-R-320, p. 38). 📚 Go deeper: EMP Commission Executive Report — the plain overview; NOAA A Profile of Space Weather; Wikipedia: nuclear EMP · geomagnetic storm · Carrington Event.

🔬 What the tests actually found | Claim | What testing showed | | "Every car will die." | 37 cars and 18 trucks were tested up to about 50 kV/m. Vehicles that were off: no effects. Of running cars, 3 stalled (at 30 kV/m or more) and needed a restart; one had dashboard electronics damaged; most just had blinking lights. Of running trucks, 3 stalled — 2 restarted at once, 1 needed towing (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). | | "All electronics fry." | Handheld and vehicle radios — stored, idle or operating — had no damage up to 50 kV/m; some locked up and worked after switching off and on (EMP Commission 2008, p. 169). Plugged-in household gear: at 6.7 kV/m 20% were upset (fixed by power-cycling); at 16.6 kV/m about 6% were damaged — mostly items on antenna cables (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). | | "Pocket radios are useless after." | Small battery radios weren't damaged unless near cables carrying huge currents (DCPA 1975). | | "Solar panels get destroyed." | Panels hit with up to 100 kV/m showed only very minor change (Sandia, p. 39); rooftop microinverters survived 20–60 kV pulses (Sandia microinverter tests). The surge travels down the panel wires toward the charge controller/inverter — that's the part to keep a spare of. | | "A surge strip or the breaker protects me." |

surge travels down the panel wires toward the charge controller/inverter — that's the part to keep a spare of. | | "A surge strip or the breaker protects me." | Lightning-rated surge suppressors don't stop E1 (Sandia TVSS tests); circuit breakers survive but give no real protection — some pulse passes even when they're off (Sandia, p. 6). | | "Ham radios are toast." | 15 ham stations survived repeated simulated pulses when the power cord was unplugged and the coax disconnected; with protectors on both lines they were also fine (NCS TIB 85-10). | | "Networked computers will be fine." | They're the weak point — dispatch computers began failing at 3–6 kV/m, and every industrial control system tested failed (EMP Commission 2008). | 📚 Go deeper: EMP Commission Critical Infrastructures Report — vehicles, p. 131; Consumer Electronics Testing.

🔌 Rule one: unplug and disconnect Wires are the antennas. Even a few feet of cable can pick up thousands of volts from E1; long power and antenna lines pick up far more (Low Cost EMP Protection (Navy 1982)). (CISA guidelines, p. 44) - Unplug at the device — power, data and antenna cables — not just at the wall. Coil any cable you can't remove. - Pull battery packs from small electronics in storage; turn phones and radios off and take them off chargers. - Disconnect outdoor antennas and coax from radios when not in use. - Unplug everything or nothing: pulling only a TV's power cord while it stays on cable or phone lines removes its ground path (NIST Surges Happen, p. 11). - Backup generators: don't leave one connected to the grid through an automatic transfer switch without strong surge protection — the utility line can carry the pulse in (CISA, p. 45). A generator stored disconnected is far better off. - Surge protectors still help with lightning and the surge when power comes back — just don't count on them for E1. Keep spare protectors and fuses. 📚 Go deeper: CISA EMP Protection and Resilience Guidelines — Level 1 steps, p. 44; NIST Surges Happen; MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 2 — grounding and surge arresters.

🗑️ Faraday containers: building one that works How it works: a closed metal shell keeps the pulse on the outside. It only works if the shell is continuous — the leaks are at seams, lid edges and holes, and a long narrow slot leaks far more than a round hole. Seams must be bare metal touching bare metal (no paint) (MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1, p. 275). A plain metal box is not automatically a Faraday cage — ordinary cabinets gave little protection until their seams were taped and gasketed (Navy 1982). Options, best to simplest (CISA, pp. 45, 86): 1. Metal can with a tight metal lid (galvanized trash can, paint can, cookie tin, steel ammo can): - Wrap each item in a plastic or paper bag or cardboard so it doesn't touch the metal. - Seal the lid seam with conductive tape (aluminum or copper foil tape — the kind with conductive glue) all the way around. Trash cans leak at the lid, handles and base unless sealed. - Ammo cans: the rubber gasket breaks metal contact — scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes. 2. Foil wrap: item in a plastic bag, then 2 or more layers of heavy-duty foil, every seam folded and overlapped, any cables

No wires passing through. Don't drill holes. 2. Foil wrap: item in a plastic bag, then 2 or more layers of heavy-duty foil, every seam folded and overlapped, any cables inside the wrap. 3. Nesting adds protection: a foil-wrapped item inside a sealed metal can is better than either alone. 4. Microwave oven (unplugged, never switched on): an expedient shield for small items — test it first. Weak or useless: Mylar food bags (little protection); refrigerators (plastic liner and rubber gasket); many cheap "Faraday bags" (the closure leaks). Does it need a ground wire? No — a closed storage container doesn't need to be grounded (rule of thumb). How good is good enough? For stored spare electronics, CISA considers 20 dB of shielding adequate (CISA appendix, p. 126); critical military gear uses 80 dB (DHS 2022). Testing yours (and what it doesn't prove): - Put a phone inside and call it, and a battery AM/FM radio tuned to a station. If the call won't ring and the radio goes silent, the shell has no big leaks at those frequencies. - This is a rough check, not a measurement — silence just means the signal dropped below what the radio can hear. The AM test matters most (low frequencies are hardest to block). Close the lid the same way every time (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: CISA guidelines — foil

hear. The AM test matters most (low frequencies are hardest to block). Close the lid the same way every time (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: CISA guidelines — foil and container methods, pp. 45 & 86; MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1 — seams and slots, p. 275; Wikipedia: Faraday cage.

📦 What to keep in it From CISA's list plus practical extras (rule of thumb where not cited): - A second copy of this library on a USB drive or small SSD — and a cheap laptop or tablet with its charger to read it. - Battery AM/FM/NOAA weather radio, and a handheld ham or GMRS radio with a spare antenna (CISA, p. 44). - Spare solar charge controller and a small inverter — the parts of a solar system most at risk. - Multimeter, LED flashlights/headlamps, rechargeable batteries and a small USB solar charger. - Spare fuses (vehicle, equipment, solar), spare surge protectors and MOVs. - Small spare electronics you depend on (a phone, a radio's spare power supply). - For older vehicles, a spare ignition module or electronic part if you can get one. Handheld gear with no long wires attached is fairly tough anyway; the container is cheap insurance (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: ORNL — radio communications and spare-equipment procedures; Radio guide.

☀️ When a solar-storm warning comes NOAA rates geomagnetic storms G1 to G5 (NOAA Space Weather Scales): | Level | How often (per 11-year cycle) | What happens | | G3 strong | ~200 | Grid voltage corrections; GPS and HF radio come and go; auroras as far south as Oregon | | G4 severe | ~100 | Widespread grid voltage problems; some protection systems trip; GPS degraded for hours | | G5 extreme | ~4 | Grid collapse and transformer damage possible; HF radio out 1–2 days; GPS degraded for days | For a G4–G5 warning (rule of thumb): 1. Charge batteries, power banks, radios and laptops; fill water containers; get fuel. 2. Unplug sensitive electronics from the wall — the risk is outages and surges when power returns. 3. Disconnect long outdoor antennas and feedlines. 4. Expect GPS and HF radio to be unreliable; have paper maps (Maps\) and use VHF/UHF locally. 5. Solar panels don't need protecting from a solar storm — their wiring is far too short. (S5 "solar panel damage" on NOAA's scale means satellites.) 6. Have the generator ready, connected only through a transfer switch or interlock — never backfeed. 📚 Go deeper: NOAA scales, p. 1; LANL May 2024 storm study; Wikipedia: May 2024 solar storms.

🔧 After an event: check and repair 1. Power-cycle anything that's locked up — in tests most "upsets" cleared this way (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). 2. Vehicles: restart. If one won't run, disconnect the battery for several minutes to reset the electronics, then check fuses (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). 3. Fuses and breakers: a surge protector firing can blow the equipment's fuse — check and replace. Breakers are likely fine; reset them (ORNL radio study; Sandia breakers). 4. Surge protectors fail one of two ways: no power, or power with no protection left. Replace any that took a hit (NIST Surges Happen, p. 7). 5. Look and sniff: burnt smell, scorch marks, swollen or leaking capacitors. Discharge big capacitors before touching (inverters, microwaves, power supplies). 6. Radios: if dead, suspect the antenna input stage and power supply first — those took the damage in tests (ORNL radio study). 7. Solar: panels are probably fine; test the charge controller and inverter; swap in shielded spares. 8. Generators: check the output breaker, brushes and voltage regulator — see the Engines guide. 9. Expect the grid to stay down a long time — the EMP Commission expected months to years for recovery (Executive Report, p. 27). Switch to off-grid power, radios and the rest of this library. 🌱 Your Seed Bank: Grow, Harvest and Save Seed How to keep a heirloom seed bank alive for good in the Illinois Valley: store it so it lasts, test it, plant each variety at the right time here, keep varieties from crossing, and save your own seed every year — including seed from the fruits (tomatoes, cucumbers, melons, squash, peppers). It ends with the calorie crops the kit is missing and how to propagate fruit trees and berries, whose seeds don't grow true. The manuals are in Gardening-Food\Seed-Saving, Gardening-Food\Fruit-Propagation and the rest of Gardening-Food\. Written for the Heaven's Harvest "10 Year" seed bank. The company's list has 39 varieties (they note some may be swapped when seed is short), so check your own packets — the rules below are by crop, so they still apply. ### The five rules of a seed bank 1. Don't plant it all. Plant part of each packet; keep the rest sealed as a backup. 2. Start saving seed in year one — the short-lived ones first: onions, leeks, sweet corn, peppers and okra keep only 1–2 years. 3. Test germination every winter so you know what still sprouts before you need it. 4. Know which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes,

which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes, dry beans, a flour corn and grains. Every variety in this kit is open-pollinated (heirloom): seed you save grows the same plant as long as it didn't cross with a relative. Hybrids ("F1" on a packet) don't come true — don't save from those. (OSA Seed Saving Guide, p. 5)

🗄️ Keeping the seed bank alive Seed dies from heat and damp. Two rules from seed-storage research (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9): - Every 10 °F cooler roughly doubles seed life. - Every 1% less moisture in the seed roughly doubles it too. - Quick test for a storage spot: temperature (°F) + relative humidity (%) should add up to less than 100. (OSA, p. 17) Where to keep it here: - Not in a shed, garage, attic or vehicle — Illinois Valley summers top 100 °F. - Best: the coolest, driest room of the house, a closet on a north wall, or a dry root cellar. - Fridge or freezer only for very dry seed in an airtight jar. Let the jar warm to room temperature before opening, or moisture condenses on the cold seed. Very dry seed (about 5% moisture) held below 20 °F still sprouted well after 20 years. (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9) - Once you open a Mylar packet, reseal it, or move the seed into a glass jar with a desiccant packet (silica gel). Label every jar with the variety and year. Store spare seed in the freezer. | | 3 | Asparagus, beans, broccoli, carrot, celery, pea, spinach | Grow out and replace by year 3. | | 4 | Beet, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower, eggplant, kale, mustard, pumpkin, rutabaga, squash, tomato, turnip, watermelon | Replace by year 4. | | 5–6 | Cantaloupe, collards, cucumber, radish (5), lettuce (6) | The long keepers. | The "10 year" label is possible only with very cool, dry storage — in ordinary storage most of these last 3–5 years, so a seed bank survives by being grown and re-saved, not by sitting. 📚 Go deeper: OSA — where and how to store seed, p. 17; Seed Processing and Storage — drying with silica gel, p. 9; Seed Ambassadors zine — drying and freezing, p. 7.

🧪 Germination test ("rag doll") Do this every winter, and before planting any packet more than a year old. (OSA, p. 18; Univ. of Illinois, p. 1) 1. Dampen a paper towel — damp, not dripping. 2. Lay out 10 seeds (more is more accurate) spaced apart, roll the towel up, and put it in a plastic bag with a little air. Label it. 3. Keep it warm: about 70 °F for most crops; 75–80 °F for peppers, eggplant, melons. Lettuce and celery sprout better with some light. 4. Check from day 3; remove sprouted and moldy seeds and count them. Slow crops (peppers, parsley-type seeds) can take up to 3 weeks. 5. Read the result: 10 of 10 — plant normally. 7–9 — sow thicker. 6 or fewer — this packet is failing: plant it now and save fresh seed this year. Fresh spinach, lettuce and pepper seed can be dormant for a few months — retest before giving up on it. 📚 Go deeper: OSA germination test, p. 18; McCormack — germination testing, p. 20.

🏡 Growing it here - Raised beds with good soil. Many valley soils are serpentine (high magnesium, low calcium) or slow-draining clay. Build raised beds, get a soil test before adding amendments, and add lots of compost. (OSU Soil Test Guide; Improving Garden Soils) - Water is the summer limit. Only 5–7 in of rain falls April–September. Rogue Valley gardens can lose ½ inch of water a day in hot wind (Growing Your Own, p. 21). Apply 1–1.5 in per watering (EC 871, p. 9), use drip lines, and mulch thickly. - Frost pockets: cold air drains to low ground. Plant warm crops on the warmest, sunniest ground you have, and keep row cover or old sheets ready for late-May frosts. - Heat: lettuce, spinach and cabbage-family crops bolt or go bitter in July heat. Grow them in spring and fall, or under shade cloth on the north side of taller crops. - Deer and gophers: a 7–8 ft fence for deer; hardware-cloth bottoms on raised beds or wire baskets around roots for gophers (rule of thumb). - Bugs: encourage beneficial insects rather than spraying (PNW 550). 📚 Go deeper: Growing Your Own — Rogue Valley section, p. 21; Drip Irrigation in the Food Garden; Food Gardening with Less Water; Josephine County soil survey.

❌ Which of your seeds cross — and what to do Plants that are pollinated by insects or wind cross with relatives of the same species flowering nearby. The seed looks fine; the next generation is a mix. Self-pollinating crops rarely cross. Rutabaga crosses with them only rarely, but separate it anyway (zine, p. 16) | | Squash (C. pepo) | Zucchini × crookneck × Jack O'Lantern pumpkin | One per year, or hand-pollinate (below). ✋ Hand-pollinating and caging Squash, pumpkin and cucumber — save pure seed even when relatives grow nearby (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 12): 1. In the evening, find male and female flowers that will open tomorrow (yellow showing at the tips; the female has a tiny fruit behind the flower). Tape or tie them shut. 2. Next morning, once the dew is off, pick a male flower, peel back its petals, and rub its pollen onto the center of the opened female — use 2–3 males. 3. Tape the female shut again and tie a tag or yarn on its stem. Save seed only from tagged fruit. Corn: cover young ear shoots with paper bags before silks appear; when silks show, bag a tassel that's shedding pollen, shake the pollen into the bag the next morning, pour it onto the silks and re-bag (OSA sweet corn guide, p. 6). Cabbage family, carrots, peppers: cover them with a cage of row cover on hoops. Cabbage-family plants need insects to set seed (they can't pollinate themselves), so put flies or bees in the cage — or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12–17; OSA sweet corn hand pollination, pp. 5–8; Isolation Distances — caging, p. 17.

🍅 Saving seed from the fruits Fruit crops have wet seed: let the fruit get riper than you'd eat it, scoop out the seeds, clean them, and dry them. (OSA, pp. 15–16, 21–24) Tomatoes — ferment them: 1. Pick fully ripe fruit from several healthy plants of the variety. 2. Squeeze the seeds and juice into a jar; add a little water if thick. Label it. 3. Leave it at about 70–80 °F for 2–3 days, stirring 2–3 times a day. A white mold on top is normal — it eats the gel coat that keeps seed from sprouting. Stop before any seed sprouts, and keep it out of high heat (liquid in the high 80s °F can kill half the seed). (Tomato Seed Production, p. 11) 4. Add water and stir: good seed sinks; pour off the mold, pulp and floaters. Rinse in a strainer. 5. Spread thin on a plate or screen to dry (paper towels stick). Cucumbers: leave the fruit on the vine 4–5 weeks past eating stage, until it's big, yellow to orange-brown and slightly soft. Scrape the seeds and pulp into a jar and ferment about 3 days at 70–75 °F like tomatoes; good seed sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 18) Melons and watermelon: seed is ripe when the fruit is ripe to eat. Scoop the seeds, rinse them in a strainer (watermelon can ferment

sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 18) Melons and watermelon: seed is ripe when the fruit is ripe to eat. Scoop the seeds, rinse them in a strainer (watermelon can ferment 2–3 days), and dry. (OSA, pp. 22, 24) Squash and pumpkins: leave on the vine until hard — a thumbnail won't dent it — and the stem dries. Summer squash for seed gets "about the size of your leg." Then store winter squash and pumpkins about 2 months (summer squash a few weeks) before cutting them open: the seed keeps filling out. Scoop, rinse, dry. Ferment no more than a day, if at all. (OSA, p. 24; Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 15) Peppers: pick at full color (red for both kit peppers), hold them 7–10 days at room temperature, then cut them open and scrape out the seeds. Good seed is ivory, not brown. Seed from green peppers often won't sprout. Wear gloves for jalapeños. (OSA, p. 23; Pepper Seed Production, p. 9) Eggplant: leave the fruit until it turns dull brown and hard, 2–3 weeks past eating. Grate or blend the seedy end with water; good seed sinks. (OSA, p. 21) Drying all of them: a thin layer out of direct sun, below 95 °F (dark seeds in sun can overheat at 80 °F), stirred daily. Small seeds are dry when they snap instead of bend. 🫘 Saving seed from dry crops These dry on the plant; harvest, thresh (beat or stomp the seed out), and winnow (pour in a breeze to blow off chaff). (OSA, pp. 19–24) - Beans and peas: let pods dry on the plant; pull plants when 70–80% of pods have turned color and finish drying under cover. Freeze shelled seed 3 days to kill bean weevils. (zine, p. 6) - Lettuce: let a few of the best plants bolt (don't save from the first to bolt). When heads look fluffy ("feathered"), shake them into a paper bag; repeat a week or two later. In our hot summers, lettuce must flower by May or early June or seed set suffers. (OSA, p. 21; Climatic Considerations — Rogue Valley, p. 19) - Radish: dig the best roots, replant them, and let them flower; harvest when 60–70% of pods are brown and papery. (OSA, p. 23) - Spinach: sow early (it bolts as days lengthen); harvest when most seed is brown. (OSA, p. 23) - Onions and leeks: cut the seed head when about a quarter-sized patch of black seeds shows; dry 10–14 days on paper. (OSA, p. 22) - Sweet corn: let ears dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Save from at least 100 plants if you can — corn weakens fast when inbred. (zine, p.

dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Save from at least 100 plants if you can — corn weakens fast when inbred. (zine, p. 9) - Okra: let a few pods dry on the plant until they rattle. - Asparagus: female plants make red berries in fall; mash, rinse and dry the black seeds. 📚 Go deeper: OSA crop-by-crop tips, pp. 19–24; OSA Bean Seed Production; OSA Lettuce Seed Production; OSA Spinach Seed Production.

🥕 Biennials: seed in the second year Carrots, beets, onions, leeks, celery, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, collards, kale, turnips and rutabagas flower only after a winter — they need 8–12 weeks below 50 °F. (OSA, p. 4) - Leave them in the ground where winters rarely drop below about 14 °F — true for most of the valley, but use well-drained raised beds so roots don't rot, and watch for voles. - Or dig and store the best roots ("stecklings") at 35–38 °F and high humidity — in moist sand in a root cellar — and replant them in early spring. This lets you choose the best-looking roots. (OSA, p. 4; OSA Carrot Seed Production, p. 7) - Carrots for seed: sow in June, not April, so roots are small going into winter (small roots survive cold better). (zine, p. 15) - Cabbage: overwinter a loose, full-size head; in spring cut an X in the top so the flower stalk can get out. Kale and collards: sow June 20–July 15 and overwinter them in place. (OSA, pp. 20–21) - Beets: small roots (1–1.5 in) overwinter best. (OSA Beet Seed Production) 📚 Go deeper: OSA Carrot Seed Production; OSA Beet Seed Production; Climatic Considerations — Rogue Valley, pp. 19–20.

🌾 Filling the calorie gap This kit is mostly vegetables — vitamins and variety, but not many calories. To live from a garden you also need: - Potatoes — the most food per square foot in this climate. Save your own "seed potatoes": keep healthy, egg-sized tubers cool and dark over winter (rule of thumb). - Dry beans — protein that stores for years. Your Provider and Blue Lake beans can be left to dry and eaten as dry beans. (OSU Preserving Dry Beans) - Winter squash — your butternut and pumpkin store for months. - Flour or flint corn — Golden Bantam is a sweet corn; it dries for parched corn but makes poor meal. - Grains (wheat, oats, barley) and garlic — see the Food From Scratch guide for growing, threshing and milling. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics — Food; Growing Your Own — amounts for a family of four, p. 9.

🍎 Fruit trees and berries: seeds don't come true An apple seed grows a new, different apple tree — usually a poor one. Fruit trees are kept true by grafting a twig ("scion") of the variety you want onto a rootstock. (Univ. of Minnesota Grafting and Budding; Univ. of Kentucky, p. 1) - Grow rootstocks from seed: apple and pear seeds need 70–90 days cold and moist (in damp sand or a damp paper towel in a sealed bag in the fridge); peach 90–120 days. Then plant them; graft when the seedling is about pencil-thick. (Mississippi State Basic Grafting, p. 3) - Collect scionwood while trees are dormant (here, January–February, before buds swell): last year's growth, pencil-thick, a foot or more long. Wrap in damp (not wet) paper towel or sawdust in a sealed bag, label it, and keep it at 34–38 °F. Never store scions with apples or pears — the gas they give off ruins them. (Mississippi State, p. 3; Kentucky, p. 4) - When to graft: whip-and-tongue Feb–early March while dormant; cleft graft late Feb–March; bark graft in spring once the bark slips. Budding (a single bud under the bark) in July–September. (Mississippi State, pp. 3–4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43) - Peaches and apricots from seed often give usable fruit, but not the same as the parent (rule of thumb). - Berries and grapes are easier:

FB 1567, p. 43) - Peaches and apricots from seed often give usable fruit, but not the same as the parent (rule of thumb). - Berries and grapes are easier: - Raspberries and blackberries: bury a cane tip in late summer — it roots ("tip layering") — or dig suckers. (Virginia Tech, p. 4) - Strawberries: root the runners. (Virginia Tech, p. 5) - Grapes: dormant hardwood cuttings. (USDA Grape Propagation) - Currants, gooseberries, apple rootstocks: mound or stool layering. 🥔 Root Cellars & Food Storage Without Power How to keep a year's harvest with no refrigerator: root cellars, storage rooms, pits and buried barrels, cooling with water and evaporation, sun and solar drying, curing and smoking meat, fermenting, and keeping eggs. The manuals are in Food-Storage\ (Root-Cellars-Pits, Cooling-Without-Power, Drying, Curing-Smoking, Fermenting-Eggs-Vinegar); canning and freezing are in Gardening-Food\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent food poisoning and losses - Low-acid food in sealed jars needs pressure canning — never "water bath" or "oven can" vegetables, meat or beans, and never can wild mushrooms. Follow the USDA canning guide exactly. - Cured meat needs exact amounts. Weigh salt and any curing salt (nitrite/saltpeter) — too little lets meat spoil, too much nitrite is poisonous. Follow one tested recipe; don't mix them. - Cold-smoked fish is not cooked. Hot-smoke fish to 150–160 °F inside for 30 minutes (PNW 238) unless it's heavily salted and dried. - Green potatoes are toxic — store potatoes in the dark and cut away green parts. - Check stored food weekly. One rotting apple or potato spreads; remove it at once.

🌡️ The Illinois Valley problem: warm ground Old root-cellar books assume cold ground. Deep soil stays near the average yearly air temperature, and across most of the U.S. that's 49–58 °F; at 6 ft down clay still swings about ±11 °F through the year (MSU Earth Tempering, p. 2). Here the yearly average is roughly 54 °F (rule of thumb, from Cave Junction's average highs and lows). So: - A cellar here idles around 50–58 °F. That's perfect for winter squash, pumpkins, sweet potatoes, and fine for a few weeks of most other crops. - To get it down to the 32–40 °F that potatoes, carrots, cabbage and apples want, you must cool it with cold night air in winter: open the vents on cold nights, close them on warm days (USDA FB 1939 (1960), p. 5; Agriculture Canada Pub. 1478, p. 12). November–February nights here regularly fall into the 20s and 30s. - In a 50–60 °F space, root crops keep only 3–4 weeks loose — about twice as long packed in damp (not wet) sand or soil (USDA FB 1939 (1943), pp. 29–30). - Mild winters are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below), so you need less cellar than people in cold country. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) — storage in a 50–60 °F space, p. 29;

all winter (see below), so you need less cellar than people in cold country. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) — storage in a 50–60 °F space, p. 29; MSU Earth Tempering — ground temperature map, p. 2; PNW 548 — winter vegetables west of the Cascades.

Below about 38 °F they turn sweet; above 40 °F they sprout sooner; they freeze near 30 °F. Keep them dark. (USDA Ag Handbook 66, p. 517) - Winter squash and pumpkins: cure about 2 weeks at 80–85 °F (a sunny porch in October), then store at 50–55 °F — colder than 50 °F damages them. (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 30; AH 66, p.

weeks at 80–85 °F (a sunny porch in October), then store at 50–55 °F — colder than 50 °F damages them. (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 30; AH 66, p. 525) - Sweet potatoes: cure about 10 days at 85 °F and high humidity, then store at 50–55 °F (USDA FB 1442). - Garlic: keeps 1–2 months at room temperature, 9+ months near freezing (AH 66, p. 343). - Nuts: dry hazelnuts to a crisp kernel; they keep about 2 years below 50 °F (AH 66, p. 761). 🏗️ Building a root cellar The essentials (Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar, pp. 2–6; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar): 1. Drainage first. Pick a slope or high ground. On the wet valley floor, build at or above ground level and heap earth over it rather than digging into a winter water table; lay a drain pipe along the footings (Novia, pp. 8–9). 2. Earth cover: at least 3½ ft of soil and straw over the roof (layers of ~6 in straw and 8–12 in soil), carried well past the sides. Add soil as the straw rots. 3. Two vents at opposite ends, about 12 in square for a 10×14 ft cellar: - Intake: brings outside air down to about 1½ ft above the floor. - Outlet: starts at the ceiling and rises well above the roof (warm air leaves high). - Both adjustable, and screened against rodents and insects. 4. Double doors about 4 ft apart act as an air lock. Face the door north and keep it shaded so summer sun doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13–14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel — it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around everything. 6. A thermometer and a humidity gauge inside (or a wet rag test: if things shrivel, it's too dry — sprinkle the floor). Simpler options: - Basement-corner storage room: about 10×10 ft with an outside window. Insulate the two inside walls and the ceiling (vapor barrier on the warm side), and run an intake duct from the window down to about 18 in above the floor (Pub. 1478, pp. 8–12). - Above-ground and part-underground cellars: plans in USDA FB 1939 (1960). - Unheated outbuilding, porch or garage: works for squash, onions and dry goods — not for the cold & moist group. 📚 Go deeper: Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar — full plan, p. 2; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar — photo step by step; USDA FB 1939 (1943) — cellars, pits and banks; Wikipedia: root cellar.

🕳️ Pits, clamps, buried barrels — and the garden itself - Cone pit (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 16): on well-drained ground, dig 6–8 in deep, line with straw or leaves, pile the vegetables in a cone, cover with straw, then 2–3 in of earth, thickened as winter comes. Leave a tuft of straw sticking out the top as a vent and cap it with a board. Open a pit all at once and use a new spot each year (FB 1939 (1960), p. 9). - Clamp (long mound) for potatoes: a straw bed, a vent duct along the bottom, about 8 in of packed straw and up to 12 in of soil; in mild climates use more straw and less soil (FAO Prevention of Post-Harvest Losses). - Buried barrel or trash can: a clean food-safe barrel laid in the ground on a slant so water runs out, mouth facing the path, covered with straw and earth (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 18). Line or wrap it with ¼-inch hardware cloth against gophers and voles (rule of thumb). - Leave it in the ground: parsnips, carrots, beets, leeks, kale, collards and rutabagas can stay in the garden through most Illinois Valley winters — in raised or ridged beds so roots don't rot in waterlogged soil, with straw over the roots in hard cold (FB 1939 (1960), pp. 14–17; PNW 548).

Valley winters — in raised or ridged beds so roots don't rot in waterlogged soil, with straw over the roots in hard cold (FB 1939 (1960), pp. 14–17; PNW 548). Gophers and voles are the main risk. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) — pits, banks and barrels, pp. 16–18; FAO — potato clamps.

❄️ Cooling without power - Springhouse: water from a spring or deep well sits near ground temperature — about 52–55 °F here (rule of thumb). Run it through an insulated tank or a shaded stone trough and stand crocks, milk cans and butter in it (USDA FB 976). See springhouse. - Evaporative cooler — made for our dry summers: a screened cabinet covered in flannel or burlap, kept wet by wicks from a pan of water on top, in shade and breeze. In hot, dry weather it can hold about 50 °F inside; it works poorly in humid weather (USDA The Iceless Refrigerator). Bigger versions use a wall of wet charcoal, or a double brick wall with wet sand between (about 400 bricks keeps 220 lb of produce), wetted twice a day (Practical Action Evaporative Cooling, p. 2). The clay-pot zeer is the small version (Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools). - Ice house: ice packed in at least 15 in of sawdust on all sides, on a drained floor, keeps through summer (USDA FB 475, pp. 6, 12–13). Valley ponds rarely freeze thick, but the bulletin shows freezing ice in metal cans on cold nights. Realistically a small ice store is a winter-only luxury here. 📚 Go deeper: USDA The Iceless Refrigerator; Practical Action — charcoal and brick coolers; USDA FB 475 Ice Houses.

☀️ Drying food Our hot, dry late summer is ideal drying weather. Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air; dependable drying needs several days in a row near 95 °F (PNW 651, p. 16). - Trays: wooden frames with food-safe screen (not galvanized); cover with cheesecloth or netting against insects; bring trays in at night so dew doesn't re-wet the food (USDA FB 984, pp. 13–14). - Solar dryer: a dark box with a clear top, vents low and high, and screened trays — a 3×6 ft dryer serves a household of 4–6 (Practical Action A Simple Solar Dryer); more designs in the Peace Corps solar food technologies manual and Practical Action Solar Drying. - Is it dry? Fruit is leathery with no moist center; vegetables are brittle. Squeeze a handful of fruit: it should spring apart "like rubber bands." Then condition it 1–2 weeks in a covered jar, shaking daily — if moisture beads up, dry it more (USDA FB 984, p. 47; PNW 651, pp. 17–19). - Don't dry outdoors in wildfire smoke — ash settles on the food (rule of thumb). - Jerky: PNW 632. Store everything dry in sealed jars. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 651 Drying Project Manual — fruit-by-fruit and vegetable-by-vegetable; USDA FB 984 Farm and Home Drying — sun driers and evaporators.

🥓 Curing and smoking meat Dry-cured country ham and bacon keep without refrigeration once cured, smoked and aged. - Cure in the cold season: meat must stay 36–40 °F for the whole cure — warmer risks spoilage, colder stops the salt from soaking in (USDA Curing Pork Country Style, p. 5). Here that means December–February, in a cellar or shed vented on cold nights. Carver's bulletin covers curing where winters are too warm (Carver 1912). - The cure: about 8 lb salt + 2 lb sugar per 100 lb of meat, rubbed in, repeated after about a week; 1½–2 days per pound of ham (Virginia Tech 458-223, p. 3; Kentucky ASC-213). Curing salt (nitrite) must be weighed exactly — use a commercial premix by its label. - Smoke with hardwood (never pine) at 100–120 °F for cured pork (Leaflet 273, p. 8). A barrel smoker at the top of a sloping covered trench, fire at the bottom, is the simplest smokehouse (USDA AWI-68). - Store: wrap cooled hams, bag in muslin or paper, and hang in a dark, dry, airy, rat-proof place; skipper flies don't breed below 45 °F (Leaflet 273, p. 8). - Fish: dry-salting keeps longer than brining in warm weather (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 5); hot-smoke fish to safe temperatures (PNW 238). 📚 Go deeper: Kentucky How to Make a Country Ham — modern step by step;

in warm weather (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 5); hot-smoke fish to safe temperatures (PNW 238). 📚 Go deeper: Kentucky How to Make a Country Ham — modern step by step; USDA Curing Pork Country Style; Fishery Leaflet 18; Wikipedia: country ham.

🥬 Fermenting, salting, eggs and vinegar - Sauerkraut: 2½% salt — 1 lb salt to 40 lb cabbage (about 3 Tbsp per 5 lb); pack in a crock, weight it so brine covers the cabbage, skim scum. Ferment 3–4 weeks at 70–75 °F or 5–6 weeks at 60–65 °F; below 60 °F it may not ferment, above 75 °F it goes soft (USDA FB 1438, p. 14; USDA canning Guide 6). Old bulletins say 86 °F and paraffin seals — don't. - Salted vegetables (beans, greens, corn) in crocks: recipes in the 1918 Food Administration bulletin. - Eggs for 6–9 months: fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs in a crock of 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, with 2 in of liquid over them; or clear lime water. Prick the shell before boiling (USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs). - Vinegar: fruit juice → alcohol (yeast) → vinegar (air-loving bacteria). Leave the container open to air under cheesecloth and keep it at least 70 °F (USDA FB 1424). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1438 Fermented Pickles and Sauerkraut; USDA canning Guide 6 — fermented foods; Wikipedia: sauerkraut.

🐀 Keeping rats, mice and bugs out - Mice get through ¼-inch gaps. Use ¼-inch hardware cloth on vents and storage bins (rule of thumb); line corncribs and grain bins with galvanized hardware cloth (USDA Rat Proofing Buildings, p. 10). - Foundations: concrete curtain walls 2 ft below ground, and metal or stucco on lath 2 ft up the walls, stop burrowing rats (Rat Proofing, p. 8). - Grain, beans and dried food in metal or glass with tight lids. Freeze dry beans and grain 3 days (or heat them) to kill weevils — not the old chemical fumigants. - Cats, traps and tidiness — no open feed, no clutter for nesting. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Rat Proofing Buildings and Premises; Food From Scratch — storing grain.

Cure onions and garlic in shade, then braid or bag. | | Oct | Cure winter squash and pumpkins on a sunny porch, then into a 50–55 °F room. Cure potatoes 1–2 weeks, then into the dark. | | Nov | Start night-venting the cellar as nights drop into the 30s. Move apples, potatoes, carrots, beets and cabbage in as it cools. Mulch roots left in the garden. | | Dec–Feb | Coldest stretch: cure hams and bacon; make sauerkraut slowly; check stored food weekly. | | Mar–Apr | Use up cellar crops before they sprout; replant the best roots for seed (see the Seed Bank guide). 🐴 Horses, Mules and Draft Animals How to keep, feed, handle, ride, shoe and pack horses, mules and donkeys, and how to put them to work in harness — written for a time when there may be no feed store, vet or farrier. The manuals are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ (Care-Feeding, Riding-Training, Hoof-Care-Shoeing, Packing-Travel, Draft-Harness). Horse health, vital signs, colic and first aid are in Animals\ and the Animals and vet care section of the Illinois Valley page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - A horse can kill you without meaning to. Stay where it can see you, speak before you touch it, keep a hand on it as you move around the hindquarters, and never stand directly behind or in front of it. - Never wrap a lead rope or reins around your hand or body, and never tie a horse with a knot you can't pull loose. Never tie with a chain lead. (4-H Horse Project PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety) - Wear a helmet and boots with a heel when riding. - The old books here (1867–1940s) teach good handling and shoeing but also harsh "breaking" methods and dangerous old medicines (purges, firing, chloroform). Use them for skills, not for doctoring.

🐎 Choosing an animal - For a first horse, pick an older, calm, well-trained one over a young or green horse — the 4-H manual says 6 to 18 years suits most purposes, and "a young horse and an inexperienced rider do not learn together" (PNW 587, p. 24). For hard work, not much under 5; with good care many stay useful past 20 (USDA FB 779, p. 8). Check it sound before you take it: walk and trot it on hard ground, look for limping, swellings, bad feet and bad habits. (USDA How to Select a Sound Horse) - Age by the teeth: after about 12 years the front teeth turn triangular and slant forward. (USDA AIB 353, p. 18; PNW 587, p. 48) - Mules are tough, sure-footed, eat less and handle heat and rough country better; they tend to stand and fight rather than bolt. A well-trained mule is very steady; a badly trained one is hard work. Donkeys need shelter always — their coats aren't waterproof, which matters in our wet winters. (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 44) - Who's who: a mule is a mare bred to a jack (male donkey); a hinny is a jenny bred to a stallion and is smaller and rarer. Mules are hardy but can still founder, and they fret if stabled long or kept alone. Donkeys live just over 30

bred to a stallion and is smaller and rarer. Mules are hardy but can still founder, and they fret if stabled long or kept alone. Donkeys live just over 30 years and should be kept with a companion. (Donkey Care Handbook, pp. 15–19) 📚 Go deeper: 4-H Horse Project (PNW 587) — choosing a horse, breeds, behavior; USDA How to Select a Sound Horse — unsoundness, blemishes and vices to check; Donkey Care Handbook — how donkeys and mules differ from horses; USDA Mule Production — breeding and raising mules.

🌾 Feeding and water - Total feed: 1.5–2.5% of body weight a day, most of it hay or pasture. Never less than 8–10 lb of hay a day for a 1,000-lb horse; an idle horse holds weight on about 18 lb of good hay. (Nebraska G1781, pp. 1–2; FM 25-5, p. 101) - Weigh a horse with a string: weight (lb) = heart girth (in) × heart girth (in) × body length (in) ÷ 330. Body length is point of shoulder to point of buttock. (G1781, p. 1) - Working horses: about 1.1 lb grain + 1.25 lb hay per 100 lb of body weight a day, grain split into 3 feeds. Keep each grain meal under about 5 lb for a 1,000-lb horse. Feed by weight: a quart of oats ≈ 1 lb, a quart of corn ≈ 1.7 lb. (USDA FB1419, p. 9; G1781, p. 3; UGA B1356) - Water: 5–15 gallons a day, double in heat or hard work (an idle horse drinks about 10–12 — G1781, p. 4). Give an exhausted horse small drinks every 5–10 minutes until it recovers. In cold weather, take the chill off the water or salt the feed (1–2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: about 3 oz a day; loose salt-mineral beats a block. Western Oregon soils are low in

it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: about 3 oz a day; loose salt-mineral beats a block. Western Oregon soils are low in selenium — use a mineral that contains it. (Rule of thumb) (AIB 353; UGA B1356, p. 3) - Army feeding rules that prevent colic: water before feeding (or wait an hour after); never grain a hot horse (hay is fine); a little hay before grain; change feeds gradually over 1–2 weeks; never feed moldy or dusty hay. - Turning out onto lush spring grass: a few hours a day for 2–3 days, then half days for 2–3 days, then full time — or fill them up on hay first (G1781, p. 4). - Never feed cattle feed containing Rumensin — it kills horses (G1781, p. 4). - A horse that bolts its grain: put a few fist-sized rocks in the feed box (USFS Horse Packing, p. 3). - Plan the winter hay: at 1.5–2% of body weight, a 1,000-lb horse eats 15–20 lb of hay a day — roughly 450–600 lb for every month off pasture (arithmetic from G1781's table). 🦷 Teeth and worms - Teeth: check at least yearly (twice for older horses). Sharp edges form on the outside of the upper molars and inside of the lowers — float (rasp) them or the horse drops feed and loses weight. (PNW 587, p. 46; Merillat Animal Dentistry) - Signs of tooth trouble: dropping grain while chewing, holding the head sideways, eating slowly, whole grain in the manure, losing condition (G1781, p. 4). - Worms: don't deworm blindly every 8 weeks. Adults need 1–2 treatments a year (one in fall for bots and tapeworms); youngsters 3–4. When dewormers run out: pick up manure, don't overgraze, rotate pastures and graze with cattle or sheep. (Penn State/SARE, pp. 1–2) - Know your high shedders: most horses carry few worms; a few shed most of the eggs. Penn State's line: deworm a horse whose fecal egg count is over about 300 eggs per gram; over 500 is a "high shedder" (Penn State, pp. 1–2). Foals need a special schedule — ask the books, not guesswork. - Kill eggs without drugs: a manure pile that heats to 130–150 °F kills most parasites, flies and weed seeds (OSU EC1558, p. 16); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass it to horses — worm them together (Donkey Care

in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass it to horses — worm them together (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 16). 📚 Go deeper: Penn State Managing Equine Parasites — the egg-count method and when to treat; 4-H PNW 587 — teeth and aging; Merillat Animal Dentistry — floating and dental work by hand (old book: skills only).

🦶 Hoof care and shoeing - Pick out the feet every day. A healthy frog feels like firm rubber. Thrush) (black, stinking rot in the frog) comes from wet, dirty footing — trim away dead tissue, apply an antiseptic, and get the horse onto dry ground. In our wet winters, give horses a dry gravel or wood-chip standing area. (TM 2-220, p. 97; PNW 587; OSU EC1558, p. 2) - Hooves grow about ⅜ inch a month. Trim barefoot horses every 6–12 weeks, donkeys and mules every 6–10; the Army reset shoes every 3–6 weeks. (NMSU B-707, p. 2; Donkey Care Handbook, p. 14; TM 2-220) - Going barefoot (when shoes and nails run out): leave the sole, balance the wall, round off the outer edge so it doesn't chip, and check weekly. Most horses do fine barefoot on soft ground; hard rocky work wears feet faster than they grow. (TM 2-220, p. 98) - Making and fitting shoes: TM 2-220 The Horseshoer teaches forging shoes from bar stock, fitting and nailing, and even shoeing in the field with a ground fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference. Pair with the Blacksmithing guide. Taking shoes off for good (TM 2-220, p. 97): 1. Pull the shoes, then trim to balance and round the edge of the wall. Leave the dead sole. 2.

guide. Taking shoes off for good (TM 2-220, p. 97): 1. Pull the shoes, then trim to balance and round the edge of the wall. Leave the dead sole. 2. Expect the hoof to break away and the horse to go a bit tender for the first few weeks. It isn't serious and passes as new horn grows. 3. On rough, rocky pasture, leave the front shoes on for the first few days while the horse settles, then pull them. 4. Even shod horses do better with 2–3 months a year barefoot. Mud is the enemy here. Wet ground softens hooves and soles, leading to cracks, stone bruises, abscesses and thrush; mud also causes "mud fever" (scratches) — crusty scabs on the lower legs (OSU EC1558, p. 2). For the dry lot, lay down twice as much footing as you have mud: landscape fabric, 3 inches of ¾–1½-inch crushed rock, then 6 inches of gravel or sand or up to 12 inches of wood chips (p. 5). Field tips from the Army farrier: store horseshoe nails wrapped in an oiled cloth in a watertight can, and a worn rasp can be re-sharpened with a three-cornered file and re-hardened (TM 2-220, p. 99) — see the Blacksmithing guide. 📚 Go deeper: The Horseshoer TM 2-220 — care of shod and unshod feet, field expedients; Lungwitz Text-Book of Horseshoeing — hoof anatomy,

🤠 Handling, saddling and riding - Leading: from the left side, right hand near the halter, slack folded (never wrapped) in your left hand. If the horse rears, let go with the hand nearest the halter so you stay on the ground. (PNW 587, p. 51) - Tying: use a quick-release knot, about 3 ft of rope, tied at or above withers height to something solid. Any rope around the neck gets a bowline (it can't tighten), never a slip knot. Untie before taking the halter off. (PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety, p. 3) - Saddle fit: with pad and rider on, the gullet must clear the withers. After a sweaty ride, even sweat marks = good fit; dry spots = pressure. A sliding saddle needs a breast collar, not a tighter cinch. Dry spots with raised skin lead to saddle sores and white hair — fix the fit now (UF Saddle Fit, p. 3). - Cinching: snug it gradually until a flat hand just slips under, walk the horse a few steps, then recheck after a short ride — many horses puff up their bellies. On the trail, stop after 1–2 miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse, sit deep with heels down. Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse, sit deep with heels down. The 4-H manual (PNW 587) and FM 25-5 walk through riding step by step. - Starting young horses: handle foals early and teach them to lead before weaning. Light harness or saddle work at 2–3 years; no heavy work until they're nearly mature. First tie with a neck rope through the halter ring, tied with a bowline.
