🩺 Health checks and first aid Normal vital signs at rest — the sources differ a little, so learn your own horse's normal by taking it twice a day for a week (PNW 587, p. 28): | | Temperature | Pulse (beats/min) | Breaths/min | | 4-H PNW 587 | 99–101 °F (102+ = sick) | 32–48 (over 50 = distress) | 8–20 | | Raising Healthy Horses | 99–101.5 °F | 40–48 | 10–14 | | UGA B1356 | 99.5–101.5 °F | 32–36 | 8–12 | Take the pulse under the jawbone for 15 seconds × 4. A pinched fold of neck skin should flatten in 1–2 seconds; gums should be pink and moist; a healthy horse passes several piles of manure a day (PNW 587, p. 28). Act fast (no vet coming? treat these as emergencies) — temperature 102 °F or more, signs of colic, a deep puncture, a wound near an eye, joint or tendon, severe lameness, choking, off feed 12–24 hours, worsening cough, persistent diarrhea, or a mare in trouble foaling (PNW 587, p. 29). Colic (belly pain) — looking at or kicking at the belly, pawing, rolling, getting up and down, sweating, little or no manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3–4): - Take away all feed. Let it stand or lie quietly; walk it only briefly if it's throwing

manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3–4): - Take away all feed. Let it stand or lie quietly; walk it only briefly if it's throwing itself around — don't walk it to exhaustion. - Don't syringe in oil or water, and never put a hose down its nose or throat — the fluid goes into the lungs. Don't repeat painkillers without advice. - Water: sources disagree — UF lets the horse drink; the 4-H manual says no food or water until the vet sees it. - If it recovers on its own, no feed for 12–24 hours, then small meals over 3–5 days, and watch for manure (8–12 piles a day is normal) (UF VM275, p. 4). Choke (feed stuck in the gullet) — saliva and feed running from the nose, retching, sometimes a lump you can see or feel in the neck. It can still breathe. Remove all feed and water, keep it on bare ground or muzzle it, gently massage a visible lump; many cases clear in a couple of hours. Watch for fever over 101.5 °F or coughing in the days after — food in the lungs causes pneumonia (UF VM275, pp. 4–5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet; a horse can lose up to 4 gallons of blood

4–5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet; a horse can lose up to 4 gallons of blood without severe stress. Watch for proud flesh (red, lumpy tissue) in wounds over joints (PNW 587, p. 30). Eyes: rinse gently with saline (1 teaspoon salt in a pint of boiled water — Raising Healthy Horses, p. 9) or weak-tea-colored dilute betadine. Never alcohol or chlorhexidine near the eye, and no steroid ointments. Put on a fly mask (UF VM275, pp. 5–6). Swollen face, noisy breathing (snakebite, bee sting): horses can't breathe through the mouth. Cut two pieces of soft hose as long as from the inner corner of the eye to the nostril, lubricate them, slide one into each nostril and tape them in place (UF VM275, p. 6). Donkeys hide illness. A dull donkey off its feed is an emergency — it can fall into hyperlipaemia (fat flooding the blood) and die. Coax it to eat with fresh grass or favorite food and warm water. When a donkey loses its companion, let it stay with the body until it loses interest, and watch it closely for three weeks (Donkey Care Handbook, pp. 108–110). 🚜 Harness and draft work - What an animal can pull all day: about one-tenth of its body weight in steady draft (a big horse pulling 150 lb at 2½ mph ≈ 1 horsepower). Donkeys pull about a fifth of their weight for 3–4 hours. A cart donkey should pull no more than twice its weight, cart included, on the flat. (Peace Corps Animal Traction, p. 20; Donkey Care Handbook) Sources differ: Starkey quotes 15% of body weight as normal pulling power for horses (Starkey, p. 118). - Collar fit: a flat hand should just pass between the collar and the windpipe. A short collar chokes; a long one bruises the shoulders. Give each horse its own collar and wipe it after every use. Sore shoulders are the #1 harness problem. (USDA FB1419; FM 25-5) - Harness, hitching, driving pairs and teams, carts, plows and sledges: FM 25-5, Mounted Instruction for Field Artillery, the Peace Corps Animal Traction manual and Starkey's Harnessing and Implements. Big-team hitches and eveners: Sommerfeld's How to Hitch Horses. Preventing sore shoulders, step by step (USDA FB1419, pp. 17–20): 1. Fit: flat hand at the windpipe, fingertips at the sides of the neck just above the shoulder points. A narrow collar pinches; a wide one rubs. 2. Skip sweat pads — they cause more sore shoulders than a clean, smooth collar. 3. Set the hames snug

shoulder points. A narrow collar pinches; a wide one rubs. 2. Skip sweat pads — they cause more sore shoulders than a clean, smooth collar. 3. Set the hames snug so the pull comes about one-third of the way up from the point of the shoulder. 4. Spring toughening: for the first 2–3 weeks of work, wash the shoulders after work with warm water and mild soap, then rinse with cold water with a little salt in it. 5. At midday, lift the collar forward, wipe off sweat and dirt, and let the shoulders cool. 6. Harness care: hang it in a dry room; wipe the collar face after every use; once a year take it apart, soak 15 minutes in lukewarm water with mild soap, clean, oil and restitch. Keep a repair kit: punch, rivets, awls, needles, waxed thread, a clamp, spare leather, snaps and buckles (FB1419, p. 18). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB1419 Farm Work Horses — collar fitting, sore shoulders, harness care; Peace Corps Animal Traction — choosing and training draft animals, yokes, plows and carts; Starkey Harnessing and Implements — harness systems and draft-force data; Hasluck Harness Making — making collars and harness by hand. ☠️ Local dangers - Toxic plants: tansy ragwort, poison and water hemlock, foxglove and bracken fern — hungry horses on overgrazed pasture eat them. (Wild-Plants\ and Animals\ sheets) - Wildfire: evacuate horses early and in daylight; practice loading into a trailer ahead of time. See the Illinois Valley page. | Plant | Watch for | Why it matters | | Tansy ragwort | Yellow daisy-like flowers in flat clusters, ragged leaves, bad smell | Horses are especially sensitive. As toxic dried in hay as fresh — and tastier. Liver damage shows up months later (WSNWCB, p. 24) | | Poison hemlock | Hollow stems with purple blotches, fern-like leaves, rank smell when crushed | Less than a pound can kill a 1,000-lb animal in 2–3 hours; stays toxic in hay up to 3 years (WSNWCB, p. 34) | | Water hemlock | Wet ground; thick, chambered stem base | A single mouthful can kill in 15 minutes; roots most toxic (WSNWCB, p. 34) | | Bracken fern | Big triangular fronds, in woods and open ground | 2–5 lb a day for weeks causes staggers; also toxic in hay (WSNWCB, p. 36) | | Yellow starthistle | Gray-woolly plant, yellow flowers with inch-long spines | "Chewing disease" — horses can't eat or drink; poor outlook (WSNWCB, p. 26) | | Foxglove | Tall spikes of spotted pink-purple bells | Heart

flowers with inch-long spines | "Chewing disease" — horses can't eat or drink; poor outlook (WSNWCB, p. 26) | | Foxglove | Tall spikes of spotted pink-purple bells | Heart poison, fresh or dried (WSU, p. 28) | | Yew | Flat glossy needles, red berries — garden shrubs | Hedge trimmings thrown to stock kill fast (WSU, p. 2) | If you suspect poisoning (WSNWCB, p. 4): move the animal to shade with clean water and clean hay and keep it calm; collect a sample of the plant (gloves, sealed bag with a dry paper towel); find the source. ⛽ Fuel Guide How long gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane keep, how to tell when fuel has gone bad, what can be rescued, how to store fuel for the long haul — and how to get fuel out of gas-station underground tanks, drums and vehicles when there's no grid power. The manuals are in Fuel\ (Fuel-Quality-Storage, Station-Tanks-Pumping, Military-Fuel-Handling, Other-Fuels). Wood gas, biodiesel and alcohol fuel are in Homestead-Skills\Fuels. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent fires and deaths - Gasoline vapor explodes. No flames, smoking or sparks within 50 feet of open fuel. Use only pumps made for gasoline — ordinary electric motors spark. (FM 10-67-1, p. 21) - Static sparks ignite fuel. Touch bare metal with your bare hand before opening any cap. Keep the nozzle touching the can or tank the whole time you pour. Fill portable cans on the ground, never in a truck bed or on carpet (rule of thumb). (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21–23) - Never climb into a tank sump, manway or tank. Fuel vapor pushes out oxygen and can kill without any smell or warning; the lids are heavy. Work from ground level. (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 5; DoD UFM 3-460-03, p. 24) - Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. Smell gas: put out flames, get out,

Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. Smell gas: put out flames, get out, close the tank valve if it's safe. (Texas RRC Propane Safety, p. 11) - Empty cans and drums are more dangerous than full ones — they are full of vapor. (FM 10-67-1, p. 14) - Fuel-soaked clothes can burst into flame from static when you pull them off. Wet them with water first, and never take off a jacket or sweater within 50 feet of open fuel. (FM 10-67-1, p. 23)

Storage that makes fuel last: fill containers nearly full (less air), keep them cool and out of the sun, use metal or approved cans with tight caps, add stabilizer the day you buy the fuel, label the date, and use the oldest first. Keep fuel outside living areas. Heat and sun cost you fuel. Temperature swings also pull in moist air that condenses as water. Stand them in a plastic or rubber tub to catch drips. - Keep propane tanks and cylinders at least 6 metres (about 20 ft) from petroleum tanks. - A filter on a bulk tank's outlet should be about 10 microns — fine enough to stop rust, sand and lint. 📷 Jerrycan. 📚 Go deeper: Alberta Farm Fuel Storage and Handling — farm tanks, siting, evaporation, inventory; K-State MF3068 — ethanol fuel and stored small engines; FEMA P-1019 — keeping generator fuel from going bad.

🔍 Is this fuel still good? - Jar test: pour a sample from the bottom of the can or tank into a clean clear jar. Good fuel is clear and bright. Let it stand 15 minutes. Haze, droplets or a second layer at the bottom = water. Water fully settles out in about a day. (FM 10-67-2, p. 36; p. 97) - Bad signs: darker color, a sour or varnish smell, or a drop on glass that leaves a sticky film when it dries (gum). Gum sticks valves and clogs carburetors. - E10 with a bottom layer has phase-separated: the bottom is ethanol plus water, not just water. E10 at 60 °F holds only about 4 teaspoons of water per gallon (3.8, to be exact) before this happens — less in the cold. Humid air rarely causes it; rain and water sitting in tanks do. (EPA phase-separation memo, p. 2; pp. 4–5) What the jar tells you: | You see | It means | Do this | | Clear and bright | Good fuel | Use it | | Haze or tiny droplets | Water mixed in | Let it settle a day, take fuel off the top, filter | | A separate bottom layer | Free water — or, in E10, ethanol + water | Drain the bottom off; see "Rescuing" below | | Grit, rust or black specks

| A separate bottom layer | Free water — or, in E10, ethanol + water | Drain the bottom off; see "Rescuing" below | | Grit, rust or black specks | Dirt, rust or microbe slime | Settle, then filter through a fine filter | | Dark, sour, sticky | Old, gummy fuel | Blend small amounts with fresh, or don't use | 📚 Go deeper: FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing — Army fuel tests and what the results mean; EPA Water Phase Separation — how much water E10 can hold.

🔧 Rescuing old fuel (FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing, p. 97) - Water and dirt can be fixed: let the fuel settle a few hours to a day, then pour or siphon off the top, leaving the bottom inch behind, and filter it. The Army lets gasoline and diesel settle at least 2 hours after a tank is filled; water drops out in about 24 hours. - Phase-separated E10: the layers won't remix. Drain off and discard the bottom layer. The top is weaker (lower-octane) gasoline — fine for lawn, farm and older carbureted engines. - Stale but clean gasoline: blend it with fresh. The Army mixes a small test batch ("pilot blend") first and tests it. In its worked example, gummy old gasoline needed about 6 parts fresh to 1 part old to come back within limits. (FM 10-67-2, p. 98) Rule of thumb: 1 part old to 4 or more parts fresh for mildly stale gas, and use it in simple engines (generators, mowers, older trucks) — not modern high-compression or turbo engines. The staler it is, the more fresh fuel it needs. Blending can't save fuel that's bad in many ways at once. (FM 10-67-2, p. 97) - Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel. Diesel normally won't catch fire at storage temperatures, but a little gasoline in it changes that — and

Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel. Diesel normally won't catch fire at storage temperatures, but a little gasoline in it changes that — and gasoline in diesel can badly damage a diesel engine. (FM 10-67-1, p. 17; Alberta, p. 12) Diesel mixed into gasoline is usually less serious for a gas engine. (Alberta, p. 12) - Starting on old gas: a little fresh gas or starting fluid in the carburetor helps it catch; stale gas has lost the light parts that make it start. (Rule of thumb) - First tank of ethanol gas in an old engine: it may loosen old deposits and start running rough. Changing the in-line fuel filter often fixes it. (K-State, p. 2) 📚 Go deeper: FM 10-67-2 — reclaiming, blending and downgrading fuel; Oklahoma BAE-1746 — old fuel and small engines; Engines guide — cleaning a gummed-up carburetor.

🛢️ Diesel care - Water is the enemy. Drain water from the bottom of tanks and drums regularly, and check for it every time you gauge — the Army checks with water-finding paste every time and drains water the day after new fuel comes in, before it rises high enough to be drawn into the outlet. Keep drum bungs tight and covered so rain can't seep in. (FM 10-67-1, p. 141) - "Diesel bug": yeast, fungus and bacteria grow where fuel meets water — brown, black or gray slime that clogs filters and eats tanks. A puddle of water in the tank bottom is enough to feed big colonies, and it's worst in hot, humid weather. Prevent with zero water and a biocide; badly slimed tanks must be drained and scrubbed. Tanks left unused for a long time collect water at low points. (DoD UFM 3-460-03, pp. 29–30) - Expect old station diesel tanks to be corroded inside. EPA found moderate or severe corrosion in 83% of the diesel tanks it inspected, and ethanol had crept into 90% of the diesel samples. (EPA Corrosion in USTs with Diesel, p. 8; p. 10) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every day (a heater or tractor) so the fuel turns over. Keep spare filters. (FEMA

Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every day (a heater or tractor) so the fuel turns over. Keep spare filters. (FEMA P-1019, p. 91) - Cold gelling: thin diesel with No. 1 diesel or kerosene (the Army blends kerosene in for winter — FM 10-67-2, p. 98) or add a cold-flow additive — before it gets cold; additives won't un-gel it. Additives don't change the temperature at which wax first clouds the fuel; they only help it keep flowing through filters a few degrees colder. (NREL Biodiesel Handling Guide, p. 29) "Summer" diesel bought in July can gel on a frosty valley morning — buy diesel in the season you'll burn it. (Alberta, p. 12) - Substitutes: diesel engines can run on No. 2 heating oil, which is nearly the same fuel (FEMA P-1019, pp. 91, 106). Kerosene and Jet A are close to No. 1 diesel. Kerosene is "dry" (low lubricity) and harder on modern injection pumps; older mechanical-pump diesels tolerate substitutes best. (Rule of thumb) 📚 Go deeper: DoD UFM 3-460-03 Petroleum Fuel Systems Maintenance — water, microbes and tank cleaning; EPA Corrosion in Diesel USTs — what's happening inside old diesel tanks; NREL Biodiesel Handling and Use Guide — cold weather and storage for diesel and biodiesel.

🏪 Getting fuel out of gas-station tanks Why this matters here: a 2016 emergency exercise in Portland on a Cascadia earthquake found it would have catastrophic impacts on Oregon's petroleum infrastructure and make resupply very hard. Once delivery trucks stop, the fuel already in local station tanks may be all there is. (NASEO Petroleum Shortage Planning, pp. 7–8) What's under the concrete (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets; North Dakota training): - Each tank is usually 8,000–20,000 gallons, about 8–10 ft across, with its bottom roughly 10–14 ft below the pavement. (Rule of thumb) - Fill pipes sit inside small round spill buckets (5–25 gallons, lids 1–2 ft) (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 7). The cap colors usually tell you the fuel: white = regular, blue = mid-grade, red = premium, yellow = diesel; orange marks vapor-recovery pipes, not fuel. (Rule of thumb — check by gauging.) - A large manhole (3–4 ft lid) right over each tank covers the turbine-pump sump — the pump, piping and leak sensor. Other small risers are the tank gauge, spare ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy — get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below. Expect fuel vapor when you open them. (EPA, pp. 5, 8) - Bail out the spill bucket first. Rain and snowmelt fill them;

and smash the pump or piping below. Expect fuel vapor when you open them. (EPA, pp. 5, 8) - Bail out the spill bucket first. Rain and snowmelt fill them; if you open the fill cap under water, the water runs into the fuel. (Vermont Simple Suction manual, p. 4) Step 1 — measure what's there (EPA Doing Inventory Control Right): - Use a long wooden stick (won't spark), marked in inches (the EPA uses ⅛-inch marks), with zero at the very end. Varnish keeps fuel from creeping up the wood. (EPA, p. 6) - Lower it slowly down the fill pipe or gauge port, let it touch bottom gently, then bring it up quickly, and read the wet line. Wipe it and do it twice. (EPA, p. 8) - Water-finding paste on the tip changes color where there's water in the bottom; fuel-finding paste smeared where you expect the fuel line makes the reading sharper. A tank chart (if you can find one in the station office) converts inches to gallons. (EPA, pp. 6–7) Step 2 — the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. A check valve just under that pump keeps the line full ("primed") between uses. (Vermont, p. 3) - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible turbine in

pumps. A check valve just under that pump keeps the line full ("primed") between uses. (Vermont, p. 3) - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible turbine in the sump, usually 240-volt, ¾–2 hp (rule of thumb), plus the dispenser's electronics. That takes a stout generator. Connect only through the station's transfer switch — never by backfeeding. Several states have paid to prewire stations with generator hookups or "quick connects" (Florida required some by law in 2006). (NASEO, pp. 71–73; Florida SB 528 analysis) If the owner is around, work with them: they know their tanks and may already have a generator hookup. Step 3 — no power: pump it up by hand. - A siphon won't work — the fuel is below you, and a siphon only flows downhill. - Hose down the fill pipe: there's a drop tube inside with a flapper valve (it slams shut when the tank is about 95% full). The drop tube ends close to the tank bottom — within 6 inches in Vermont's manual, within 1 foot in EPA's. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the separate gauge port is another way in. (Vermont, p. 5; EPA Inventory Control, p. 7) - Suction lift is the limit. Air pressure can push water up at most about 33 feet in a perfect vacuum

in. (Vermont, p. 5; EPA Inventory Control, p. 7) - Suction lift is the limit. Air pressure can push water up at most about 33 feet in a perfect vacuum at sea level, and real pumps do far worse; gasoline's own vapor pressure cuts the lift further, especially when it's hot. (FM 10-67-1, pp. 485, 487) Hand and 12-volt suction pumps typically lift gasoline 10 feet or less (less in hot weather — gasoline boils in the hose). They work while the tank is fairly full and fail as it drops. (Rule of thumb, from the physics in FM 10-67-1) - For a deep or low tank, use a pump that goes down into the tank — a 12-volt submersible fuel-transfer pump rated for gasoline on a long hose — or a hand pump on a long rigid pipe. - Keep the hose end a few inches off the bottom to avoid water and sludge, pump into metal cans on the ground, keep everything bonded (metal-to-metal contact or a ground wire), and filter through a water-separating funnel. Bonding and grounding, the Army way (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21–22): - Bond = connect the two metal things (nozzle to can, pump to tank) so no spark can jump between them. Make the bond before you open the cap and keep it until the cap is back on. - Ground = a wire

tank) so no spark can jump between them. Make the bond before you open the cap and keep it until the cap is back on. - Ground = a wire from the equipment to a metal rod driven down to permanently damp soil, clamped to clean, bare, unpainted metal. Rod depth by soil: clean sand or gravel 6 ft, clay 4 ft, silt, silty sand, peat or muck 3 ft. - In dry or rocky ground, dig a hole about 1 ft deep and 3 ft across, pour in 5 lb of salt dissolved in 5 gallons of water, drive the rod there and keep it damp. If hand pumping goes wrong (rule of thumb, except where a page is given): | Problem | Likely cause | Try this | | Pump sucks air, never primes | Fuel level too far down; air leak at a hose joint | Tighten joints; switch to a pump that goes down into the tank | | Flow sputters and foams on a hot afternoon | Gasoline boiling in the suction hose | Work in the cool early morning; shorten the lift (FM 10-67-1, p. 487) | | Hose stops partway down the fill pipe | Hitting the drop-tube flapper | Turn and wiggle gently, or use the gauge port | | Water or sludge in the can | Hose end too low |

🚗 Drums and vehicles - Drums: a rotary or lever drum hand pump threads into the 2-inch bung; the Army's have a bonding wire and a strainer. Keep the drum grounded, and cover the pump's suction pipe when it's not in use. (FM 10-67-1, p. 353) - Open bungs slowly on a drum that's sat in the sun or been bumped around — pressure can spray out fuel and vapor. (FM 10-67-1, p. 14) - Cars and trucks: most modern fillers have an anti-siphon screen or rollover valve, so a hose won't reach the fuel. It's usually easier to disconnect the fuel line at the engine and let the car's own fuel pump push fuel into a can (key on, or power the pump relay) — or drain from the fuel-filter or tank fittings underneath. Older vehicles and many diesel trucks have no screen. (Rule of thumb) - Gas in old vehicles goes stale too — jar-test it before trusting it. 📷 Drum pump. 📚 Go deeper: FM 10-67-1 — drum pumps and handling; TM 9-8000 Principles of Automotive Vehicles — how vehicle fuel systems are laid out.

🔥 Kerosene and propane Kerosene heaters (CPSC Kerosene Heater Safety, pp. 1–2): - Only water-clear 1-K kerosene, never gasoline (even a little is dangerous). Store it in blue cans that have never held gasoline, away from other fuel cans. - Refuel outdoors with the heater off and cool, and don't fill above the "full" mark — that space lets the fuel expand. - Keep it at least 3 feet from furniture and clothes. - Unvented heaters make carbon monoxide: run it with the room's door open to the rest of the house, and crack a window about an inch if the door must be closed or the house is tight. - Keep the wick clean and set at the right height. - If it flares up, don't carry it and don't throw water on it. Use its shut-off switch; if that fails, get everyone out. Propane (Texas RRC Propane Safety Tips): - Store cylinders outdoors and upright, never in a closed building; vapor is heavier than air and pools low. (p. 4) - Never put your head over a tank's valves — the relief valve can pop. Liquid propane causes frostbite on skin and eyes. (p. 4) - Keep big tanks painted white or silver; a dark, rusty tank heats up and can vent through its relief valve. Cap every line not connected to an appliance. (p. 5) - Reading

tanks painted white or silver; a dark, rusty tank heats up and can vent through its relief valve. Cap every line not connected to an appliance. (p. 5) - Reading the tank gauge: the 5–95 dial is percent full, not gallons. A 500-gallon tank at 40% holds about 200 gallons. (p. 6) - How much is in a grill cylinder: run a wet finger down the side — the streak dries faster over the empty part. Don't use a dented, bulged, burned or badly rusted cylinder. (p. 8) - Before a flood or storm: close the tank valve and turn off pilots. After a flood, have tanks and lines checked before use — a regulator or appliance control that's been under water must be replaced. (p. 10) - If you smell gas: put out flames, don't flip any switches or use phones inside, get everyone out, close the tank valve, and don't turn it back on until the leak is fixed. (p. 11) 📷 Kerosene heater. 📚 Go deeper: CPSC Kerosene Heater Safety — one-page heater rules; MSU Portable Kerosene Heaters — choosing and running kerosene heaters; Texas RRC Propane Safety Tips — tanks, gauges, leaks and floods.

🌲 When the stored fuel runs out These are big projects — read the books before you build anything. - Wood gas: in World War II, cars, trucks and stationary engines in Europe ran on gas made by burning wood in a sealed canister. FEMA's plans fit 4-stroke gasoline engines of 10–150 hp; a diesel can run mostly on wood gas with a little diesel to light it. (FEMA Simplified Wood Gas Generator, p. 19) Wood gas is about 20% carbon monoxide. Many people died of "generator gas poisoning" in WWII. The danger is greatest when refueling, idling, or after shutdown — the unit keeps making gas after the engine stops — so keep it away from closed or poorly aired spaces. (FEMA, pp. 8, 73–74) - Alcohol: a farm still makes about 190-proof ethanol — too wet to mix with gasoline, but it runs most spark-ignition engines after you advance the timing, enlarge the carburetor jets and add preheat for cold starts. A gallon replaces about ⅔ gallon of gasoline. It's a poor diesel fuel on its own. (USDA Small-Scale Fuel Alcohol Production, p. 23) - Biodiesel is made from vegetable oil with methanol and lye — methanol is poisonous (it can blind or kill) and highly flammable, and lye burns skin and lungs. Goggles, gloves and good ventilation every time. (Penn State Biodiesel Safety, pp. 5, 8) -

(Penn State Biodiesel Safety, pp. 5, 8) - Charcoal and firewood don't run engines but do cook and heat — see Homestead-Skills\Fuels. 📷 Wood gas generator. 📚 Go deeper: FEMA Construction of a Simplified Wood Gas Generator — full build plans and safety; USDA Small-Scale Fuel Alcohol Production — making and using fuel alcohol; Practical Action Biodiesel Technical Brief — small-scale biodiesel basics; Peace Corps Charcoal Making — kilns and pits.

⚒️ Blacksmithing and Hand Tools How to set up a simple forge, pick the right scrap steel, forge and heat-treat it, and make or repair basic hand tools — chisels, punches, tongs, knives, axes — plus how to sharpen and re-handle the tools you already have. The full books are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ (Blacksmithing, Heat-Treating-Steel, Hand-Tools); axe and crosscut-saw manuals are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws. Farm blacksmithing (plow shares) and a short Practical Action brief are in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst injuries - Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel. Assume everything near the forge is hot; pick things up with tongs, and set hot pieces down where no one will grab them. - Eye protection at the anvil, grinder and when quenching. Never use a cracked grinding wheel, never wear gloves at the wheel, stand aside when you switch it on. (Navy Steelworker, p. 22) - Never heat galvanized (zinc-coated) metal indoors — the fumes cause "metal fume fever." Strip the zinc first (rule of thumb: soak overnight in vinegar) and work outdoors. Drinking milk does not help, despite old advice (TM 10-440, p. 60 still recommends it — ignore that). - Quench oil can catch fire. Use a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an

a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an oil fire — smother it with the lid. (Rule of thumb) Oil fires usually start when there's too little oil for the piece. (Practical Action Blacksmithing, p. 3) - A coal or charcoal forge makes carbon monoxide — work outdoors or under an open-sided roof. - Fire season: Illinois Valley summers are dry. Keep a full water bucket or trough by the forge for embers as well as quenching (Practical Action, pp. 1–2), clear dry grass and leaves well back from the forge, and never leave a fire unattended. (Rule of thumb) - Oily rags can catch fire by themselves. Throw them out or keep them in a bucket of water. (USFS An Ax to Grind, p. 34)

🔥 A simple forge and anvil Rule-of-thumb setups; the books have full plans. - Forge: anything that holds a fist-sized pile of burning fuel with air blown up into the middle — a brake drum or steel tub lined with clay, or a brick or stone hearth with a pipe coming in at the bottom (the "tuyere"). The ICS Shop Equipment book and the Peace Corps manual show how to build forges and bellows. (ICS, p. 21) - Air: a hand-crank blower, homemade bellows, a hair dryer or a small fan with a valve or gate to control it. Too much air wastes fuel and burns steel. - Fuel: charcoal (easy to make — see Homestead-Skills\Fuels), or coal turned to coke in the fire. Keep the fire clean: rake out clinker (glassy lumps), and work in the hot center. Screen coke to get rid of dust before you use it. (Practical Action, p. 2) - Anvil: a real anvil is best, but a chunk of railroad rail, a big block of steel, or a sledgehammer head set in a stump works. Set the face at about knuckle height when you stand with your arm hanging. Practical Action also shows a stone with an iron insert and an old casting used as anvils. (Practical Action, p. 3) - First tools: a 2–3 lb cross-peen hammer, a pair of tongs (or make

stone with an iron insert and an old casting used as anvils. (Practical Action, p. 3) - First tools: a 2–3 lb cross-peen hammer, a pair of tongs (or make them — they're a classic first project), a bucket of water, a file, and a magnet. - Water trough: big enough to sink the whole piece — at least about 5 gallons. (Practical Action, p. 2) Running the fire (TM 10-440, pp. 26–27): - The hottest spot is about 5–7 inches above the tuyere. Keep the fire just big enough to surround the piece with glowing coals. - A thin fire lets unburned air reach the steel and covers it in scale (an "oxidizing" fire). A deep fire uses up the air first — slower, but it doesn't scale the steel. - Pack wet, unburned fuel around the edges to keep the fire from spreading; it cokes there and feeds the center as you need it. | Fire problem | Likely cause | Fix | | Steel comes out heavily scaled | Fire too thin, too much air | Build the fire deeper; less blast | | Fire won't get hot | Clinker choking the tuyere; wet or dusty fuel | Rake out clinker; screen fuel | | Fire spreads and wastes fuel | Too much loose fuel, no banking | Pack damp fuel around the edges | 📷 Anvil,

| Rake out clinker; screen fuel | | Fire spreads and wastes fuel | Too much loose fuel, no banking | Pack damp fuel around the edges | 📷 Anvil, Tuyere, Bellows, Swage block, Hardy tool. 📚 Go deeper: ICS Blacksmith Shop Equipment — forges, blowers, bellows and anvil tools; Peace Corps Basic Techniques of Blacksmithing — building a forge and tools from scrap; TM 10-440 — fuel and fire management; Peace Corps Charcoal Making — making forge charcoal.

🌡️ Heat colors (in shade, not sunlight) | Color | About °F | What it's for | | Dull red | 1,050–1,175 | Stop hammering — steel worked colder than this cracks. | | Cherry red | 1,250–1,375 | Hardening temperature for most carbon steel; bending. | | Orange to yellow | 1,725–1,975 | Normal forging heat — hammer here. | | Bright yellow-white, "flowing" surface | about 2,000 | Forge welding (mild steel and wrought iron, about 2,000 °F). | | White with sparks shooting off | 2,200 and up | Burned. The steel is ruined — cut that part off. | (°F from TM 10-440's color table, p. 25; colors look different in different light and to different eyes, so learn them on your own forge.) High-carbon steel burns at a lower heat than mild steel, so forge tool steel no hotter than orange-yellow. Burned steel can't be fixed by any later heat treatment. Keep hammering until the steel cools to a low red — forging refines the grain and makes it tougher. (TM 10-440, p. 24) Basic moves: drawing out (hammering thinner and longer), upsetting (hammering the hot end to make it thicker), bending over the anvil horn or edge, punching holes hot, cutting on a hardy (a chisel set in the anvil), twisting, and forge welding. Ilgen's Forge Work and the Selvidge Shop Manual walk through

horn or edge, punching holes hot, cutting on a hardy (a chisel set in the anvil), twisting, and forge welding. Ilgen's Forge Work and the Selvidge Shop Manual walk through each one step by step. Punching a hole (TM 10-440, p. 33): center-punch the spot, heat to a good working heat, drive the punch two-thirds of the way through, flip the piece, and punch out from the other side over the anvil's round (pritchel) hole. Cool the punch often so it doesn't soften, and drop a little dry coal in a deep hole to stop the punch sticking. Forge welding, step by step (Selvidge, pp. 45–47; TM 10-440, pp. 30–31): 1. Prepare: upset each end to about 1½ times its thickness, then hammer a scarf (a bevel) on each, slightly rounded, not hollow, so scale squeezes out from the middle. 2. Clean fire, clean anvil: rake out clinker, have plenty of coke ready, brush scale off the anvil face, and set your hammer where you can grab it. 3. Heat slowly under a covering of live coals, turning the pieces so both heat evenly. 4. At bright red, sprinkle flux — borax or clean sand — on the scarfs; it keeps air off and melts the scale so it can squeeze out. 5. Keep heating until the surface looks wet and flowing. Pull both pieces, knock off loose scale, lap

keeps air off and melts the scale so it can squeeze out. 5. Keep heating until the surface looks wet and flowing. Pull both pieces, knock off loose scale, lap the scarfs and strike light blows first, then heavier. 6. Don't keep hammering once it drops below welding heat. If it doesn't stick, cut off the tips, re-scarf and try again. Use as few heats as possible. | Forging problem | Likely cause | Fix | | Cracks while hammering | Worked below dull red | Reheat sooner; stop at dull red | | Sparks and a crumbly end | Burned | Cut back to sound metal | | Weld won't stick | Not hot enough, dirty fire, no flux, scale between faces | Clean fire, flux at bright red, reach full welding heat | | Weld lets go later | Hammered after it cooled; hollow scarfs trapped scale | Round the scarfs; weld in fewer, hotter heats | | Thin tip burns before the thick part is hot | Fast heating | Heat slowly and keep the thin end back from the hot spot (Drew, p. 63) | 📷 Forge welding. 📚 Go deeper: Selvidge Blacksmithing Shop Manual — every basic operation as a one-page job sheet; Ilgen Forge Work — drawing, upsetting, bending and welding explained; TM 10-440 — heat colors, forging and welding in brief.

🔩 Which scrap steel to use (Peace Corps Basic Techniques of Blacksmithing, p. 31) | Steel | Found in | Good for | | Low carbon — won't harden | Car body panels, most rebar, nails, bolts, rail spikes, pipe, drums | Hooks, hinges, brackets, tongs, anything that bends instead of cuts. Forge-welds easily. | | Medium carbon — hardens | Leaf and coil springs, axles, torsion bars, shock-absorber rods | Chisels, punches, hammers, axes, hoes, pry bars, springs. The best all-round tool stock. | | High carbon — hardens hard | Old files, saw blades, drill bits, dies, bulldozer blades | Knives, scrapers, wood chisels, plane irons — tools that must hold a keen edge. | Sources disagree on springs. The Peace Corps puts car springs, axles and torsion bars in the medium-carbon group; Practical Action calls coil springs, leaf springs and torsion bars high carbon. Test each piece and treat springs as hardening steel either way. Practical Action also warns that rebar often has a bit more carbon than true mild steel. (Practical Action, p. 5) - Quick test: heat the tip to light cherry red and quench it in water. If a file skates over it like glass, it will harden. If the file bites, it's low-carbon. (Peace Corps, p. 32) - Spark test on a grinder: low-carbon steel throws long streams with few forks; high-carbon throws

glass, it will harden. If the file bites, it's low-carbon. (Peace Corps, p. 32) - Spark test on a grinder: low-carbon steel throws long streams with few forks; high-carbon throws shorter, bushier streams full of bright bursts; cast iron throws short dull red sparks. Practice on known pieces first. In the Navy Steelworker's pictures the low-carbon stream runs about 70 inches, high-carbon about 55 inches with more volume, and gray cast iron only about 25 inches, red near the wheel and straw-colored at the end. Watch a spot about a third of the way back from the tip of the stream. (Steelworker, pp. 22–24) - Other clues (Peace Corps, p. 32): drop it on concrete and compare the ring with known pieces; see whether a cold chisel nicks it easily; and think about its old job — anything that had to be springy, tough or wear-resistant is probably medium or high carbon. 📷 Spark testing, Leaf spring. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps manual, scrap identification — what's in scrap and how to test it; Navy Steelworker Vol 1 — spark and chip tests with pictures; Practical Action Blacksmithing brief — mild, medium and high carbon steel from old vehicles.

🧪 Hardening and tempering 1. Anneal (soften) old steel before reshaping it cold or filing it: heat slowly to red, then bury it in dry wood ashes, lime or powdered charcoal and leave it until cold. (Selvidge, p. 56) 2. Harden: heat evenly to cherry red — rule of thumb: just past the point where a magnet stops sticking to it — and quench. - Plain carbon steel (springs, files, most scrap): water or brine (about ¾ lb salt per gallon) cools fastest and most evenly. Thin or very high-carbon pieces (files, knives) can crack in water — warm oil (80–150 °F; vegetable oil works) is gentler. (Steelworker, pp. 35–36) - Alloy steels: oil only. - Keep the piece moving in the quench. Steam and gas bubbles otherwise cling to it and leave soft spots, which can later crack or warp. (Selvidge, p. 57; Steelworker, p. 35) - The steel is now glass-hard and brittle — temper it right away, before it's fully cold. The Navy Steelworker manual takes parts out of the quench at about 200 °F — still too hot to touch — rather than letting them cool through the "cracking range" below that. (Steelworker, p. 31) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven) and watch the colors run. Quench

Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven) and watch the colors run. Quench when the edge reaches the color you want: | Color | About | Use | | Pale yellow | 430 °F | Engraving and lathe tools, scrapers | | Straw | 460 °F | Taps, punches, dies, knives for a very hard edge | | Brown-yellow (deep straw) | 500 °F | Wood chisels, drills, plane irons, hammer faces | | Purple | 530–540 °F | Light cold chisels, shears, axes | | Blue tinged with purple | 550 °F | Ordinary cold chisels | | Blue | 570–600 °F | Springs, picks | The further toward blue, the softer and tougher. Books disagree a little — one old table puts most chisels and knives at light blue — so test your tool and adjust. (Bacon, p. 263; Selvidge, p. 59; TM 10-440, p. 26) One-heat method for chisels and punches: heat the working end to cherry red, quench only the tip inch or so (bob it up and down), pull it out, quickly polish the tip, and watch the heat from the shank run colors toward the edge. When the right color reaches the edge, quench the whole tool. (Steelworker, p. 34; Selvidge, p. 58) Many pieces at once:

heat from the shank run colors toward the edge. When the right color reaches the edge, quench the whole tool. (Steelworker, p. 34; Selvidge, p. 58) Many pieces at once: temper them in a pot of oil over the fire with a thermometer instead of by color — steadier and more even. (Bacon, pp. 263–264) If the tool doesn't work right: | Problem | Likely cause | Fix | | Edge chips or breaks in use | Too hard | Reheat gently to the next softer color and quench (Selvidge, p. 59) | | Edge bends or dulls fast | Too soft — tempered too far, or never got hard | Re-harden and temper less (rule of thumb) | | File still bites after quenching | Low-carbon steel, or not hot enough | Test the steel; heat to full cherry red | | Soft spots | Steam pockets in the quench | Move the piece in the quench; use brine | | Cracked in the quench | Too hot, quench too harsh, thick-and-thin shape, sharp inside corners | Harden at cherry, not hotter; use oil for thin or high-carbon pieces | | Warped | Uneven heat or uneven entry into the quench | Heat evenly; plunge straight in, thick end first (Drew, p. 64) | 📷 Tempering colors). 📚 Go deeper: Bacon Forge Practice and Heat Treatment of Steel —

🛠️ Making basic tools - Cold chisel (first real project): a 6–8 inch piece of coil spring or axle. Straighten it, draw one end to a wedge, grind or file the edge to about 60°, harden and temper to purple at the edge (one-heat method). Leave the striking end soft. (TM 10-440, pp. 33–34) - Hot chisel vs cold chisel: a hot chisel is left soft and used only on hot steel; a cold chisel is hardened and tempered and used only on cold steel. Don't swap them. (Practical Action, p. 4) - Center punch / drift: same steel, drawn to a round taper; temper the point straw to brown. - Tongs: two matching pieces of mild steel, forged with jaws and a boss, punched and riveted together. Richardson Vol 2 and Selvidge have patterns. - Knife: from an old file or saw blade. Anneal first, forge or grind to shape (on a grinder, dip often — blue on the edge means you've ruined the temper), harden in oil, temper straw to brown. - Axe, hoe, hammer: the Peace Corps manual covers forging each from scrap, including punching the eye with a drift. - Fullers (grooving tools) and other top and bottom tools can be made of plain mild steel. (Practical Action, p. 4) - Repairing tools ("dressing"): reforge mushroomed chisel heads, re-point picks, and redraw worn hoes and drill

and bottom tools can be made of plain mild steel. (Practical Action, p. 4) - Repairing tools ("dressing"): reforge mushroomed chisel heads, re-point picks, and redraw worn hoes and drill bits — ICS Shop Equipment, Hand Forging and Tool Dressing. Sharpening a plow share — gardens and fields here depend on it (Drew Farm Blacksmithing, pp. 62–64): 1. Use a round-faced 2½–3 lb hammer. Draw the edge out by hammering the top side while the bottom lies flat on the anvil. 2. Don't burn the edge while heating — it's thin and heats fast. 3. If the point bends over, rest the edge on a hardwood block, not the anvil, while you drive it back. 4. Harden a good-steel share at full red, plunging it thick side first into water or brine. For stony ground, leave it less hard so it doesn't chip. 5. A worn-out point can be replaced by welding on a piece of old plow steel (not a rasp — too high in carbon to weld easily), using borax as flux. Practice on scrap first. Skip the old book's chemical hardening powder. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps manual — axe, hoe, tongs and hammer projects; ICS Tool Dressing — reforging and re-tempering worn tools; Drew Farm Blacksmithing — farm repairs, chisels and plow work; Richardson Practical Blacksmithing Vol 2 — tongs and shop-made tools.

🪓 Keeping hand tools working Hanging an axe handle (USFS An Ax to Grind): - First check whether you need a new handle at all — often just a new wedge will do. (An Ax to Grind, p. 28) - Line the edge up with the center of the handle. Laid flat, the blade should touch the table one third of the way from the heel. (p. 24) - Saw the wedge slot about two-thirds of the depth of the eye. Drive the head on by striking the end of the handle on a block, not the head. (pp. 30–31) - Drive a hardwood wedge in until it stops, leaving ¼–½ inch, then trim. No metal wedges, screws or epoxy. Soaking a loose head in water only works for a day. (pp. 32–33) Soaking the head in linseed oil is a better temporary fix. (p. 33) - Good handle woods: straight-grained ash (Oregon ash grows here), hickory, oak. (Rule of thumb) The grain should run straight along the handle and in line with the wedge slot. (p. 26) Sharpening: - Never sharpen an axe on a fast dry bench grinder — it draws the temper (the edge turns blue). Use a file (cuts on the push stroke only; lift on the return, wear gloves and use a knuckle guard), a slow wet grindstone, then a whetstone. File until a burr

a file (cuts on the push stroke only; lift on the return, wear gloves and use a knuckle guard), a slow wet grindstone, then a whetstone. File until a burr forms, then switch sides. Aim for about 25°, slightly convex. (An Ax to Grind, pp. 34–36; Handtools for Trail Work, p. 22) - If you do blue an edge, the temper is gone for at least 3/16 inch back — grind or file past it. On a pedal grindstone, keep it wet and turn it toward you, into the edge. File in a fan shape 2–3 inches back from the middle of the edge, and hone every morning you use the axe. (An Ax to Grind, pp. 34–36) - Chisels and plane irons: grind at about 25°, then hone on an oilstone or water stone until a fine burr forms, flip and flatten the back, and strop. The grindstone shapes; only the stone sharpens — hone at a hair steeper angle than you ground. (Griffith Essentials of Woodworking, pp. 68–69) - Hand saws (Disston): clamp with the gullets just above the jaws. Joint the teeth level with a flat file, set them (never deeper than half the tooth), then file. Crosscut: every other tooth with the file angled about 45° toward the handle, then turn the saw around for the rest. Rip: straight across at 90°. (Disston, pp. 35–38) -

Crosscut: every other tooth with the file angled about 45° toward the handle, then turn the saw around for the rest. Rip: straight across at 90°. (Disston, pp. 35–38) - Files: keep them dry and separate (files dull each other), clean them with a file card or a nail, and use chalk on the teeth for soft metals. 🍄 Mushroom Guide How to identify, use, preserve and grow mushrooms in the Illinois Valley — and how not to die doing it. The field guides, poisoning reports and growing manuals are in Mushrooms\ (Identification, Poisoning-Safety, Uses-Growing-Preserving). Wild-Plants\ also has the Forest Service Wild Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest and death cap ID sheets. ### ⚠️ The rules that keep foragers alive 1. Only eat a mushroom you have identified with complete certainty — every feature, including the spore print and the base of the stem. "Pretty sure" is how people die. 2. No folk test works. Silver turning dark, a peeling cap, animals or insects eating it, soaking in salt water, cooking — none of these tell you anything. Cooking, drying, freezing and canning do not destroy the deadly toxins. (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 218) 3. The deadliest ones taste fine and make you sick late — 6 to 24 hours or more after eating. By then the toxin is already in your liver or kidneys. 4. Dig up the whole mushroom — the cup or bulb at the base is what tells you it's a deadly Amanita. Never eat unopened "buttons" of gilled mushrooms; nobody can tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in

tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in moderation, and keep one uncooked specimen in the fridge in case someone gets sick. (PNW/BC White Paper, p. 10)

🔎 How to identify a mushroom Check all of these, every time: - Underside: gills (thin blades), pores (a sponge of tubes — boletes), teeth or spines (hedgehogs), or blunt ridges (chanterelles). (See gills).) - Stem base: dig it up. A cup (volva) or bulb at the base, plus a ring on the stem and white gills, means Amanita — leave all of them alone. (FB 796) (See volva) and ring).) - Spore print: cut off the stem of a mature cap, lay the cap gills-down on half white, half dark paper, cover with a glass, and wait a few hours. The color (white, pink, brown, rusty, purple-black) places the mushroom in its family. (Thomas Field Book; Atkinson, p. 373; pictures: Spore print) - Where it grows: on wood or soil, under which trees (oak, tanoak, Douglas-fir, pine), alone or in clumps, and the season. - Flesh, smell and bruising: does it stain when cut? Is the flesh brittle or stringy? Fruits in fall, but in summer where lawns or orchards are watered (BCCDC briefing, p. 8). - How little it takes: a lethal dose can be as low as 0.1 mg per kg of body weight, and one mushroom can hold up to 15 mg (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). Half a cap can kill a small child (White Paper, p. 8). - Boiling and pouring off the water doesn't help (BCCDC, p. 5). - Young death caps look like puffballs — see the puffball slice test below. - Dogs die from it too — puppies especially (BC Forests, p. 8). Poisoning timeline — deadly Amanita, Galerina, Lepiota: nothing for 6–24 hours, then violent vomiting and diarrhea, then a false recovery around day 1–2, then liver (and kidney) failure at day 3–5. 10–20% die

deadly Amanita, Galerina, Lepiota: nothing for 6–24 hours, then violent vomiting and diarrhea, then a false recovery around day 1–2, then liver (and kidney) failure at day 3–5. 10–20% die even with hospital care. (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3) Sources differ on the death rate: BC public health says 10–30% even with treatment (BCCDC, p. 5); NAMA's records show about 11% of people who got sick (NAMA 2018–20, p. 3); FDA says 50–90% for people who reach care late, about 10% for those treated almost at once (Bad Bug Book, p. 219). Without a hospital, expect the worst. When did the symptoms start? 🚑 If someone may have eaten a bad mushroom - Get medical help immediately, even if they feel fine — the dangerous ones are delayed. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222. - Bring the mushroom — leftovers, the uncooked ones, even scraps from the trash — in a paper bag (they rot in plastic). A photo is far less useful than a sample. (White Paper, p. 6; Michigan sheet, p. 2) - The main hospital treatment for amatoxin is aggressive IV fluids — NAMA calls it "by far the best single intervention" (NAMA 2018–20, p. 4; CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). Liver drugs such as silibinin (from milk thistle) are tried, but proof is thin. Sources disagree on activated charcoal: FDA lists it as part of prompt treatment (Bad Bug Book, p. 229), CDC says it has no proven benefit for amatoxin, and NAMA says it's useless more than about 1 hour after eating. With no hospital: replace fluids constantly (oral rehydration solution — see the Medical guides), give activated charcoal only if they ate the mushroom within the last hour or so, and rest. Survival odds are much worse without a hospital — which is why rule 1 matters so much. - Don't be fooled by the false recovery. In the 2016 California outbreak, people sent home with "stomach flu" came back in liver failure (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). One Québec

Don't be fooled by the false recovery. In the 2016 California outbreak, people sent home with "stomach flu" came back in liver failure (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). One Québec man with orellanine poisoning put up with mild symptoms for 18 days before his kidneys failed (NAMA 2021, p. 2). - Write down (rule of thumb): what was eaten and how much, raw or cooked, the time of the meal, the time symptoms started, who else ate it, and any alcohol. Check everyone who shared the dish — and any pets. 📚 Go deeper: CDC MMWR 2017 death cap outbreak — 14 real cases, hour by hour; NAMA 2018–2020 summary — what treatments work and which don't; BCCDC Wild Mushrooms May Be Poisonous — one-page symptoms and what to do.

A Verpa cap hangs free like a thimble; a Gyromitra is wrinkled like a brain, never pitted (Michigan sheet, pp. 1–2). - Gyromitra fumes: its toxin boils off at about 190 °F, so the cook breathing the steam can be poisoned, and it lingers in the cooking water. 🫙 Cooking, drying and storing - Cook all wild mushrooms — never raw, and morels especially well done. Don't mix alcohol with morels the first time (some people react). - Eat a few mouthfuls, not a plateful, of any wild mushroom, and not several days running — big servings cause reactions even with "safe" kinds like morels (White Paper, pp. 10–11). In 1991, 77 of 483 guests at a Vancouver banquet got sick from morels served raw (p. 10). - Fresh storage: in the refrigerator (40 °F or colder) in a paper bag — CDC's advice for morels (CDC 2024, p. 5). Don't freeze them raw — bacteria keep growing (NAMA 2018–20, p. 2). - Dry slices about ½ inch thick at about 120 °F with good airflow until crisp; morels lose about 90% of their weight. Store airtight. Rehydrate in hot water. Ventilate while drying — spores can trigger asthma. (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2; USFS PNW-GTR-710, pp. 66–67) - No dehydrator? In warm, dry weather, dry on screens, threaded on fishing line, or in a single layer on a tarp, turning them; or use the warm air near a wood stove with a fan. Moving dry air matters more than heat — don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66–67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note 13,

more than heat — don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66–67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4). - Freeze after sautéing (best) or steam-blanching. To steam: soak 5 minutes in 1 teaspoon lemon juice per pint of water, then steam whole 5 minutes, quarters 3½, slices 3, cool in ice water, pack and freeze (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2). - Never can wild mushrooms — only store-type button mushrooms have tested canning times (OSU SP 50-919, p. 1). Improperly canned chanterelles gave diners botulism in Vancouver in 1987 (White Paper, p. 10). - Recipes from the old books — fine for cooking ideas once the mushroom is safely identified: McIlvaine's 15-page recipe chapter (p. 813), Mrs. Rorer's recipes in Atkinson (p. 379), Gibson (p. 321) and Thomas (p. 381). Skip their raw-mushroom salads and anything about canning. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Preserving Mushrooms SP 50-919 — freezing, drying and why only button mushrooms can be canned; Morels of Western North America — drying with and without power; McIlvaine recipe chapter — old-time cooking and drying methods.

🪵 Growing your own - Shiitake on logs: fresh hardwood logs (oak is among the best) 4–6 inches across, cut in the dormant season while the bark is tight. Drill holes 7/16 inch wide, 1¼ inches deep, 3 inches apart in a diamond pattern, plug with spawn, seal with wax. Keep shaded and moist. Mushrooms start in 6–18 months; after that, soak a log 24 hours and it fruits about a week later. Rest logs 8–12 weeks between soaks. (UVM/Cornell, p. 20; USDA Agroforestry Note 13, p. 3) - Oysters on straw: chop straw 4–5 inches, soak overnight, pasteurize at 165 °F for 1–2 hours, mix in 5–10% spawn, pack into bags with holes, keep warm and humid. Fruits in weeks. (UF IFAS SS662, p. 2) - Keep your strain going: a piece of a fruiting log or colonized straw can start the next batch, so you don't need to buy spawn again. Shiitake details: - Logs: 3–8 inches across and 2–4 feet long. A 4-foot, 8-inch log can weigh 80 lb. Cut from live trees roughly Thanksgiving to St. Patrick's Day, and inoculate within two weeks (Agroforestry Note 13, pp. 2–3). - Hole spacing: the sources differ — Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches apart with one row fewer (p. 3).

says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches apart with one row fewer (p. 3). Either way, stagger the rows in a diamond pattern. - Spawn: one 5-lb bag of sawdust spawn does about 20–25 logs 4–6 inches by 3 feet (Cornell-UVM, p. 21). - Laying yard: 75–100% shade all year — under conifers is best; the north side of a house or shed works for a few logs. Keep logs above 30% moisture; in a dry spell soak them a few hours or sprinkle them (Cornell-UVM, p. 23). - Harvest when caps are 60–75% open, edge still slightly curled under (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4; Cornell-UVM, p. 39). Logs keep producing for up to 6 years; about 10 logs feed a family. - Check every brown mushroom on your logs. Deadly Galerina can pop up on shiitake logs. Make a spore print: shiitake is white, Galerina brown; shiitake never has a ring (Cornell-UVM, p. 41). Oyster details (UF SS662, pp. 2–4): incubate filled bags in the dark at 75–77 °F and 80–90% humidity until white all through (2–3 weeks); then give them light, about 68 °F, 90% humidity and fresh air. Pick clusters by twisting. Expect 2–4 more flushes. If this goes wrong: | Problem | What to do | | Logs haven't fruited

🌿 Medicinal mushrooms Turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake have real research behind them as add-ons to treatment — turkey-tail extract (PSK) is a prescribed cancer add-on in Japan — but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. They are not cures. Turkey tail and reishi are traditionally simmered for hours as tea. (VA Mycomedicinals, pp. 1–3) - Making the tea: simmering or boiling in water for 20 minutes to 2 hours breaks down the tough cell walls and releases the active compounds (VA, p. 1). - Who should be careful: people with leukemia or lymphoma, after a bone-marrow transplant, or on drugs that suppress the immune system — these mushrooms act on the immune system (VA, p. 3). - No panacea: in one mouse study a reishi extract made tumors grow faster (GTR-309, p. 31). 📚 Go deeper: VA Mycomedicinals — what the research shows for turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake; Agroforestry Note 13 — growing lion's mane on logs.The old mushroom books here (1895–1928) are great for pictures, descriptions and recipes, but some of their safety advice is wrong and has killed people: Marshall's Mushroom Book lists false morels as edible, Thomas says the parasol has no poisonous look-alike, and USDA FB 796 recommends raw mushrooms and old first aid. ☢️ Nuclear Fallout Guide What to do if there is a nuclear detonation or a radiation release: how to shelter, how long, how to protect food, water and animals, how to clean up, and when potassium iodide (KI) helps. The full manuals — shelter plans, the homemade KFM fallout meter, farm and livestock guides — are in Nuclear-Radiation\. ### The three rules 1. Get inside. Stay inside. Stay tuned. Most deaths from fallout are avoidable just by being behind enough mass in the first day or two. 2. Fallout is dust. It hurts you from what lands on and near you, so put mass and distance between you and the roof, walls and ground outside. 3. Time is on your side. Radiation from fallout drops fast — 90% in the first 7 hours, 99% in 2 days.

⚡ The first minutes - If you see a flash: drop behind anything solid, face down, cover your head, and don't look at it — the flash can blind you even when you are too far away for the blast to hurt you (FEMA H-20, p. 14). The blast wave can arrive many seconds later — stay down until it passes. Being outdoors in the first minute can mean burns, cuts from flying glass and broken bones (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 76). - Fallout near a blast can start arriving in 15–30 minutes; 100–200 miles downwind, often 5–10 hours or more. Use the time before it arrives to put out small fires, bring people, pets and water inside, and move to the best shelter you can reach. (FEMA Protection in the Nuclear Age, H-20, p. 7) - Officials will tell everyone within about 50 miles to shelter until they know where the fallout is going. (FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed., p. 54) - Know the sirens. A 3–5 minute steady blast means "turn on the radio." A 3–5 minute wavering tone (or short blasts repeated) is the attack warning — go to shelter now. (FEMA H-20, p. 12) First-hour checklist: get people and pets inside; close doors, windows and blinds; take a few minutes to check the house for fires — stamp out smoldering drapes, throw burning furniture outside (FEMA

get people and pets inside; close doors, windows and blinds; take a few minutes to check the house for fires — stamp out smoldering drapes, throw burning furniture outside (FEMA H-20, p. 26); fill containers and tubs while the taps run (rule of thumb); carry food, water, radio, medicines and the toilet bucket to the shelter spot. 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 Protection in the Nuclear Age — warning signals, the flash, fallout timing, fires; FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed. — today's official "Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned" advice.

🏠 Where to shelter Best to worst: a basement (especially a corner below ground level) → the middle floors and center of a large concrete or brick building → a crawl space or interior room of a house → a vehicle (poor). Most homes in the Illinois Valley are one-story wood frame with no basement. FEMA says these, and vehicles, are not adequate shelter on their own (Planning Guidance, p. 76). Plan now: a nearby building with a basement or thick masonry, a crawl-space shelter you can shield, or an outdoor trench shelter (plans in MP-79, In Time of Emergency, and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix A). - Inside any building: get as far from the roof and outside walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go) - No need to tape windows or hang plastic sheeting — fallout shelters don't have to be airtight. A building with minor damage still works if it is structurally sound. (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 31; Planning Guidance, p. 76) - Stuck in a poor shelter? If a good one is under 15 minutes away, move within about 30 minutes of the blast, before heavy fallout arrives. If you're already in a moderate shelter, stay 1–2 hours, then move. (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 77)

(FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 77) "Adequate" means it cuts your dose 10× or more. Concrete, brick, stone and earth stop a lot; wood, drywall and sheet metal stop little (Planning Guidance, p. 76). Adding shielding — each of these stops about as much as 4 inches of concrete (FEMA H-20, p. 22): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5–6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete block (sand-filled) | 8 in (6 in) | | Water | 10 in | | Books or magazines | 14 in | | Wood (firewood stack) | 18 in | Pile it on the floor above you and around the walls of your shelter spot: earth-filled drawers and boxes, water jugs, firewood, books, heavy furniture. Every extra ~4 inches of packed earth roughly halves what gets through — about 3 feet of earth cuts it around 1,000× (Nuclear War Survival Skills, 1979, p. 23: one "halving thickness" of packed earth is 3.6 in). Crawl space: shelter under the center of the house, ring yourself with blocks or earth-filled containers, and pile mass on the floor above. Quick shelters, step by step (FEMA H-20, pp.

space: shelter under the center of the house, ring yourself with blocks or earth-filled containers, and pile mass on the floor above. Quick shelters, step by step (FEMA H-20, pp. 23–25; HS-4, p. 67): 1. Table shelter: a sturdy table or workbench in the most-underground basement corner, loaded on top and walled around with shielding. Crawl in and block the opening. 2. Door-roof shelter: walls of dressers or appliances, a roof of heavy doors propped and piled with shielding. Fill drawers and boxes with earth after they're in place — full ones are too heavy to carry. 3. Crawl-space shelter: cut an access now. Under the middle of the house, wall a spot with blocks or earth-filled containers up to the joists and pile mass on the floor above. Make sure no heavy appliance sits right above you. Dig down so you can sit up. 4. Last resort: dig a trench beside a slab house and tunnel no more than 4 feet under the slab; shore it and pile shielding on the slab inside. Ventilation: a crowded, sealed shelter gets dangerously hot in warm weather. Kearny's homemade air pump (KAP) — plans in Nuclear War Survival Skills and the ORNL Expedient Shelter Handbook — moves air without bringing in fallout dust. In a heat wave, plan on about 4 quarts of water and 10 grams of salt per person a

Expedient Shelter Handbook — moves air without bringing in fallout dust. In a heat wave, plan on about 4 quarts of water and 10 grams of salt per person a day and as few clothes as practical (NWSS 1979, p. 62). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 — shielding table and home expedient shelters; FEMA HS-4 Citizen's Guide — rating and upgrading your house; Expedient Shelter Handbook ORNL-4941 — trench and log shelters, plus full Kearny Air Pump plans; MP-79 — construction drawings for homes without basements.

🧰 Stocking the shelter FEMA says to have at least two weeks of water, food and supplies ready to carry to the shelter (H-20, p. 13). | Item | How much / what kind (FEMA H-20, pp. 29–31) | | Water | At least 1 quart per person per day, more is better. Kearny says store 15 gallons per person for two weeks (NWSS 1979, p. 71). | | Food | Canned or sealed, no cooking needed. Most adults do fine on half their usual amount — not children or pregnant women. | | Toilet | Bucket with a tight lid, liner bags, a second lidded can, bleach, toilet paper. | | Radio and light | Battery radio, flashlight, spare batteries — the radio "may be your only link." | | Medicines, babies | Two weeks of regular medicines and a first-aid kit; formula or canned milk and diapers. | | Tools | Shovel, pick, saw, hammer, crowbar, broom, nails, wire (H-20, p. 18). | - Water hiding in your house: the water heater (20–60 gallons), toilet tanks (not bowls) and the pipes — shut the main valve, open the highest faucet, draw from the lowest (H-20, pp. 31–32). Don't ration drinking water below thirst — nothing is gained by it. - Never burn charcoal indoors; any stove used inside needs good ventilation. - Toilet routine: a little bleach after

ration drinking water below thirst — nothing is gained by it. - Never burn charcoal indoors; any stove used inside needs good ventilation. - Toilet routine: a little bleach after each use, lid back on; when you can step out briefly, bury the waste 1–2 feet deep (H-20, p. 33). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20, Part 4 "Shelter Living" — supply lists, water, food and sanitation; Expedient Shelter Handbook Appendix C — emergency water storage, lights and sanitation; Shelter Management Handbook H-16 — running a shelter with a group.

⏳ How long to stay in The 7-10 rule: every 7× increase in time after the blast cuts the radiation 10× (once the fallout has finished falling). (FEMA H-20, p. 8) | Time after blast | Radiation level (example) | | 1 hour | 1,000 R/hr | | 7 hours | 100 R/hr | | 2 days | 10 R/hr | | 2 weeks | 1 R/hr | - Stay sheltered at least 12–24 hours unless officials say otherwise or fire, collapse or a medical emergency forces you out (FEMA Planning Guidance, pp. 53, 76). In heavy fallout areas it can be several days to two weeks, with only short trips out once levels drop (H-20, p. 9). USDA adds that where fallout is light or moderate you might be able to come out for part of each day after 2–3 days (PA-515, p. 6). - Late fallout decays more slowly where you are — if it arrives 8 hours after the blast, it takes about two days to fall to one-tenth (KFM report ORNL-5040, p. 69). - Gritty dust on ledges, cars or walks after an attack = assume fallout (H-20, p. 33). - Without a meter, listen for official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below. Dose yardsticks — what a short-term whole-body dose does to a group of people (DCPA home-study

official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below. Dose yardsticks — what a short-term whole-body dose does to a group of people (DCPA home-study course, p. 49): | Dose received over a short time | What to expect | | 50 R | No visible effects | | 75–100 R | Brief nausea the same day in about 1 in 10 people | | 200 R | Up to half get some radiation sickness; 5–10% need care; deaths not expected | | 450 R | Serious sickness in most; about half die within 2–4 weeks | | 600 R | Serious sickness in all; nearly all die within 1–3 weeks | Sources set the line differently: the old civil-defense course says keep short-term doses under 100 R (DCPA, p. 50); today's EPA guideline for emergency workers is 5 rem, up to 25 rem only to save lives (EPA PAG Manual, p. 46). Treat 1 R of fallout as about 1 rem (rule of thumb). Lower is always better — the dose adds up. 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 — the 7-10 rule and radiation sickness by dose; DCPA Introduction to Radiological Monitoring — dose effects and how to predict decay; EPA PAG Manual — official dose thresholds for sheltering, KI, food and water.

🧼 Cleaning yourself up (decontamination) (CDC Decontamination; EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 32) - Taking off your outer layer of clothes removes up to 90% of the fallout on you. Do it before you enter the shelter if you can, and do it gently so dust doesn't shake loose. Bag the clothes and put them away from people and pets. - Shower with soap and shampoo — no conditioner (it glues particles to hair). Don't scrub hard or scratch the skin; keep cuts covered. Keep suds out of your mouth and don't swallow the water. - No shower? Wipe exposed skin, blow your nose, wipe eyelids, ears and face with a damp cloth. - Clothes from closed drawers and closets are fine to wear. No clean clothes? Take off the outer layer, shake or brush it off, put it back on, then rewash your hands and face. - A cut or wound with fallout in it: flush with plenty of clean water or saline, or keep it covered (EPA Q&A, p. 33). - Visitors: have them strip the outer layer, bag it, and wash before coming in — then they're no danger to you (EPA Q&A, p. 33). Radiation sickness is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing gloves and a dust mask, keep your cuts (and theirs) covered,

is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing gloves and a dust mask, keep your cuts (and theirs) covered, rinse completely, then wash yourself (EPA Q&A, p. 44). - Fallout looks like sand, ash or grit. Brush or hose it off roofs and away from the house after levels drop; wear a dust mask, gloves and a hat, and wash afterward. If you must be out while dust is in the air, cover nose and mouth with a cloth (EPA Q&A, p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: CDC Decontamination for Yourself and Others — the one-page picture guide; EPA Protective Action Q&A — self-decontamination, visitors, wounds, pets and service animals.

💊 Potassium iodide (KI) - KI only protects the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. It does nothing against other fallout. Take it only when health officials say to — or, with no officials, when you have reason to believe fresh fallout or a reactor plume is arriving. Table salt and iodine tincture are not substitutes (tincture is poisonous to swallow). Iodine dietary supplements aren't either — use only FDA-approved KI. (CDC How KI Works; FDA, p. 12) - One dose protects about 24 hours. It works best just before or as the plume arrives and still helps 3–4 hours after. Avoid repeat doses for newborns and pregnant or breastfeeding women. (FDA, pp. 9–11) FDA dose by age (one dose per day) (FDA 2001, p. 9): | Who | Dose | 130 mg tablets | 65 mg tablets | | Adults over 18 (including pregnant or breastfeeding) | 130 mg | 1 | 2 | | Ages 12–18 (130 mg if 154 lb or more) | 65 mg | ½ | 1 | | Ages 3–12 | 65 mg | ½ | 1 | | 1 month – 3 years | 32 mg | ¼ | ½ | | Birth – 1 month | 16 mg | ⅛ | ¼ | Adults over 40 need it only for a very large expected exposure. To make liquid doses for small children

– 1 month | 16 mg | ⅛ | ¼ | Adults over 40 need it only for a very large expected exposure. To make liquid doses for small children from tablets, use the two FDA sheets in Nuclear-Radiation\Government-Guidance. Making liquid KI for children — the two FDA sheets give the same recipe for one 130 mg tablet or two 65 mg tablets (FDA, one 130 mg tablet; FDA, two 65 mg tablets): 1. Put the tablet(s) in a small bowl with 4 teaspoons of water. Soak 1 minute. 2. Crush with the back of a spoon until there are no large pieces. 3. Stir in 4 teaspoons of milk, chocolate milk, orange juice, cola, formula, raspberry syrup or water. You now have 8 teaspoons of KI liquid. 4. Give once a day: 19 and older — 8 tsp; 13–18 years and 150 lb or more — 8 tsp; 13–18 under 150 lb — 4 tsp; 4–12 years — 4 tsp; over 1 month to 3 years — 2 tsp; birth to 1 month — 1 tsp. 5. Keep leftover liquid in the refrigerator; throw it out after 7 days. (The liquid sheet uses 150 lb for teens; the 2001 FDA guidance says 70 kg, about 154 lb. Either way a near-adult-size teen gets the adult dose.) - A nursing mother's KI does not protect her baby — the baby

FDA guidance says 70 kg, about 154 lb. Either way a near-adult-size teen gets the adult dose.) - A nursing mother's KI does not protect her baby — the baby needs its own dose, and newborns given KI should see a doctor afterward if one can be found (FDA, pp. 9–10; EPA Q&A, p. 38). - Repeat daily only while the risk of breathing or eating radioactive iodine continues (FDA, p. 9). Once the cloud has passed, FDA says the protection is controlling the food — especially fresh milk — not more KI. Stored grain and canned milk or vegetables kept weeks to months carry no radioiodine risk (FDA, p. 11). - Too much is dangerous too — don't double up "to be safe" (CDC). 📚 Go deeper: FDA KI dosing guidance — the official dose table and timing; FDA liquid KI sheet — step by step for children; CDC How KI Works — what it does and doesn't do.
