🥫 Food and water (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 29; FDA; Nuclear War Survival Skills Ch. 8) - Food that was indoors is fine. Sealed cans, jars and bags that were outside are fine after wiping the outside — bag the wiping cloths. Stored grain and canned food have no radioactive-iodine risk. - Don't eat garden produce or anything left uncovered outdoors until levels have dropped and it's declared clear — then wash and peel it. Leafy vegetables: strip the outer leaves of cabbage and lettuce and wash the rest thoroughly. Roots and tubers: normal washing and peeling is enough. Fruit: wash before eating. (FB 2107, p. 14; PA-515, p. 7) - Don't drink fresh milk from animals grazing fallout-covered pasture for the first weeks (radioactive iodine concentrates in milk). Milk made into cheese and aged two months or more is fine — the radioactive iodine decays away (it loses half its strength every 8 days — USDA Ag Handbook 234, p. 9; USDA puts the wait at 30–60 days — PA-515, p. 8). If you have a baby, keep canned or dry milk in a protected place. - Water: bottled and sealed water is certain. Covered wells, tanks and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil,

cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil, let it settle several hours, and pour off the clear water — or filter it through a bucket of packed earth. Both remove most fallout particles. Then disinfect as usual. - Cover rain barrels, tanks and well heads ahead of time. Water sources, safest first (NWSS 1979, pp. 76–77): deep wells and covered tanks → covered shallow wells → deep lakes → shallow ponds → streams (worst after the first heavy rains) → roof runoff → melted snow. With the power off, a well can still be used with a homemade bail-can on a rope. Settling method (NWSS 1979, pp. 78–79): 1. Fill a bucket three-quarters full of the doubtful water. 2. Dig clay or clayey soil from at least 4 inches below the surface (fallout stays near the top). 3. Stir in about 1 inch of dry clay for every 4 inches of water until it's all suspended. 4. Let it settle at least 6 hours. The clay carries the fallout down. 5. Dip or siphon off the clear water, then disinfect it. (USDA says settle a day, then strain through cloth; for stock, stir up a pond's mud bottom and let it settle — PA-515, p. 8.) Earth

water, then disinfect it. (USDA says settle a day, then strain through cloth; for stock, stir up a pond's mud bottom and let it settle — PA-515, p. 8.) Earth filter (NWSS 1979, pp. 77–78): 1. Punch about a dozen nail holes, from the bottom upward, within 2 inches of the center of the bottom of a 5-gallon can or bucket. 2. Put in 1½ inches of washed pebbles, then one layer of towel or burlap cut a bit bigger than the can. 3. Add 6–7 inches of crumbled soil with some clay in it, dug from 4+ inches deep, pressed down in layers. Not pure clay (too tight) or sand (too loose). 4. Cover with one layer of towel held by a few stones. Set the can on sticks over a pan. 5. Pour in (settled) water. Expect about 6 quarts an hour at first, 2 quarts an hour later. If it runs faster than a quart in 10 minutes, repack the soil. Replace the soil after about 50 quarts. Disinfect the filtered water. Disinfecting afterward: boil, or use plain unscented bleach — 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon, double if cloudy or very cold, wait 30 minutes (EPA Emergency Disinfection, pp. 1–2). 📚 Go deeper: Nuclear War Survival Skills 1979, Ch. 8 — water sources, bail-can, settling and earth filter; USDA

or very cold, wait 30 minutes (EPA Emergency Disinfection, pp. 1–2). 📚 Go deeper: Nuclear War Survival Skills 1979, Ch. 8 — water sources, bail-can, settling and earth filter; USDA PA-515 Fallout and Your Farm Food — cleaning home-grown food; FDA Accidental Radioactive Contamination of Food and Feeds — official food and milk limits.

🐄 Livestock and gardens (USDA FB 2107, pp. 8–14, PA-516; Oregon ODOE, p. 2) - Shelter animals if you can (a barn helps), and take them off pasture. Feed protected feed — hay from inside the stack, covered silage, grain from closed bins. - Water from a covered well, tank or flowing spring is best; open pond water clears more slowly but improves quickly. - Hold off on slaughter, fresh milk and eggs until levels drop. - Gardens: stop harvesting; after levels drop, wash and peel produce. Fallout on soil decays and is diluted by digging it in. More from USDA FB 2107 (pp. 8–14): - Animals are as sensitive to radiation as people. Crowd them into the barn — they shield each other; ventilation, not floor space, is the limit. Dairy animals first — milk them before fallout arrives if you can, and turn calves in with the cows (pp. 9–11). - Feed: fallout only coats the outside of a haystack or stack of feed bags. Peel off the outer layer and feed the inside; a tarp over a field stack ahead of time is enough (p. 10). - Tanks and ponds: use what's already in a covered tank first. Pond water usually clears in a few days — keep stock off it a few days longer if it rains (pp. 9–10). - Poultry stand about twice the radiation

first. Pond water usually clears in a few days — keep stock off it a few days longer if it rains (pp. 9–10). - Poultry stand about twice the radiation cattle do; eggs clear soon after hens get clean feed (PA-515, p. 8). - Meat: an animal exposed only to outside radiation can be eaten if slaughtered before it shows sickness; keep hide and gut contents off the meat. Wash fallout off animals with any water, wearing coveralls, gloves and boots (p. 12). - Pasture: lightly contaminated pasture can be grazed again after one to a few weeks (p. 13). Bees: don't move or harvest hives until checked (ODOE, p. 2). Long-term garden choices: radioactive strontium acts like calcium. Liming acid soil cuts how much plants take up. Alfalfa, clover, soybeans and leafy greens take up more than grains, grasses, corn, potatoes and fruit — favor the latter on contaminated ground (FB 2107, p. 13). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 2107 Defense Against Radioactive Fallout on the Farm — livestock, feed, water, milk and crops; USDA Ag Handbook 234 — the science of fallout on soil, crops and animals; USDA Radiological Monitoring Handbook — checking pasture, water and livestock with a meter.

📟 Measuring radiation - A meter turns guessing into decisions — when to leave the shelter, which room is safest, whether the water is clear. - KFM (Kearny Fallout Meter): a homemade meter from a can, foil and paper. Build it before you need it. The patterns must print exactly to scale — check against a ruler; OISM warns online copies of the templates aren't fully reliable and recommends the printed book. Full patterns and tables: ORNL-5040 and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix C. - Old civil-defense meters turn up at sales: the yellow CD V-715 reads high levels (fallout); the CD V-700 is a low-range Geiger counter for checking food, water and people. Manuals and a home-study course are in Nuclear-Radiation\Measuring-Radiation. What a KFM is made of (ORNL-5040, pp. 33, 39): an 8-ounce can (or a cut-down soup can), 2 square feet of aluminum foil, clean thread, clear plastic, doorbell wire. A drying agent goes in the bottom — gypsum from heated drywall, or silica gel, not calcium chloride or salt. Charge it by rubbing a plastic ruler on dry paper. Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69–73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the paper scale. 2. Hold it on a stick about 3 feet above the ground for a set time — 1 minute if you have no idea of the level

the paper scale. 2. Hold it on a stick about 3 feet above the ground for a set time — 1 minute if you have no idea of the level — then read again. The table on the meter turns the drop into a dose rate. 3. Dose = dose rate × time. At 1,200 R/hr, a 30-second dash outside is 10 R. 4. Keep a daily dose record for every person, and use the meter indoors to find the lowest-dose spot in your shelter, then add shielding there. Above about 90% humidity it can't be charged — make and use the dry-bucket (ORNL-5040, pp. 65, 73). Check the drying agent. | | Leaves leak charge fast | Modern thread and floss may

📍 Our area - The region's only operating nuclear power plant is the Columbia Generating Station at Hanford, Washington — roughly 350 miles from the Illinois Valley, far outside its planning zones. (Oregon ODOE, p. 1) Its zones are a 10-mile plume zone (Oregon is not in it) and a 50-mile ingestion zone that reaches parts of northern Oregon (ODOE, p. 2). - The more realistic threats here are fallout drifting from detonations elsewhere and fallout carried across the Pacific on west winds. After Chernobyl, radioactive iodine showed up in milk in northwest Oregon. (Nuclear War Survival Skills, 1987) Even in the 1960s, Chinese test fallout put measurable radioactive iodine in American milk (NWSS 1979, pp. 117–118). Winds across the U.S. run mostly west to east, but change day to day (FEMA H-20, p. 7). - OISM, publisher of Nuclear War Survival Skills, is in Cave Junction — the printed edition (with accurate KFM patterns) may be easy to get locally. - Stay tuned locally: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts on seven frequencies, 162.400–162.550 MHz (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 167). Which stations reach the valley, and local AM/FM, are on the Illinois Valley page. 📚 Go deeper: Oregon ODOE Hanford pamphlet — Oregon's zones and farm steps; Nuclear War Survival Skills 1987 (OISM, Cave Junction) — trans-Pacific fallout and the corrected KFM patterns; FEMA Planning Guidance — emergency alert channels.The 1987

(CPSC Portable Generator Hazards, p. 1) - Never refuel a hot or running engine. Keep the can touching the tank while pouring (stops static sparks). (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding") — use a transfer switch or interlock. It can kill someone working on the lines. - Capacitors bite. Motor capacitors (and microwave ovens) can hold a deadly charge after unplugging. Discharge across the terminals with an insulated screwdriver or a resistor before touching. - Pull the spark plug wire before working on a mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns. - Keep away from diesel injection lines while the engine turns. The injection pump pushes fuel at 4,000–10,000 psi (Practical Action

mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns. - Keep away from diesel injection lines while the engine turns. The injection pump pushes fuel at 4,000–10,000 psi (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 13). Never hold a hand or face near a cracked line or a nozzle that is spraying. (Rule of thumb) - Never carry a chainsaw or fuel in the passenger part of a vehicle. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training, p. 34)

⛽ Small gas engines: why it won't start Every engine needs three things: compression, spark and fuel. Find which one is missing. (MAVCC Small Engine Repair, p. 590) 1. Fuel: pull the plug, cover the hole with a finger and pull the starter 2–3 times. A wet finger means fuel is arriving. If dry, check: fuel in the tank, shutoff valve open, cap vent not blocked, carburetor bowl (drain it — water or gum?), fuel filter and line. (MAVCC, pp. 595–598) 2. Spark: put a spare plug on the plug wire, rest it against the metal head and crank. A bright blue spark is good. Yellow, weak or none = clean or replace the plug, check the kill-switch wire, then the coil/magneto. (MAVCC, pp. 599–600) 3. Compression: spin the flywheel backward against compression — a sharp rebound is good. Weak = loose plug or head, stuck valve, worn rings. With a compression gauge, crank at least six times before you read it. (MAVCC, pp. 602–603) Quick troubleshooting chart (MAVCC, p. 592): | What it does | Look at these first | | Won't start, plug dry | Empty tank, fuel valve shut, plugged tank vent, stuck or clogged float valve, blocked filter or line, choke not closing | | Won't start, plug wet | Choke stuck or overused, stale fuel, water in fuel, flooded (mixture too rich), too much oil

blocked filter or line, choke not closing | | Won't start, plug wet | Choke stuck or overused, stale fuel, water in fuel, flooded (mixture too rich), too much oil in 2-stroke mix, fuel-soaked air filter | | Won't start, no spark | Kill button or wire grounded, bad plug, bad plug wire, dirty or wrongly gapped points (older engines), bad coil | | Won't start, weak compression | Loose plug or head bolts, blown head gasket, valve stuck open, worn rings or bore | | Starts but lacks power | Dirty air filter, carburetor out of adjustment, clogged muffler or exhaust port, low compression, governor fault | | Overheats | Cooling fins or blower blocked, engine overloaded, clogged muffler, late ignition timing | | Smokes or uses oil | Wrong oil, oil diluted by a rich mixture, worn rings, clogged crankcase breather, wrong 2-stroke mix | | Kicks back when you pull it | Ignition timing off, sheared flywheel key, loose blade | Old fuel is the #1 problem. Gas goes stale in about 60 days without stabilizer (sooner with ethanol). For longer storage, drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, or add stabilizer and run it a few minutes so it reaches the carburetor. Keep cans sealed — water in ethanol gas separates and ruins engines. (Oklahoma Extension BAE-1746, p. 2) - Ethanol is a solvent. In

few minutes so it reaches the carburetor. Keep cans sealed — water in ethanol gas separates and ruins engines. (Oklahoma Extension BAE-1746, p. 2) - Ethanol is a solvent. In an old, neglected engine it can loosen years of deposits that then clog the filter and tiny carburetor passages — the main reason for "ethanol trouble." Older engines (before about 1995) may also have rubber or cork parts that suffer. (BAE-1746, pp. 1–2) Cleaning a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with air. (AAVIM, p. 97) - Plastic or nylon parts no more than 30 minutes; never soak cork or coated floats. (AAVIM, p. 95; p. 93) - Don't poke jets with wire — it enlarges them. Use a bristle, fishing line or air. - Always fit new gaskets. Float too high = floods; too low = starves. A metal float with gasoline sloshing inside, or a crushed one, must be replaced. (AAVIM, pp. 92–93) Two-stroke fuel (chainsaws, trimmers): mix oil at the ratio printed on the engine or in its manual (MAVCC, p. 186). Never run straight gas — it seizes the engine in minutes. Rule of thumb: most modern saws are 50:1 (about 2.6 oz of 2-stroke oil per gallon); older gear is often 16:1–32:1. Don't

gas — it seizes the engine in minutes. Rule of thumb: most modern saws are 50:1 (about 2.6 oz of 2-stroke oil per gallon); older gear is often 16:1–32:1. Don't mix mineral and synthetic 2-stroke oils. Routine care: check oil every use (4-strokes), clean the air filter often (a choked filter makes an engine run rich and weak), keep cooling fins clear, replace the plug yearly. Replacing a starter rope: for a wrap-around (non-recoil) starter, use 3/16-inch braided nylon rope, usually 4–5 feet long — enough to wrap the pulley 3–5 times plus about 6 inches. Singe the cut ends with a match so they don't fray, and tie a figure-eight or double overhand knot in each end. (AAVIM, pp. 14–15) Recoil starters take thinner rope — most often 5/32 inch — that fills the pulley groove without binding. (AAVIM, p. 20) 📷 What the parts look like: Carburetor, Spark plug, Magneto. 📚 Go deeper: MAVCC Small Engine Repair — full troubleshooting unit and job sheets; AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2 — carburetor, starter and valve repair step by step; TM 9-2805-262-14 6 HP engine — Army maintenance checks for a small engine; Oklahoma BAE-1746 — ethanol fuel in small engines.

🚜 Diesel engines Diesels have no spark plugs — squeezing the air makes it hot enough to light the fuel. So a diesel needs compression and clean fuel with no air in the lines. (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 5) Diesels usually need less maintenance than gasoline engines because they have no ignition system. (FM 5-424, p. 114) Won't start or keeps dying: suspect air in the fuel lines (an "air lock"), an empty tank or a clogged filter. (Practical Action, p. 12) Bleed the air out (p. 16): 1. Fill the tank with clean diesel and open the tank valve. 2. Loosen the bleed screw on the fuel filter (and on the injection pump) until fuel runs out in a steady stream with no bubbles. Tighten it. 3. Loosen the injection line nut at the injector and crank the engine until fuel comes out without foam. 4. Tighten the nut and check every joint for leaks. What the smoke and symptoms tell you (Practical Action, pp. 11–14): | Symptom | Common causes | | Lots of black smoke | Faulty injector (p. 14) | | Overheating | Low coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank or lines, clogged air cleaner, wrong valve timing, overload, lots

water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank or lines, clogged air cleaner, wrong valve timing, overload, lots of stopping and starting, idling when not needed | | Burns oil | Worn or wrongly fitted piston rings, worn cylinder, damaged seals or head gasket | | Knocking or noise | Poor-quality fuel, loose connecting rod, worn or badly adjusted parts | Cleaning an injector nozzle: soak the nozzle valve and body in clean diesel, scrub the soot off with a copper (not steel) wire brush, and check the needle slides freely. (Practical Action, p. 15) Don't run a diesel generator lightly loaded for long. It runs too cool, soot builds up in the engine and exhaust ("wet stacking"), and over time this can permanently damage it. (FEMA P-1019, p. 150) Give it a real load when you run it. Diesel fuel catches fire less easily than gasoline, but once burning a diesel fire is fierce (Practical Action, p. 6). Cold-weather gelling, water and fuel substitutes are in the Fuel guide. 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair and Maintenance — short, plain-language diesel fault-finding; Navy Construction Mechanic — diesel fuel systems, governors and bleeding; TM 9-8000 Principles of Automotive Vehicles — how every engine and vehicle system works.

🪚 Chainsaws, crosscut saws and axes - A sharp chain throws chips; a dull one makes dust — and dust clogs the filter and raises kickback risk. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course, p. 25) - The four chain rules: sharp, depth gauges set right, correctly tensioned (more bar and chain trouble comes from wrong tension than anything else), and well oiled. The chain should not hang below the bar but should still turn freely by hand. (USFS, p. 31) - Filing: use the file size for your chain, with a guide. Hold the file level with about one-fifth of it above the cutter's top plate, guide mark parallel to the chain. File from the inside of each cutter outward, all of one side, then turn the saw around. Keep all cutters the same length. If the chrome is chipped, file until the chip is gone. (USFS, pp. 33–34) - Depth gauges (the little humps in front of each cutter): check with a gauge tool every few sharpenings, file down only to the tool, and round off the front. Never file one lower than the tool. (USFS, p. 34) - After several hand filings, the angles drift. The Forest Service then grinds the chain on a chain grinder to restore them — if you have none, file slowly and check angles against a new chain. (USFS, p. 32)

Forest Service then grinds the chain on a chain grinder to restore them — if you have none, file slowly and check angles against a new chain. (USFS, p. 32) Cleaning a saw (USFS, p. 31): - Take off the bar and chain. Clean the bar groove from the tip toward the base, clear the oil holes, check the rails for wear or flared edges, grease the nose sprocket, and turn the bar over when you refit it so it wears evenly. - Air filter: tap it gently clean. Never blow it out with an air hose and never wash it in saw fuel — a damaged filter lets grit into the engine. - Spark plug: the tip should be tan (beige), not black, and dry. - Spark arrester screen in the muffler: replace it if it has any holes. Illinois Valley summers are fire season — a saw spitting sparks into dry grass can start a wildfire. - Check the chain brake, loose bolts, and the rubber anti-vibration mounts. Things that make kickback more likely (USFS, p. 32): a loose or dull chain, wrong filing angles, depth gauges filed too low or left square, loose rivets or cracked links, and anti-kickback parts removed. Running out of fuel isn't the end of cutting. A sharp crosscut saw and ax still fell and buck trees. Raker depth for a crosscut: 0.008

and anti-kickback parts removed. Running out of fuel isn't the end of cutting. A sharp crosscut saw and ax still fell and buck trees. Raker depth for a crosscut: 0.008 in for hard, dry wood up to 0.030 in for soft, springy wood; start at about 0.012 in. (USFS Crosscut Saw Manual, p. 16) Set the teeth only enough to stop binding — about 0.010 in is a good first try; up to 0.030 in for soft, punky wood. (Crosscut Saw Manual, p. 21) More in Saws That Sing and An Ax to Grind. 📷 Chainsaw, Crosscut saw. 📚 Go deeper: USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course — maintenance, felling and bucking; MAVCC Chain Saw Repair — engine, clutch and oiler repair; USFS Crosscut Saw Manual — filing and setting a crosscut; USFS Saws That Sing — using crosscut saws safely.

🔋 Generators Where to put it (CPSC, p. 1): - Outdoors, far from doors, windows and vents, exhaust pointed away from buildings. Put a battery-powered CO alarm in the house. - In rain, run it under an open, canopy-like roof on dry ground where water can't puddle under it. Dry your hands before touching it. - Use heavy outdoor extension cords rated for more than the total watts on them, with all three prongs and no cuts. Don't pinch them in doors or windows. - Turn it off and let it cool before refueling. Keep its fuel outside living areas. - Set it nearly level — the Army 3 kW set allows no more than 15° of tilt — on planks or timbers if the ground is soft. (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) Maintenance (rule of thumb — the generator's own manual comes first): oil change every 50–100 hours (sooner when new), clean air filter, fresh or stabilized fuel, run it under load for 20–30 minutes once a month. Machines that sit idle for long periods should be "exercised" on a schedule to keep oil moving and moisture out. (TM 5-683, p. 41) Load: add up the running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second — rule of thumb). Keep steady load under

you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second — rule of thumb). Keep steady load under about 80% of the generator's rating. - Motors need extra generator size. When a big motor starts, voltage dips and other motors can stall. Unplug the other loads, start the big motor, then plug the small loads back in. (FM 5-424, p. 113) - A generator feeding only heaters, cookers or light bulbs (a "resistive" load) can carry only about 80% of its kVA rating — e.g. a 6.25 kVA Army set carries 5 kW. (FM 5-424, p. 115) Grounding: follow the generator's own manual. The Army 3 kW set procedure (TM 5-6115-271-14, pp. 60–61): - Drive a ground rod — or a ¾-inch copper or steel pipe — at least 8 ft into the ground. - In rock or hard ground, a buried metal plate can stand in (the manual gives sizes). - Soak the ground around the rod with water to help it conduct. - Run copper wire from the rod to the generator's ground stud — braided cable is best, No. 6 or heavier solid wire will do — and tighten it securely. No output but the engine runs? Check the breaker on the generator, then the brushes and voltage regulator (most small generators). A generator that

do — and tighten it securely. No output but the engine runs? Check the breaker on the generator, then the brushes and voltage regulator (most small generators). A generator that sat unused can lose its residual magnetism — see "flashing the field" below. 📚 Go deeper: CPSC Portable Generator Hazards — CO, shock and fire rules on one page; TM 5-6115-271-14 3 kW generator — grounding, troubleshooting tables and field flashing; FM 5-424 Electrical Systems — picking and loading a generator, wiring and grounding; FEMA P-1019 — generator sizing and fuel planning.

⚙️ Electric motors: testing and repair When a motor won't run, check the simple things first, in this order (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, pp. 24–25): 1. Power: is the right voltage reaching the motor terminals? Check fuses, breakers and the switch. 2. Load: take the belt off. If the motor now runs, the machine it drives is stuck. 3. Bearings: power off, turn the shaft by hand. If it won't turn freely, a bearing is dry, worn or stuck. 4. Thermal protector: many motors have a red reset button; others reset themselves once cool. A tripped protector means something else is wrong — find it. 5. Starting switch: a motor that hums but won't start, yet runs if you spin the shaft by hand, has a fault in its starting circuit (see below). 6. Windings: a burned winding has a strong burned smell, and you may see charred insulation. Single-phase motor hums but won't start (pumps, compressors, shop tools): suspect the start capacitor or the centrifugal start switch, which should click open at about ¾ speed (Illinois, p. 28). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure. Replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage (rule of thumb). Switch contacts can

or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure. Replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage (rule of thumb). Switch contacts can be dirty, burned or pitted, or a wire can burn in two. (Illinois, p. 24) Basic winding checks with a meter (Navy Electrician's Mate): - Windings must have no opens (infinite ohms through a winding), no shorts (much lower reading than its twin), and no grounds (any reading from a winding to the frame). - The three windings of a 3-phase motor should read nearly the same resistance; a high reading between any two leads means an open winding. (Navy Electrician's Mate, p. 237) - Insulation test (megger): right after shutdown while warm and dry, with capacitors disconnected. At least 0.5 megohm for motors 250 V and under, 1 megohm up to 1000 V. Write readings down — a steady fall over months warns of trouble even above the minimum. (TM 5-683, p. 54) - Armatures (brushed motors): test bar-to-bar on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). (Navy EM, pp. 238–239) Bearings: a rumbling or hot bearing is the most common motor failure. Replace with the same number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to no more than about 200 °F (oil bath or

is the most common motor failure. Replace with the same number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to no more than about 200 °F (oil bath or oven, not a flame). (Navy EM, p. 225) Never wash sealed bearings in solvent — factory-sealed bearings shouldn't be disturbed. Open bearings get repacked half to two-thirds full of motor bearing grease; too much grease makes heat. (Illinois, p. 23; TM 5-683, p. 58) Brushes and commutators (drills, saws, mixers, car starters, DC motors): replace brushes that stick, are chipped, or are worn to about half their original length (or to within ⅛ inch of a riveted clip). (Navy EM, p. 228) Seat new brushes by pulling fine sandpaper (grit toward the brush) under them in the direction the motor turns, lifting the brushes on the return stroke, then blow out the carbon dust. (Navy EM, p. 229) A blackened, grooved commutator can be cleaned with a commutator stone or fine sandpaper — never emery cloth; emery dust conducts electricity and causes shorts (Illinois, p. 24) — or turned lightly on a lathe (no more than 0.010 in per cut). (Navy EM, p. 233) Keeping spare motors (salvage is your parts store): wipe them clean, lubricate the bearings, grease the bare shaft against rust, wrap them in heavy paper, and store them dry. (Illinois, pp. 23–24) Rewinding a burned motor

parts store): wipe them clean, lubricate the bearings, grease the bare shaft against rust, wrap them in heavy paper, and store them dry. (Illinois, pp. 23–24) Rewinding a burned motor (Braymer & Roe Rewinding Small Motors; DOE Repair Specifications): - Before stripping, record everything: turns per coil, wire size, coil span (slots), how coils connect, and lead markings. Photograph each step. (Braymer & Roe, p. 12) - Strip old windings at no more than about 680 °F (360 °C) or the iron core is damaged. (DOE Repair Specifications, p. 8) - Rewind with the same total copper area per turn and same turns (two thinner wires in parallel can replace one thick one). Varnish and bake below about 195 °F to dry. (DOE, p. 9; p. 11) - Small burned motors are often easier to replace from salvage than to rewind — keep a stock. 📷 Commutator), Centrifugal switch, Megger. 📚 Go deeper: Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use — plain-English motor types, care and fault-finding; Navy Electrician's Mate — bearings, brushes, armature and stator tests; TM 5-683 — insulation tests and full troubleshooting tables; Braymer & Roe Rewinding Small Motors — rewinding step by step.

🔁 Motors as generators What works best, easiest first: 1. Permanent-magnet DC motors (treadmill motors, wheelchair, scooter, some cordless tool motors): spin them and they make DC directly. Output voltage rises with speed, so choose one that makes at least 14–15 V at the speed you can actually turn it to charge a 12 V battery. Add a blocking diode so the battery can't run it as a motor. (Rule of thumb) 2. Car alternators: built-in rectifier and regulator, but they need high speed (rule of thumb: about 1,500+ rpm — step-up pulleys or belts for wind, water or pedals) and a battery connected to power their field — they are not self-starting. The field draws about 3 A, which wastes a lot at low power. (Alternator and Regulator Servicing, p. 11) 3. Induction motors (ordinary AC motors) as generators: drive it about 1–5% faster than its synchronous speed — e.g. a motor rated 1725 rpm (1800 synchronous) is driven at about 1820–1890 rpm. Output rises with the extra speed. (DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 54) On its own (not tied to the grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. Sources disagree here: the DOE handbook (same page) and the European hydro guide say an induction generator can't run cut off from the grid (ESHA Layman's Guidebook Pt 2, p. 30), while village hydro

DOE handbook (same page) and the European hydro guide say an induction generator can't run cut off from the grid (ESHA Layman's Guidebook Pt 2, p. 30), while village hydro schemes run them off-grid with a capacitor bank and controller (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M, p. 23). Expect some trial and error. - Rule of thumb: start with run capacitors whose current at rated voltage roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70–80% of the motor's rating as output (rule of thumb). Needs a ballast (dump) load or controller so voltage doesn't swing as loads switch. Aging capacitors make frequency creep up; a capacitor running hotter than the others is failing — feel them once a month. Too many capacitors overheat the generator. (Practical Action, pp. 23–26) 4. Build a permanent-magnet alternator from magnets and magnet wire for a wind turbine or slow water wheel — full plans in Hugh Piggott's Axial Flux Alternator and PMG Construction Manual. His PMG makes about 180 W (15 A at 12 V) at only 420 rpm — slow enough to drive directly from blades. (Piggott PMG Construction Manual, p. 4) Rules for any homemade generator: - Never let a wind or water generator run with no load — it overspeeds and can destroy itself. Use

PMG Construction Manual, p. 4) Rules for any homemade generator: - Never let a wind or water generator run with no load — it overspeeds and can destroy itself. Use a diversion (dump-load) charge controller, not a solar controller (solar controllers disconnect the source). The dump load can be light bulbs or a heating element — a water-heater element puts the spare power to use. (DFID-ITDG Small Wind Systems, p. 16; DOE Wind Power for Farms, p. 122) - Watch the battery voltage. Over about 14 V on a 12 V battery means it's charging too hard — use more power or divert it. (Piggott Axial Flux, p. 41) - Flashing the field: if a generator won't build up voltage, it may have lost its residual magnetism. The Army 3 kW set does it with two 1.5 V flashlight batteries touched momentarily to the regulator terminals (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 73); village hydro operators use a 6 V or 12 V battery on brush-type generators (Practical Action, p. 26). Use the lowest voltage that works, touch it only briefly, then try again. (Rule of thumb) - Creek power in Oregon: under Oregon law all water belongs to the public — owning creek frontage doesn't by itself give you the right to divert it, and a hydro project needs a license (OWRD Water Rights in Oregon, p. 7; OWRD Minor Hydroelectric License

creek frontage doesn't by itself give you the right to divert it, and a hydro project needs a license (OWRD Water Rights in Oregon, p. 7; OWRD Minor Hydroelectric License Guide, p. 1). Screen your intake so fish aren't pulled in (ODFW Fish Screening Criteria). - Old method: the 1939 North Dakota circular shows turning a car generator into a 6-volt wind charger, and the DOE Wind Power for Farms handbook covers matching any generator to a rotor. 📷 Induction generator, Car alternator). 📚 Go deeper: Piggott PMG Construction Manual — build a slow-speed permanent-magnet generator; DFID-ITDG Small Wind Systems — controllers, dump loads and batteries; Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M — running and fixing a small hydro plant; North Dakota Homemade Six-Volt Wind-Electric Plants — 1939 car-generator wind charger.

🚑 The first few minutes When someone is hurt, check in this order and act on the first problem you find (FM 4-25.11, p. 18–19): 1. Protect yourself — gloves or a clean plastic bag on your hands if there's blood. 2. Responsive? Tap and ask "Are you OK?" 3. Breathing? If not, open the airway and give rescue breaths. 4. Bleeding? Press hard on the wound with a thick, clean cloth. A tourniquet is the last resort, for an arm or leg that keeps bleeding through a pressure dressing (FM 4-25.11, p. 48). 5. Shock? Weak, fast pulse, pale cold sweat, confusion. Lay them down with feet a little raised, keep warm; unconscious = on the side, nothing by mouth (WTND — shock). 6. Neck or back injury? Don't move them unless their life is in immediate danger. There is no 24-hour ER in the Illinois Valley — see Local contacts in the Illinois Valley guide. 📚 Go deeper: FM 4-25.11 First Aid — the full casualty check; WTND — bleeding — pressure points, closing cuts.

💊 Using found or expired medicines 1. Identify it. US pills must carry an imprint code. Open Pill-Identifier\PILL-IDENTIFIER.html, type the code, then check that the color, shape and size also match — the same code can be two different drugs (e.g. "I2" is ibuprofen 200 mg or amitriptyline 25 mg depending on size; "N 4" is nitroglycerin or a diet pill). No code at all = a supplement, a foreign or compounded product, or an illegal pill. 2. Never trust street pills. Pills that didn't come from a pharmacy can be counterfeits pressed with fentanyl — fake blue "M30" oxycodone, Xanax and Adderall are common, and many contain a deadly dose. 3. Look it up before giving it. In the WHO Model Formulary or MSF Essential Drugs (Medicines\), read what it treats, the dose, who must not take it, and interactions. For children, use the WHO Formulary for Children — children's doses go by weight. Give the right dose, no more and no less; finish every antibiotic course; antibiotics do nothing for colds (WTND, p. 56). 4. Expired medicines. Most tablets and capsules kept sealed, cool and dry lose potency slowly — military testing extended most stockpiled lots by years (88% of 3,005 lots, on average by 66 months), and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date (Zilker 2019, p. 54–55). That was warehouse storage, and inhalers and

(88% of 3,005 lots, on average by 66 months), and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date (Zilker 2019, p. 54–55). That was warehouse storage, and inhalers and epinephrine often failed. But: - Don't rely on expired or badly stored: insulin (lasts only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle; WHO: discard 8 weeks after opening, p. 276), epinephrine pens (weaker when expired — but an expired pen with clear liquid is better than none in anaphylaxis), and mixed liquid antibiotics (amoxicillin suspension: 14 days in the fridge). - Throw out anything discolored, crumbling, sticky or smelling odd — especially tetracycline-family antibiotics, which can damage the kidneys when degraded. Also caked, brownish rehydration salts, and melted creams or suppositories (MSF, p. 648). - Don't raise the dose to make up for age — MSF warns of overdose. Heart and seizure medicines need exact doses, so respect their dates (p. 649). - Store medicines cool and dry (not the bathroom, kitchen or a car — a vehicle can reach 50–60 °C, MSF, p. 647), in their original containers, out of children's reach. 5. The biggest dangers - Allergy — face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. After any reaction, never use that

dangers - Allergy — face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. After any reaction, never use that medicine again (WTND, p. 70). - Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — no more than 4,000 mg a day for adults, counting every product; it's hidden in Norco, Vicodin, Percocet and many cold medicines. Too much causes liver failure (MSF, p. 244) — and an overdose needs urgent care even if the person feels fine (WHO, p. 68). - Opioids — a dose that's normal for someone used to them can stop the breathing of someone who isn't, or of a child. Never combine with benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Klonopin), alcohol or other sedatives. Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid overdose — keep some. - Children — no cough/cold medicines under age 2, no aspirin for children or teens (Reye syndrome — WHO, p. 226). - Interactions — check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 (24/7, while phones work). 6. Measure it right (WTND ch. 8): 1 g = 1,000 mg · 1 mg = 1,000 mcg · 1 grain = 65 mg · 1 teaspoon = 5 ml · 1 tablespoon = 15 ml. Kitchen spoons vary — mark one at 5 ml measured with a syringe. Check the mg on the label:

1 teaspoon = 5 ml · 1 tablespoon = 15 ml. Kitchen spoons vary — mark one at 5 ml measured with a syringe. Check the mg on the label: strengths differ. Never give medicine by mouth to someone asleep, unconscious or having a seizure (p. 62). 7. Getting rid of medicines — mix with coffee grounds or cat litter and seal; flush only what the FDA lists, like fentanyl patches — deadly to children even after use (FDA). Stock up now: ask your doctor about extra supplies of the medicines your household depends on, and keep an emergency kit (wound care, pain/fever medicine, antihistamines, oral rehydration salts, naloxone). 📚 Go deeper: WTND Green Pages — uses, doses and warnings for each medicine; MSF Essential Drugs, p. 646 — storage, spoilage and expiry; Zilker 2019 — what testing shows about old medicines.

💧 Diarrhea and dehydration: the homemade drink Most children who die of diarrhea die of dehydration. Signs: thirst, little or dark urine, dry mouth, sunken tearless eyes, skin that stays up when pinched. Start the drink at the first watery stools (WTND, p. 151–152). Rehydration Drink: in 1 liter of clean water, stir ½ level teaspoon of salt and 8 level teaspoons of sugar. Taste before adding the sugar: it must be less salty than tears. - Give sips every 5 minutes until they urinate normally — 3 liters or more a day for a large person, at least 1 liter for a small child. - Keep giving it even if they vomit. Keep feeding, and keep breastfeeding babies. - No repeat doses of medicines that can build up until they urinate normally (WTND, p. 54). - Getting worse, or other danger signs? Get medical help. 📚 Go deeper: WTND, p. 152 — the sugar and cereal recipes, with pictures; MSF Clinical Guidelines — severe diarrhea and cholera.

🌿 Medicinal plants — go carefully Signs a home remedy probably doesn't work: many different "cures" for one illness, disgusting remedies, and anything using animal or human waste — that causes infections (WTND, p. 10–11). Deadly look-alike: foxglove leaves have been mistaken for comfrey, with fatal "comfrey tea" poisonings — and comfrey itself can harm the liver (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 243). If in doubt, don't — and call the Poison Center. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Monographs Vol 1 — evidence plant by plant (Vols 1–4); WSU Poisonous Plants of the PNW, p. 28 — foxglove and other local poisons.

Recheck (WTND, p. 57) | | A child got into medicines | Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 | 📚 Go deeper: WTND — poisoning — common poisons and what to do.

Ham (Amateur), CB, Shortwave, GMRS/FRS & MURS — how they work and how to use them This guide explains, in plain language, how to communicate by radio when the internet and phones are down. It covers what each type of radio is, what it can do, which frequencies/channels matter in an emergency, and the basic procedures for calling for help. Legal note (normal times): Transmitting on ham (amateur) frequencies requires a license (easy to get — see below). GMRS requires a cheap license (no test). CB, FRS, MURS need no license. Shortwave listening needs no license (you're only receiving). In a genuine life-threatening emergency, FCC rules (47 CFR §97.405) let anyone use any means of radio to call for help. Listening is always legal. Learn and practice before you need it.

1. The quick version — what to grab and what to know | Need | Best tool | License | Range (typical) | | Talk to family nearby (same property / neighborhood) | FRS / GMRS walkie-talkie | FRS none; GMRS cheap | 0.5–2 mi (up to 5+ with GMRS + height) | | Talk across town / coordinate a group | GMRS (with repeater) or Ham VHF/UHF | GMRS cheap; Ham test | 5–50 mi via repeater | | Talk regionally / long distance / into other states | Ham HF | Ham (General class) | 100s–1000s mi | | Hear news & official broadcasts from anywhere | Shortwave receiver | none (listening) | Worldwide | | Road / vehicle convoy, truckers | CB | none | 1–15 mi | Three things everyone should know: 1. Monitor, don't just transmit. A cheap receiver tells you what's happening. 2. Higher antenna = more range. Antenna height matters more than watts. 3. Have a plan: agree on a channel/frequency and check-in times with your group in advance (write them down — see the card at the end). 📚 Go deeper: ARRL ARES Field Resources Manual, p. 6 — what to do first, checklists, message forms; NOAA Weather Radio brochure — how alerts work.

2. In the Illinois Valley 🏔️ The valley is ringed by mountains: VHF/UHF needs a repeater on a peak, and NOAA warns that mountain valleys may get little or no weather radio even inside the usual 40-mile range (NOAA brochure, p. 3). - Weather radio: try Medford 162.400, Mt. Ashland 162.475 and Brookings 162.550 MHz; SAME code 041033. - Ham: JCEC repeater 145.490 (−, tone 136.5), Eight Dollar Mtn; net Mondays 8:00 pm. - No license: Monday check-in on FRS channel 3 and MURS channel 3 after the 7:00 pm IVARC net. - HF: Oregon Emergency Net, nightly 6:00 pm, 3.980 MHz LSB. (Club websites, Nov 2026 — verify. Full lists: Illinois Valley guide.) 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 144 — radio in mountains.

3. How radio actually works (the 60-second version) - A radio turns your voice into radio waves at a certain frequency (measured in kilohertz kHz or megahertz MHz). Another radio tuned to the same frequency turns the wave back into sound. - Both radios must be on the same frequency/channel AND the same mode (e.g. FM, AM, SSB) to hear each other. - Only one person talks at a time. You press PTT (push-to-talk) to transmit, release it to listen. You cannot hear others while you hold PTT. - Frequency bands behave very differently: - VHF/UHF (high frequency numbers, ~30 MHz–3 GHz): travel in roughly straight "line of sight." Great locally, blocked by hills/buildings. Used by FRS, GMRS, MURS, and ham 2m/70cm. Extended by repeaters (see below). - HF / shortwave (low numbers, ~3–30 MHz): can bounce off the ionosphere and travel hundreds or thousands of miles ("skip"). Used by ham HF, CB (27 MHz), and shortwave broadcasters. Range changes with time of day and the sun. - Skip zone: HF can leave a zone of silence — a nearby station unheard while a far one is loud (NEETS 10, p. 106). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45). Handhelds and car whips are vertical — hold the radio upright. 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 10, p. 100 — the ionosphere

vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45). Handhelds and car whips are vertical — hold the radio upright. 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 10, p. 100 — the ionosphere by day and night; NEETS Module 12 — AM, FM and SSB.

4. CB Radio (Citizens Band) — no license, simple, vehicle-friendly - What it is: 40 channels around 27 MHz (in the HF band). No license needed. Cheap, everywhere, popular with truckers and off-roaders. - Range: usually 1–15 miles (more in flat/open terrain; occasionally hundreds of miles when "skip" conditions bounce signals off the ionosphere). - Power limit: 4 watts AM / 12 watts SSB (SSB radios reach farther). - Key channels: - Channel 9 — traditional emergency / help channel. - Channel 19 — highway / trucker channel (road conditions, traffic, convoys). - Channel 1–40 — general use; pick an unused one for your group. - Modes: Most CB is AM. Higher-end radios add SSB (USB/LSB) for more range — but both radios must use the same mode. - Good for: vehicle-to-vehicle, convoys, short local coordination with zero setup. 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 — repairing a broken whip antenna.
5. FRS / GMRS / MURS — the walkie-talkie families These are the little handheld radios ("walkie-talkies"). Great for family/group.

FRS (Family Radio Service) — no license - The blister-pack walkie-talkies. 22 channels in UHF (462/467 MHz). - Low power (0.5–2 W), fixed antenna. Range ~0.5–2 miles. - No license, no setup. Good for keeping a family/group in touch on foot.

GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) — cheap license, no test - Shares channels with FRS but allows higher power (up to 50 W), detachable antennas, and repeaters — so range can reach 5–50+ miles via a repeater. - One GMRS license (~$35, no exam) covers your entire family for 10 years. - Best all-round family emergency radio: cheap, legal, powerful, easy.

MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service) — no license - 5 channels in VHF (151/154 MHz), up to 2 W. No license. - VHF often works better outdoors/rural than FRS/GMRS UHF. Good for property/farm. In hill country: use high ground, get clear of buildings and leafy trees (they soak up more signal than evergreens), and keep away from power lines. 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 102 — choosing a good radio spot.

6. Ham (Amateur) Radio — the serious emergency option Ham radio is the backbone of emergency communications. When everything else fails, hams relay health-and-welfare traffic, weather, and coordination across towns, states, and continents.

Licensing (USA) — easier than you think Three license levels, each a multiple-choice test (questions are public — you can study the exact pool): 1. Technician — entry level. Grants VHF/UHF (local, repeaters) plus some HF. Enough for local/regional emergency comms. ~1 evening of study. 2. General — adds most HF privileges → long-distance / cross-country. 3. Amateur Extra — full privileges. Get at least a Technician license now while it's easy, and ideally General so you can use HF for long distance. In a true emergency you may legally transmit without a license to save life/property — but you'll be far more effective if you've practiced.

The main ham bands and what they do - 2 meters (144–148 MHz, VHF) and 70 cm (420–450 MHz, UHF): local simplex + repeaters. Your everyday "talk around town" bands. - HF bands (e.g. 80m, 40m, 20m): long distance. - 40m (7 MHz): reliable regional (100s of miles), day and night — great for a state/region emergency net. - 20m (14 MHz): long-distance (cross-country / international) in daytime. - 80m (3.5 MHz): regional at night.

Repeaters — how hams get range from a handheld A repeater is a radio on a tower/hilltop that receives your weak signal and re-transmits it with a big antenna and power, massively extending range. To use one you set your radio to the repeater's output frequency, an offset (so it transmits on the input), and sometimes a CTCSS "tone." Local repeater lists (and emergency nets) are worth printing out for your area.

Simplex (radio-to-radio, no repeater) If repeaters are down, you talk simplex — directly, radio to radio, line of sight. The national 2m simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz. Wilderness protocol: back-country hams listen and call on 146.52 for 5 minutes at the top of the hour, every 3 hours from 7 AM to 7 PM, so someone beyond a repeater can be relayed (ARRL manual, p. 84).

HF from a valley: "NVIS" A wire dipole hung low — 1/10 to 1/4 of a wavelength up (roughly 25–60 ft on 80m, worked from the formula in section 8) sends its signal almost straight up; it comes back down like a fountain over a few hundred miles with no skip zone, and the hills matter much less (FM 24-18, p. 279).

Nets A net is a scheduled on-air meeting. In a directed net a net control station says who talks next. Listen first, check in when invited, keep a log, and tell net control if you leave (ARRL manual, p. 7, 18).

Ham digital & data (advanced, FYI) Hams can also send text/email/images with no internet via Winlink (email over radio), FT8 (weak-signal), and APRS (position/text). Useful but needs more gear and practice. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 14 — ARES, traffic nets and RACES; FM 24-18, p. 278 — NVIS in full.

7. Shortwave (SWL) — hearing the outside world - What it is: Using a shortwave receiver to listen to broadcasts on the HF bands (roughly 1.8–30 MHz). No license needed to listen. - Why it matters: When local media and internet are down, shortwave lets you hear international news, government/emergency broadcasts, and ham traffic from far away — because HF signals bounce worldwide. - What to listen for: - International broadcasters (news from outside the affected area). - NOAA Weather Radio (VHF 162.400–162.550 MHz) — continuous US weather & emergency alerts. Every emergency kit should have a NOAA weather radio. - Ham bands (40m/20m) — to hear emergency nets and relays. - AM/FM broadcast and Emergency Alert System (EAS) on a normal radio. - Modes: Broadcasts are usually AM; ham/utility voice is often SSB (USB/LSB). A radio with SSB hears far more. - Tip: A simple long wire antenna dramatically improves shortwave reception. - NOAA Weather Radio: repeats every 4–6 minutes; a SAME radio set to your county code wakes up only for your county's alerts (NOAA brochure, p. 2). - No batteries at all: a crystal radio — wire, a homemade coil, a crystal detector and headphones — hears AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: NBS Circular 120 — build a crystal set step
AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: NBS Circular 120 — build a crystal set step by step; NBS Circular 121 — a sharper version.

8. Antennas, power & range (the practical stuff) - Antenna height beats power. Getting the antenna up high (roof, tree, mast) adds more range than buying a bigger amplifier. - Use the right antenna for the band. A proper resonant antenna (correct length for the frequency) works far better than a random wire. - Line of sight (VHF/UHF): range ≈ limited by the horizon and obstructions. Height = range. Repeaters overcome this. - HF skip: range changes with the time of day and solar conditions. Lower bands (80m) are better at night; higher bands (20m) are better in daytime. - Power: keep radios charged. Stock spare batteries, a 12V battery, a solar panel, and car-charging cables. A radio with a dead battery is a paperweight. - Grounding & safety: never put an antenna where it can touch power lines; ground equipment to reduce static/lightning risk. - EMP and solar storms: in government tests, most ham equipment wasn't damaged when its power cord was unplugged and the antenna coax disconnected (NCS TIB 85-10, p. 166) — more in the EMP Guide.

Build a wire antenna (half-wave dipole) Total length in feet = 468 ÷ MHz (3–50 MHz; FM 24-18, p. 47), cut in two equal halves with the coax at the center. 3.980 MHz (Oregon Emergency Net): 117.6 ft · 7.2 MHz: 65 ft · 14.3 MHz: 32.7 ft. 1. Any wire works in an emergency; copper or aluminum is best. 2. Insulators at the ends and center — plastic or glass (plastic spoons, bottle necks) beat wood or rope. The wire must touch nothing else (FM 24-18, p. 55). 3. Tie one end through a spring or strip of inner tube so swaying trees don't snap it. 4. Adjust length and height for the strongest signal from a distant station. ⚠️ Transmitter off before touching the antenna — it can cause serious injury (p. 56). For 2m/70cm, a J-pole from TV twin-lead is cheap (ARRL manual, p. 12). Rocky mountain ground is a poor ground, so use a dipole, or a vertical with a counterpoise — wires spread just above the ground (FM 24-18, p. 144). Set up high on a slope, not in a ravine, and away from your own generator and battery charger — they add noise (p. 102–103). Batteries: a car battery survives only about 20 deep discharges; deep-cycle batteries take 1,000 or more, and shallow use lasts far longer (about 800 cycles at 80% discharge vs

102–103). Batteries: a car battery survives only about 20 deep discharges; deep-cycle batteries take 1,000 or more, and shallow use lasts far longer (about 800 cycles at 80% discharge vs 6,000 at 20%). Recharge stored sealed batteries about every 3 months. Charging batteries give off hydrogen — no sparks or flames (Practical Action, p. 5–6). Lightning: a lightning switch grounds the antenna whenever you're not using it — No. 14 or heavier copper wire to a water pipe or ground rod, never a gas pipe (NBS Circular 120, p. 8). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 — field repair and expedient antennas; NEETS Module 10 — how antennas work.

9. How to call for help (procedure) 1. Listen first. Make sure you're not interrupting other emergency traffic. 2. Use the emergency call: - Voice distress: say "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" (life-threatening) or "PAN-PAN" (urgent but not immediately life-threatening), then your info. - On CB, call on Channel 9. On ham, break into the local emergency net or call on a repeater / 146.520 simplex. 3. Give the essentials — slowly, clearly, repeat: - Who you are (name / call sign). - Where you are (address, cross-streets, GPS coords, landmarks). - What the emergency is (injury, fire, trapped, etc.). - What you need (medical, rescue, relay a message). 4. Spell hard words with the phonetic alphabet (below). 5. Stay on, don't wander off frequency. Keep the radio on so responders can call back. Repeat your message at intervals if no answer.

NATO phonetic alphabet Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliet Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: say digits individually ("one-two-zero").

Common "pro-words" - "Over" = I'm done talking, your turn. - "Out" = conversation finished (don't say "over and out"). - "Roger" / "Copy" = I received and understand. - "Say again" = repeat (don't say "repeat"). - "Affirmative / Negative" = yes / no. - "Break" = pause / someone with emergency traffic wants in. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 58 — procedure words, phonetic alphabet, signal reports.

10. Passing messages for others Much of radio's work after a disaster is carrying short messages for people with no radio. Send in this order (ARRL manual, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life and death — when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY (important, time-limited) → WELFARE ("Is my family OK?" / "All well here") → ROUTINE (last). - Write the message down first and count the words, so the receiver can check it. - Ready-made welfare texts include "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." - Log the time, station, frequency and message. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 33–34 — welfare form, standard texts, how to write a radiogram.

11. When the radio can't reach: signals without one - Three of anything means distress: three fires in a triangle, three columns of smoke, three shots (FM 21-76, p. 238–243). In wildfire country keep signal fires small, cleared around and watched (rule of thumb). - A whistle carries up to about a mile; a mirror is the best signal on a sunny day. SOS: three short, three long, three short. - Ground-to-air symbols in a clearing: V = need help · X = need medical help · N = no · Y = yes · arrow = going this way. Make them at least 6 m (20 ft) long (the two Army manuals differ on width) (FM 3-05.70, p. 329). 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-05.70, p. 318 — signaling devices and how to use them.

12. If this goes wrong | Problem | Try this | | Nobody answers | Get higher and clear of buildings and leafy trees; hold the radio upright; try a repeater | | Repeater ignores you | Check the offset and tone | | Two radios won't talk | Same channel and same mode? Same privacy code on FRS? | | HF is dead | Lower band at night, higher in daytime (rule of thumb) | | Buzz or hum | Move away from power lines, generators, chargers (FM 24-18, p. 103) | | Broken antenna | Splice it, or replace with wire of the same length | | Battery dies fast | Lower power, transmit less, listen at set times | 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 106 — sources of interference.

13. A sensible emergency radio kit (shopping / checklist) - [ ] NOAA weather radio (hand-crank/solar + battery) — alerts & forecasts. - [ ] Shortwave receiver with SSB — hear news & ham traffic worldwide (RX only). - [ ] A pair+ of GMRS radios (and a GMRS license) — family/group, best bang for buck. FRS works with no license at shorter range. - [ ] A dual-band (2m/70cm) ham handheld (HT) — cheap; huge capability with a Technician license. Add a better antenna. - [ ] (Advanced) An HF ham radio + General license — true long distance. - [ ] CB if you travel by vehicle/convoy. - [ ] Power: spare batteries, 12V battery, solar panel, car charger. - [ ] Better antennas + coax; a roll of wire for an HF/long-wire antenna. - [ ] Printed frequency card (below), local repeater list, notebook & pencil. - [ ] Go-bag extras: earphone, mag-mount antenna, 50 ft of coax with barrel connectors, alkaline pack for the handheld. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 10–12 — basic and 72-hour go-kit checklists.

Whenever faced with a survival situation, remember the word SURVIVAL. SURVIVAL ACTIONS The following paragraphs expand on the meaning of each letter of the word survival. Study and remember what each letter signifies because you may some day have to make it work for you. Use your senses of hearing, smell, and sight to get a feel for the battlefield. What is the enemy doing? Advancing? Holding in place? Retreating? You will have to consider what is developing on the battlefield when you make your survival plan. Size Up Your Surroundings Determine the pattern of the area. Get a feel for what is going on around you. Every environment, whether forest, jungle, or desert, has a rhythm or pattern. If you act in haste, you may forget or lose some of your equipment. In your haste you may also become disoriented so that you don't know which way to go. Plan your moves. Be ready to move out quickly without endangering yourself if the enemy is near you. Use all your senses to evaluate the situation. Note sounds and smells. Be sensitive to temperature changes. This inexperience in improvisation can be an enemy in a survival situation. Learn to improvise. Take a tool designed for a specific purpose and see how many other uses you can make of it. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL All of us were born kicking and fighting to live, but we have become used to the soft life. We have become creatures of comfort. We dislike inconveniences and discomforts. What happens when we are faced with a survival situation with its stresses, inconveniences, and discomforts? This is when the will to live- placing a high value on living-is vital. The experience and knowledge you have gained through life and your Army training will have a bearing on your will to live. Stubbornness, a refusal to give in to problems and obstacles that face you, will give you the mental and physical strength to endure. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL PATTERN FOR SURVIVAL Develop a survival pattern that lets you beat the enemies of survival. This survival pattern must include food, water, shelter, fire, first aid, and signals placed in order of importance. For example, in a cold environment, you would need a fire to get warm; a shelter to protect you from the cold, wind, and rain or snow; traps or snares to get food; a means to signal friendly aircraft; and first aid to maintain health. If injured, first aid has top priority no matter what climate you are in. Change your survival pattern to meet your immediate physical needs as the environment changes. As you read the rest of this manual, keep in mind the keyword SURVIVAL and the need for a survival pattern. Page 8 of 277 Free Electricity and Water Solutions

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 2 - PSYCHOLOGY OF SURVIVAL It takes much more than the knowledge and skills to build shelters, get food, make fires, and travel without the aid of standard navigational devices to live successfully through a survival situation. Some people with little or no survival training have managed to survive life-threatening circumstances. Some people with survival training have not used their skills and died. A key ingredient in any survival situation is the mental attitude of the individual(s) involved. Having survival skills is important; having the will to survive is essential. Without a desk to survive, acquired skills serve little purpose and invaluable knowledge goes to waste. There is a psychology to survival. The soldier in a survival environment faces many stresses that ultimately impact on his mind. These stresses can produce thoughts and emotions that, if poorly understood, can transform a confident, well-trained soldier into an indecisive, ineffective individual with questionable ability to survive. Thus, every soldier must be aware of and be able to recognize those stresses commonly associated with survival. Additionally, it is imperative that soldiers be aware of their reactions to the wide variety of stresses associated with survival. This

Additionally, it is imperative that soldiers be aware of their reactions to the wide variety of stresses associated with survival. This chapter will identify and explain the nature of stress, the stresses of survival, and those internal reactions soldiers will naturally experience when faced with the stresses of a real-world survival situation. The knowledge you, the soldier, gain from this chapter and other chapters in this manual, will prepare you to come through the toughest times alive. A LOOK AT STRESS Before we can understand our psychological reactions in a survival setting, it is helpful to first know a little bit about stress. Stress is not a disease that you cure and eliminate. Instead, it is a condition we all experience. Stress can be described as our reaction to pressure. It is the name given to the experience we have as we physically, mentally, emotionally, and spiritually respond to life's tensions. Because we usually do not consider unimportant events stressful, stress can also be an excellent indicator of the significance we attach to an event--in other words, it highlights what is important to us. We need to have some stress in our lives, but too much of anything can be bad. The goal is to have stress, but not an excess of it. Too much stress can take its toll on people and organizations. Too much stress leads to distress. Distress causes an uncomfortable tension that we try to escape and, preferably, avoid. Listed below are a few of the common signs of distress you may find in your fellow soldiers or yourself when faced with too much stress: • Difficulty making decisions. • Angry outbursts. • Forgetfulness. • Low energy level. • Constant worrying. • Propensity for mistakes. • Thoughts about death or suicide. • Trouble getting along with others. • Withdrawing from others. • Hiding from responsibilities. • Carelessness. A cut artery issues bright red blood from the wound in distinct spurts or pulses that correspond to the rhythm of the heartbeat. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 5 - SHELTERS A shelter can protect you from the sun, insects, wind, rain, snow, hot or cold temperatures, and enemy observation. It can give you a feeling of well-being. It can help you maintain your will to survive. In some areas, your need for shelter may take precedence over your need for food and possibly even your need for water. For example, prolonged exposure to cold can cause excessive fatigue and weakness (exhaustion). An exhausted person may develop a "passive" outlook, thereby losing the will to survive. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 9 - SURVIVAL USE OF PLANTS After having solved the problems of finding water, shelter, and animal food, you will have to consider the use of plants you can eat. In a survival situation you should always be on the lookout for familiar wild foods and live off the land whenever possible. You must not count on being able to go for days without food as some sources would suggest. Even in the most static survival situation, maintaining health through a complete and nutritious diet is essential to maintaining strength and peace of mind. Nature can provide you with food that will let you survive any ordeal, if you don't eat the wrong plant. You must therefore learn as much as possible beforehand about the flora of the region where you will be operating. Plants can provide you with medicines in a survival situation. Plants can supply you with weapons and raw materials to construct shelters and build fires. Plants can even provide you with chemicals for poisoning fish, preserving animal hides, and for camouflaging yourself and your equipment. The basic types of root structures (Figure 9-4) are the bulb, clove, taproot, tuber, rhizome, corm, and crown. Bulbs are familiar to us as onions and, when sliced in half, will show concentric rings. Cloves are those bulblike structures that remind us of garlic and will separate into small pieces when broken apart. This characteristic separates wild onions from wild garlic. A crown is the type of root structure found on plants such as asparagus and looks much like a mophead under the soil's surface. They are mostly nocturnal in habit. You can find desert scorpions from below sea level in Death Valley to elevations as high as 3,600 meters in the Andes. Typically brown or black in moist areas, they may be yellow or light green in the desert. Their average size is about 2.5 centimeters. Nature mimics the scorpions with whip scorpions or vinegar-roons. These are harmless and have a tail like a wire or whip, rather than the jointed tail and stinger of true scorpions. There are many bat varieties worldwide, but you find the true vampire bats only in Central and South America. They are small, agile fliers that land on their sleeping victims, mostly cows and horses, to lap a blood meal after biting their victim. There are, however, a few smaller river creatures with which you should be cautious. Electric Eel Electric eels (Electrophorus electricus) may reach 2 meters in length and 20 centimeters in diameter. Avoid them. They are capable of generating up to 500 volts of electricity in certain organs in their body. They use this shock to stun prey and enemies. Normally, you find these eels in the Orinoco and Amazon River systems in South America. They seem to prefer shallow waters that are more highly oxygenated and provide more food. They are bulkier than our native eels. Their upper body is dark gray or black, with a lighter-colored underbelly. Piranha Piranhas (Serrasalmo species) are another hazard of the Orinoco and Amazon River systems, as well as the Paraguay River Basin, where they are native. DANGERS IN BAYS AND ESTUARIES In areas where seas and rivers come together, there are dangers associated with both fresh and salt water. In shallow salt waters, there are many creatures that can inflict pain and cause infection to develop. Stepping on sea urchins, for example, can produce pain and infection. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 12 - FIELD-EXPEDIENT WEAPONS, TOOLS, AND EQUIPMENT As a soldier you know the importance of proper care and use of your weapons, tools, and equipment. This is especially true of your knife. You must always keep it sharp and ready to use. A knife is your most valuable tool in a survival situation. Imagine being in a survival situation without any weapons, tools, or equipment except your knife. It could happen! You might even be without a knife. You would probably feel helpless, but with the proper knowledge and skills, you can easily improvise needed items. In survival situations, you may have to fashion any number and type of fieldexpedient tools and equipment to survive. Examples of tools and equipment that could make your life much easier are ropes, rucksacks, clothes, nets, and so on. Weapons serve a dual purpose. You use them to obtain and prepare food and to provide self-defense. A weapon can also give you a feeling of security and provide you with the ability to hunt on the move. As a field-expedient weapon, the club does not protect you from enemy soldiers. It can, however, extend your area of defense beyond your fingertips. It also serves to increase the force of a blow without injuring yourself. There are three basic types of clubs. They are the simple, weighted, and sling club. Simple Club A simple club is a staff or branch. It must be short enough for you to swing easily, but long enough and strong enough for you to damage whatever you hit. Its diameter should fit comfortably in your palm, but it should not be so thin as to allow the club to break easily upon impact. A straight-grained hardwood is best if you can find it. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL A weighted club is any simple club with a weight on one end. The weight may be a natural weight, such as a knot on the wood, or something added, such as a stone lashed to the club. To make a weighted club, first find a stone that has a shape that will allow you to lash it securely to the club. A stone with a slight hourglass shape works well. If you cannot find a suitably shaped stone, you must fashion a groove or channel into the stone by a technique known as pecking. By repeatedly rapping the club stone with a smaller hard stone, you can get the desired shape. Next, find a piece of wood that is the right length for you. A straight-grained hardwood is best. The length of the wood should feel comfortable in relation to the weight of the stone. Finally, lash the stone to the handle. There are three techniques for lashing the stone to the handle: split handle, forked branch, and wrapped handle. The technique you use will depend on the type of handle you choose. See Figure 12-1. Horseshoe Pack This pack is simple to make and use and relatively comfortable to carry over one shoulder. Lay available square-shaped material, such as poncho, blanket, or canvas, flat on the ground. Lay items on one edge of the material. Pad the hard items. Roll the material (with the items) toward the opposite edge and tie both ends securely. Add extra ties along the length of the bundle. Remember, cold weather is an adversary that can be as dangerous as an enemy soldier. Every time you venture into the cold, you are pitting yourself against the elements. REGIONS AND LOCATIONS Cold regions include arctic and subarctic areas and areas immediately adjoining them. You can classify about 48 percent of the northern hemisphere's total landmass as a cold region due to the influence and extent of air temperatures. Ocean currents affect cold weather and cause large areas normally included in the temperate zone to fall within the cold regions during winter periods. Elevation also has a marked effect on defining cold regions. Within the cold weather regions, you may face two types of cold weather environments-wet or dry. Knowing in which environment your area of operations falls will affect planning and execution of a cold weather operation. Wet Cold Weather Environments Wet cold weather conditions exist when the average temperature in a 24-hour period is -10 degrees C or above. Characteristics of this condition are freezing during the colder night hours and thawing during the day. Even though the temperatures are warmer during this condition, the terrain is usually very sloppy due to slush and mud. You must concentrate on protecting yourself from the wet ground and from freezing rain or wet snow. Dry Cold Weather Environments Page 174 of 277 Free Electricity and Water Solutions

Biological Agents and Effects Biological agents are microorganisms that can cause disease among personnel, animals, or plants. They can also cause the deterioration of material. These agents fall into two broad categories-pathogens (usually called germs) and toxins. Pathogens are living microorganisms that cause lethal or incapacitating diseases. Bacteria, rickettsiae, fungi, and viruses are included in the pathogens. Toxins are poisons that plants, animals, or microorganisms produce naturally. Toxins are poisons that plants, animals, or microorganisms produce naturally. Possible biological war-fare toxins include a variety of neurotoxic (affecting the central nervous system) and cytotoxic (causing cell death) compounds. Germs Germs are living organisms. Some nations have used them in the past as weapons. Only a few germs can start an infection, especially if inhaled into the lungs. Because germs are so Page 271 of 277 Free Electricity and Water Solutions

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL small and weigh so little, the wind can spread them over great distances; they can also enter unfiltered or nonairtight places. Buildings and bunkers can trap them thus causing a higher concentration. Germs do not affect the body immediately. They must multiply inside the body and overcome the body's defenses--a process called the incubation period. Incubation periods vary from several hours to several months, depending on the germ. Most germs must live within another living organism (host), such as your body, to survive and grow. Weather conditions such as wind, rain, cold, and sunlight rapidly kill germs. Some germs can form protective shells, or spores, to allow survival outside the host. Sporeproducing agents are a long-term hazard you must neutralize by decontaminating infected areas or personnel. Fortunately, most live agents are not spore-producing. These agents must find a host within roughly a day of their delivery or they die. Germs have three basic routes of entry into your body: through the respiratory tract, through a break in the skin, and through the digestive tract. Toxins Toxins are substances that plants, animals, or germs produce naturally. These toxins are what actually harm man, not bacteria. Botulin, which produces botulism, is an example. Modern science has allowed large-scale production of these toxins without the use of the germ that produces the toxin. Toxins may produce effects similar to those of chemical agents. Toxic victims may not, however, respond to first aid measures used against chemical agents. Toxins enter the body in the same manner as germs. However, some toxins, unlike germs, can penetrate unbroken skin. Symptoms appear almost immediately, since there is no incubation period. Many toxins are extremely lethal, even in very small doses. Symptoms may include any of the following: • Dizziness. • Mental confusion. • Blurred or double vision. • Numbness or tingling of skin. • Paralysis. • Convulsions. • Rashes or blisters. • Coughing. • Fever.
